This one, the diameter of which is nineteen feet, and the thread twenty-three feet, performs about a hundred and twenty revolutions in a second.”
“And you get then?”
“A speed of fifty miles an hour.”

“I have seen the _Nautilus_ manœuvre before the _Abraham Lincoln_, and I have my own ideas as to its speed. But this is not enough. We must see where we go. We must be able to direct it to the right, to the left, above, below. How do you get to the great depths, where you find an increasing resistance, which is rated by hundreds of atmospheres? How do you return to the surface of the ocean? And how do you maintain yourselves in the requisite medium? Am I asking too much?”

“Not at all, Professor,” replied the Captain, with some hesitation; “since you may never leave this submarine boat. Come into the saloon, it is our usual study, and there you will learn all you want to know about the _Nautilus_.”
translated_paragraphs: “先生，”尼摩船长指着自己室内墙上挂的各种仪器说道，“这些便是‘鹦鹉螺号’航行所需的装置。在这里，同在客厅里一样，它们随时都在我眼前，告诉我身处大洋何处，又准确地朝哪个方向前进。其中有些您认识，譬如温度计，显示‘鹦鹉螺号’内部的温度；气压计，指示空气的重量，预告天气的变化；湿度计，标出空气的干湿；风暴瓶，瓶内物质的分解用来预报风暴的来临；指引航向的罗盘；六分仪，靠测量太阳的高度来求纬度；航海精密时计，我据此推算经度；还有日夜两用的各式望远镜，‘鹦鹉螺号’上浮到浪面时，我用它们察看地平线四方。”
“这是常见的航海仪器，”我答道，“我知道它们的用途。可另外这些，必定是为了‘鹦鹉螺号’独有的需要吧。这个带活动指针的圆盘是压力计，对吗？”
“的确是压力计。它同海水连通，指示外部水压，因此也同时显示我们的深度。”
“那么另外这些用途猜不出的仪器呢？”
“说到这里，教授，我应该给您做一点解释。您愿意听我说吗？”
他静默了片刻，说道：
“有一种强大的力量，听从指挥，来得迅速，使用方便，能够胜任一切工作，在我船上居于无上地位。一切都凭它而成。它照明，供暖，是我全套机械的灵魂。这力量就是电。”
“电？”我惊讶地叫道。
“正是，先生。”
“可是船长，您能够达到极高的航速，这同电所能提供的动力并不相称。直到如今，它的驱动能力都受着限制，只能产生少量机械动力。”
“教授，”尼摩船长说，“我的电不是人人所用的那种电。您知道海水由什么构成。每一千克海水中，水占百分之九十六点五，氯化钠约占百分之二又三分之二。再往下，含量较少的还有氯化镁、氯化钾、溴化镁、硫酸镁、硫酸钙和碳酸钙。可见其中氯化钠占了相当大的比重。我就是从海水里提取这种钠，用来配制我所需的材料。我所有的一切都得之于海洋。海洋产生电，电给‘鹦鹉螺号’以热、光和运动，一句话，给它以生命。”
“可它供不了您呼吸的空气吧？”

“噢！所需的空气我也能制造，只是用不着，因为我要什么时候上浮换气都可以。不过即使我呼吸的空气并非由电制造，电至少也驱动了强力气泵，好把空气储存进宽大的储气舱。必要时，我愿意在海底多留多久，就能把逗留的时间延长多久。电还能给我均匀、不间断的光，太阳却不能。请您再看这座钟。它也是用电的，走得精准，最好的航海时计都难与之匹敌。我仿照意大利式的钟，把钟面分为二十四小时，因为对我没有昼夜，没有日月，只有我随身带进海底的人造光。看！现在正是上午十点。”
“正是。”
“这又是电的另一项用处。挂在正前方的这个圆盘，指示‘鹦鹉螺号’的航速。一根电线把它同螺旋桨连起来，指针标示实际速度。您看！我们此刻正以每小时十五英里的匀速飞驰。”
“真是奇妙！船长，我看您使用这种能代替风力、水力和蒸汽的动力，的确有理。”
“还没看完呢，阿龙纳斯先生，”尼摩船长站起身来，“请跟着我，咱们去察看‘鹦鹉螺号’的后部。”
这艘潜水船的前部，我已当真见过了。从船首起逐一数来，确切的分隔情形是这样：餐厅长五码，由一道水密隔舱壁同图书室隔开；图书室长五码；大客厅长十码，再由第二道水密隔壁同船长的房间隔开；船长的房间长五码，我的房间长两码半；最后还有长七码半的一间储气室，一直延伸到船头。总长三十五码，即一百零五英尺。隔壁上都有门，用橡胶密封装置可以闭得滴水不漏。万一有舱进水，它们足可保障“鹦鹉螺号”的安全。
我跟着尼摩船长穿过船腰通道，到了全船的中央。两道隔舱壁之间，有一处像井道的空间。一架铁梯以铁钩固定在隔壁上，一直通向顶端。我问船长梯子作什么用。
“通到那条小艇。”他说。
“什么！您还有条小艇？”我惊讶地叫道。
“自然有。是条很好的船，轻巧，又不会沉，可以用来捕鱼，也可以用来游玩。”
“不过您要登艇，势必得先浮到水面上来吧？”
“完全用不着。这小艇附在‘鹦鹉螺号’的船壳顶部，正好嵌在特意为它凿出的一处凹槽里。小艇有甲板，全船水密，靠结实的螺栓固定。这架梯子通向‘鹦鹉螺号’船壳上的人孔，正同小艇一侧的另一个人孔相合。我穿过这两道洞口便进了小艇。他们关好‘鹦鹉螺号’的人孔，我用螺杆压紧另一扇门。我一松螺栓，小艇就以惊人的速度升上海面。这时我才打开一直关严的甲板舱盖，竖起桅杆，升起帆，拿起桨，就出发了。”
“可您怎么回到船上？”
“不是我回去，阿龙纳斯先生。是‘鹦鹉螺号’来接我。”
“遵您的号令？”
“遵我的号令。一根电线连着我们。我发个电报，便够了。”
“当真，”我为这些奇事惊叹不已，“再简单不过了。”
经过那座通向平台的梯井，我看见一个长六英尺的小舱，康塞尔和尼德·兰德正在里面津津有味地大嚼，对那餐饭称心极了。接着有扇门通到长九英尺的厨房，厨房位于几间大储藏室之间。那里用电做一切烹调，比煤气还好。灶下的电流使海绵铂发热，热量持久而分配得很均匀。电流还加热一套蒸馏装置，靠蒸发制出上好的饮水。厨房旁边有间布置舒适的浴室，冷热水龙头一应俱全。
紧邻厨房的是一段长十六英尺的船员寝舱。门关着，我看不见内部的布置，原本也许可以借此估计“鹦鹉螺号”上到底有多少人当差。
尽头处是第四道隔舱壁，将这里与机舱分开。门开了，我便身处尼摩船长安置推进机械的舱室。这位船长一定是个造诣很高的工程师。机舱里灯光明亮，长度不下六十五英尺，分作两部。前一部是发电设备，后一部是把电力传给螺旋桨的机械。我极感兴趣地细看，想弄明白“鹦鹉螺号”的工作原理。
“您看，”船长说，“我用的是本生的装置，不是鲁姆科夫的。后者的力量本来就不够。本生的装置用的数目少，却强而大，实验证明这样最好。电流产生后传向前方，借几座巨大的电磁铁，带动一套杠杆和齿轮，将运动传至螺旋桨轴。这具螺旋桨直径十九英尺，螺距二十三英尺，每秒约转一百二十圈。”
“那样您能达到——？”
“每小时五十英里的速度。”
“我见过‘鹦鹉螺号’在‘亚伯拉罕·林肯号’跟前怎样周旋，它的速度我心里大致有数。不过光有这个还不够。我们得能看见去处，还要能向右、向左、向上、向下操纵。当水压逐渐增大，以数百个大气压来计算的时候，您怎样到达那样深的地方？怎么再回到洋面？又怎么在选中的水层保持位置？我是不是问得太多了？”
“一点也不多，教授，”船长稍稍迟疑，答道，“您也许永远离不开这艘潜水船了。请到客厅去，那是我们平常的书房。到了那里，您想知道有关‘鹦鹉螺号’的一切，都可以弄个明白。”

sections.title_zh: 上部 / 第12章　几笔数字
sections.title_en: PART ONE / CHAPTER XII — SOME FIGURES
source_paragraphs: A moment after we were seated on a divan in the saloon smoking. The Captain showed me a sketch that gave the plan, section, and elevation of the _Nautilus_. Then he began his description in these words:—

“Here, M. Aronnax, are the several dimensions of the boat you are in. It is an elongated cylinder with conical ends. It is very like a cigar in shape, a shape already adopted in London in several constructions of the same sort. The length of this cylinder, from stem to stern, is exactly 232 feet, and its maximum breadth is twenty-six feet. It is not built quite like your long-voyage steamers, but its lines are sufficiently long, and its curves prolonged enough, to allow the water to slide off easily, and oppose no obstacle to its passage. These two dimensions enable you to obtain by a simple calculation the surface and cubic contents of the _Nautilus_. Its area measures 6032 feet; and its contents about 1500 cubic yards—that is to say, when completely immersed it displaces 50,000 feet of water, or weighs 1500 tons.

“When I made the plans for this submarine vessel, I meant that nine-tenths should be submerged: consequently, it ought only to displace nine-tenths of its bulk—that is to say, only to weigh that number of tons. I ought not, therefore, to have exceeded that weight, constructing it on the aforesaid dimensions.

“The _Nautilus_ is composed of two hulls, one inside, the other outside, joined by T-shaped irons, which render it very strong. Indeed, owing to this cellular arrangement it resists like a block, as if it were solid. Its sides cannot yield; it coheres spontaneously, and not by the closeness of its rivets; and the homogenity of its construction, due to the perfect union of the materials, enables it to defy the roughest seas.

“These two hulls are composed of steel plates, whose density is from .7 to .8 that of water. The first is not less than two inches and a half thick and weighs 394 tons. The second envelope, the keel, twenty inches high and ten thick, weighs alone sixty-two tons. The engine, the ballast, the several accessories and apparatus appendages, the partitions and bulkheads, weigh 961.62 tons. Do you follow all this?”
“I do.”

“Then, when the _Nautilus_ is afloat under these circumstances, one-tenth is out of the water. Now, if I have made reservoirs of a size equal to this tenth, or capable of holding 150 tons, and if I fill them with water, the boat, weighing then 1507 tons, will be completely immersed. That would happen, Professor. These reservoirs are in the lower parts of the _Nautilus_. I turn on taps and they fill, and the vessel sinks that had just been level with the surface.”

“Well, Captain, but now we come to the real difficulty. I can understand your rising to the surface; but diving below the surface, does not your submarine contrivance encounter a pressure, and consequently undergo an upward thrust of one atmosphere for every thirty feet of water, just about fifteen pounds per square inch?”
“Just so, sir.”
“Then, unless you quite fill the _Nautilus_, I do not see how you can draw it down to those depths.”

“Professor, you must not confound statics with dynamics or you will be exposed to grave errors. There is very little labour spent in attaining the lower regions of the ocean, for all bodies have a tendency to sink. When I wanted to find out the necessary increase of weight required to sink the _Nautilus_, I had only to calculate the reduction of volume that sea-water acquires according to the depth.”
“That is evident.”

“Now, if water is not absolutely incompressible, it is at least capable of very slight compression. Indeed, after the most recent calculations this reduction is only .000436 of an atmosphere for each thirty feet of depth. If we want to sink 3000 feet, I should keep account of the reduction of bulk under a pressure equal to that of a column of water of a thousand feet. The calculation is easily verified. Now, I have supplementary reservoirs capable of holding a hundred tons. Therefore I can sink to a considerable depth. When I wish to rise to the level of the sea, I only let off the water, and empty all the reservoirs if I want the _Nautilus_ to emerge from the tenth part of her total capacity.”
I had nothing to object to these reasonings.
“I admit your calculations, Captain,” I replied; “I should be wrong to dispute them since daily experience confirms them; but I foresee a real difficulty in the way.”
“What, sir?”

“When you are about 1000 feet deep, the walls of the _Nautilus_ bear a pressure of 100 atmospheres. If, then, just now you were to empty the supplementary reservoirs, to lighten the vessel, and to go up to the surface, the pumps must overcome the pressure of 100 atmospheres, which is 1500 pounds per square inch. From that a power——”

“That electricity alone can give,” said the Captain, hastily. “I repeat, sir, that the dynamic power of my engines is almost infinite. The pumps of the _Nautilus_ have an enormous power, as you must have observed when their jets of water burst like a torrent upon the _Abraham Lincoln_. Besides I use subsidiary reservoirs only to attain a mean depth of 750 to 1000 fathoms, and that with a view of managing my machines. Also, when I have a mind to visit the depths of the ocean five or six miles below the surface, I make use of slower but not less infallible means.”
“What are they, Captain?”
“That involves my telling you how the _Nautilus_ is worked.”
“I am impatient to learn.”

“To steer this boat to starboard or port, to turn—in a word, following a horizontal plan, I use an ordinary rudder fixed on the back of the stern-post, and with one wheel and some tackle to steer by. But I can also make the _Nautilus_ rise and sink, and sink and rise, by a vertical movement by means of two inclined planes fastened to its sides, opposite the centre of flotation, planes that move in every direction, and that are worked by powerful levers from the interior. If the planes are kept parallel with the boat, it moves horizontally. If slanted, the _Nautilus_, according to this inclination, and under the influence of the screw, either sinks diagonally or rises diagonally as it suits me. And even if I wish to rise more quickly to the surface, I ship the screw, and the pressure of the water causes the _Nautilus_ to rise vertically like a balloon filled with hydrogen.”
“Bravo, Captain! But how can the steersman follow the route in the middle of the waters?”
“The steersman is placed in a glazed box, that is raised about the hull of the _Nautilus_, and furnished with lenses.”
“Are these lenses capable of resisting such pressure?”

“Perfectly. Glass, which breaks at a blow, is, nevertheless, capable of offering considerable resistance. During some experiments of fishing by electric light in 1864 in the Northern Seas, we saw plates less than a third of an inch thick resist a pressure of sixteen atmospheres. Now, the glass that I use is not less than thirty times thicker.”
“Granted. But, after all, in order to see, the light must exceed the darkness, and in the midst of the darkness in the water, how can you see?”
“Behind the steersman’s cage is placed a powerful electric reflector, the rays from which light up the sea for half a mile in front.”

“Ah! bravo, bravo, Captain! Now I can account for this phosphorescence in the supposed narwhal that puzzled us so. I now ask you if the boarding of the _Nautilus_ and of the _Scotia_, that has made such a noise, has been the result of a chance rencontre?”
“Quite accidental, sir. I was sailing only one fathom below the surface of the water, when the shock came. It had no bad result.”
“None, sir. But now, about your rencontre with the _Abraham Lincoln?_”

“Professor, I am sorry for one of the best vessels in the American navy; but they attacked me, and I was bound to defend myself. I contented myself, however, with putting the frigate _hors de combat;_ she will not have any difficulty in getting repaired at the next port.”
“Ah, Commander! your _Nautilus_ is certainly a marvellous boat.”

“Yes, Professor; and I love it as if it were part of myself. If danger threatens one of your vessels on the ocean, the first impression is the feeling of an abyss above and below. On the _Nautilus_ men’s hearts never fail them. No defects to be afraid of, for the double shell is as firm as iron; no rigging to attend to; no sails for the wind to carry away; no boilers to burst; no fire to fear, for the vessel is made of iron, not of wood; no coal to run short, for electricity is the only mechanical agent; no collision to fear, for it alone swims in deep water; no tempest to brave, for when it dives below the water, it reaches absolute tranquillity. There, sir! that is the perfection of vessels! And if it is true that the engineer has more confidence in the vessel than the builder, and the builder than the captain himself, you understand the trust I repose in my _Nautilus;_ for I am at once captain, builder, and engineer.”
“But how could you construct this wonderful _Nautilus_ in secret?”

“Each separate portion, M. Aronnax, was brought from different parts of the globe. The keel was forged at Creusot, the shaft of the screw at Penn & Co.’s, London, the iron plates of the hull at Laird’s of Liverpool, the screw itself at Scott’s at Glasgow. The reservoirs were made by Cail & Co. at Paris, the engine by Krupp in Prussia, its beak in Motala’s workshop in Sweden, its mathematical instruments by Hart Brothers, of New York, etc.; and each of these people had my orders under different names.”
“But these parts had to be put together and arranged?”

“Professor, I had set up my workshops upon a desert island in the ocean. There my workmen, that is to say, the brave men that I instructed and educated, and myself have put together our _Nautilus_. Then when the work was finished, fire destroyed all trace of our proceedings on this island, that I could have jumped over if I had liked.”
“Then the cost of this vessel is great?”

“M. Aronnax, an iron vessel costs £45 per ton. Now the _Nautilus_ weighed 1500. It came therefore to £67,500, and £80,000 more for fitting it up, and about £200,000 with the works of art and the collections it contains.”
“One last question, Captain Nemo.”
“Ask it, Professor.”
“You are rich?”
“Immensely rich, sir; and I could, without missing it, pay the national debt of France.”
I stared at the singular person who spoke thus. Was he playing upon my credulity? The future would decide that.
translated_paragraphs: 片刻之后，我和船长已在客厅的长榻上坐下，吸着烟。他给我看一张图，上面画着“鹦鹉螺号”的平面、剖面和立面。随后便这样为我说明：

“阿龙纳斯先生，这里是您所搭乘的这艘船的各项尺寸。它是一个拉长的圆柱，两端呈圆锥形。外形很像雪茄，伦敦建造的几艘同类船只已经采用过这种形式。圆柱体从船首到船尾恰好长二百三十二英尺，最宽处二十六英尺。它的构造同你们的远洋轮船不完全一样，但线条拉得足够长，曲线延伸得足够舒展，因此水可以顺畅地从船身滑过，不阻碍前进。有了这两个尺寸，简单一算，就能得出‘鹦鹉螺号’的面积和容积。它的面积是六千零三十二平方英尺，容积约一千五百立方码。换句话说，全部浸没时，排开五万立方英尺的水，重量合一千五百吨。
“设计这艘潜水船的时候，我希望在正常航行时有十分之九没在水下。因此，它只应排开相当于自身体积十分之九的水，换算为重量，也只应有相应的吨数。既按前述尺度建造，我便不能超过那个重量。
“‘鹦鹉螺号’内外两重船壳，以丁字形铁材连接，十分结实。正由于这种分格的构造，它抵抗外力时坚如一整块金属，仿佛是实心的。侧壁没处可塌。它靠结构本身结合成一个整体，不靠铆钉排得紧。材料接合得完美，使整个船体浑然一体，最凶的风浪也能抵御。
“这两层船壳都用钢板制成，密度为水的零点七至零点八倍。第一层厚不下两英寸半，重三百九十四吨。第二层外壳的龙骨高二十英寸，厚十英寸，单是它就重六十二吨。发动机、压舱物、各种附件和附属装置、隔板和隔舱壁，共重九百六十一点六二吨。到这里都跟得上吗？”
“跟得上。”
“这样，‘鹦鹉螺号’在上述状况下浮航时，有十分之一露在水面上。假如我造的水舱恰好相当于这十分之一，能容纳一百五十吨水，再往舱里灌满水，届时全船重一千五百零七吨，便完全没入水中了。教授，事情就是这样。这些水舱位于‘鹦鹉螺号’底部。我一开阀，舱里进水，方才还与海面相平的船就沉下去了。”
“好，船长，但我们这才遇到真正的困难。您要浮到水面，我能理解。可往海面以下潜时，您的潜水船岂不受着压力？每深入三十英尺水深，便承受一个大气压的向上推力，大约是每平方英寸十五磅吧？”
“确是如此，先生。”
“那么，除非把整个‘鹦鹉螺号’都灌满，我就不明白您如何能使它潜到那么深。”
“教授，您可别把静力学同动力学混在一起，否则会闹出大错。要到大洋深处去，耗力很少，因为物体都有下沉的倾向。我想知道使‘鹦鹉螺号’下沉需要增加多少重量，只用计算海水的体积随深度而发生的缩减。”
“这很明白。”
“水虽不是绝对不可压缩，能压缩的程度却极小。根据最近的计算，每加深三十英尺，相应一层大气压，缩减的比例仅有零点零零零四三六。如果我们想下沉三千英尺，我得把相当于一千英尺水柱压力下的体积缩减算进去。这很容易核算。我另备有能装一百吨水的辅助水舱，所以我能潜到相当可观的深度。想重新升到海面，我只排掉舱水。要使‘鹦鹉螺号’有总体积的十分之一露出水面，把所有水舱排空便是。”
对这番推理，我提不出什么异议。
“船长，我承认您的计算，”我答道，“既然每日的实践都证明它们有效，我要争论便是我的过错。可我觉得，前面还有一道切实的困难。”
“什么困难，先生？”
“您到了约一千英尺深处，‘鹦鹉螺号’的船壁承受一百个大气压。如果这时要抽空辅助水舱，减轻船重，好升上洋面，水泵就必须克服一百个大气压，也就是每平方英寸一千五百磅。这样一来，所需要的力量——”
“只有电才能给我，”船长迅速接口，“先生，我再说一次，我的机器动力几乎是无限的。‘鹦鹉螺号’上水泵的力量大得很。它们喷出的水柱像洪流一样冲过‘亚伯拉罕·林肯号’时，您想必已经领教过了。何况我动用辅助水舱，只是为了达到七百五十至一千英寻的中等深度，好方便操纵机器。我要是有兴致到水下五六英里深的海洋底层去拜访，另有稍慢却同样可靠的手段。”
“什么手段，船长？”
“那就得给您讲‘鹦鹉螺号’是怎样操纵的了。”
“我等不及想听了。”

“在水平面内，要使这条船朝右舷、朝左舷、向不同方向转弯，我用的是普通的舵，装在艉柱后面，通过一只舵轮和几组滑车操纵。不过我还能使‘鹦鹉螺号’在竖直方向上升而复沉、沉而复升。所用的是两块倾斜舵板，安装在两舷对着浮面中心的位置，可以向各方偏转，由船内有力的杠杆操纵。舵板若与船身平行，船就水平前进。舵板倾斜，‘鹦鹉螺号’就依其偏角，在螺旋桨的推动下，照我所愿斜向下潜或者斜向上升。要是我想更快地浮出水面，就收住螺旋桨，水的压力会让‘鹦鹉螺号’像充满氢气的气球一样笔直升上去。”
“真妙，船长！可是在水里，舵手怎样看清所走的路线呢？”
“舵手待在一座装有玻璃的舵室里。它突出在‘鹦鹉螺号’的船壳上方，设有观察用的玻璃镜片。”
“这些镜片受得了那样的压力？”
“完全受得了。玻璃挨一记敲打会碎，承受均匀压力时却可以相当坚固。一八六四年在北方海域用电灯试验捕鱼，我们见过不到三分之一英寸厚的玻璃板承受十六个大气压。我现在用的玻璃，厚度至少有它的三十倍。”
“这我承认。不过要看得见，光总得胜得过黑暗。在水里漆黑一片，您怎么看得见呢？”
“在舵手室的后方，有一盏强大的电探照灯。它的光束能把前面半英里海水都照亮。”
“啊！妙极了，船长！当初那头所谓的独角鲸发出磷光，把我们迷惑到那种地步，现在我全能解释了。再请教您，‘鹦鹉螺号’同‘斯科舍号’的那次相撞，闹出那么大动静，是偶然碰上的吗？”
“纯属意外，先生。相撞发生时，我只在水面下一英寻深处航行。幸而没酿成严重后果。”
“的确没有，先生。可是您同‘亚伯拉罕·林肯号’的遭遇呢？”
“教授，我也替美国海军这艘数一数二的好船惋惜。但他们攻击我，我势必自卫。不过我只叫巡防舰丧失了战斗力。开到最近的港口，修好并不难。”
“唉，船长！您的‘鹦鹉螺号’真是一艘不可思议的船。”

“是的，教授。我爱它，就像爱自己身上的一部分。你们的船在海上遇险，人心里头一个念头，是上天下地尽是深渊。可‘鹦鹉螺号’上的人从不会心虚胆丧。双层船壳如铁一般牢固，不怕出毛病。没有索具要照看，没有船帆会被风撕走，没有锅炉会爆炸。它用铁造的，不用怕木船上的火灾。它的机械动力只有电，不用怕用完煤。在深水里只有它独自游着，不用怕撞船。潜到水下就进入绝对的宁静，不用迎战暴风雨。先生，这才是一条十全十美的船！如果轮机工程师比造船的人更信赖自己的船，造船的人又比船长更信赖自己的船，您就该明白，我对‘鹦鹉螺号’有多少信心。因为我兼着船长、建造者和工程师三种身份。”
“可您怎么有办法秘密建造这么了不得的‘鹦鹉螺号’？”
“阿龙纳斯先生，每一项零件都来自世界不同的地方。龙骨在勒克勒佐锻造，螺旋桨轴订于伦敦的佩恩公司，船壳铁板来自利物浦莱尔德船厂，螺旋桨本身来自格拉斯哥的斯科特厂。储水舱在巴黎凯尔公司制造，发动机由普鲁士的克虏伯厂承制，船首撞角出自瑞典穆塔拉的工场，精密数学仪器是纽约哈特兄弟公司做的，等等。向这些人下单，我各用了一个不同的名字。”
“可是零件还得运到一处，装配起来呀？”
“教授，我在大洋里一座荒岛上设了自己的工场。我手下那些工人，也就是我亲自训练、亲自教导的勇士们，跟我一道，在那里把我们的‘鹦鹉螺号’装配起来。活儿一完，一把火便烧去了我们在岛上活动的一切痕迹。那点小岛，只要我乐意，都能一跃而过。”
“那么，这艘船造价很高？”
“阿龙纳斯先生，铁船每吨造价四十五英镑。‘鹦鹉螺号’重一千五百吨，算下来便是六万七千五百英镑。舾装另加八万。加上船里的艺术品与藏品，合计约二十万英镑。”
“最后再问一句，尼摩船长。”
“请问，教授。”
“您很富有？”
“极为富有，先生。即使替法国还清国债，我手头也不会觉得少了什么。”
我望着眼前这个说出这样话来的奇人。他是不是拿我的轻信寻开心？只有留给未来判明。

sections.title_zh: 上部 / 第13章　黑色的河
sections.title_en: PART ONE / CHAPTER XIII — THE BLACK RIVER
source_paragraphs: The portion of the terrestrial globe which is covered by water is estimated at upwards of eighty millions of acres. This fluid mass comprises two billions two hundred and fifty millions of cubic miles, forming a spherical body of a diameter of sixty leagues, the weight of which would be three quintillions of tons. To comprehend the meaning of these figures, it is necessary to observe that a quintillion is to a billion as a billion is to unity; in other words, there are as many billions in a quintillion as there are units in a billion. This mass of fluid is equal to about the quantity of water which would be discharged by all the rivers of the earth in forty thousand years.

During the geological epochs, the igneous period succeeded to the aqeous. The ocean originally prevailed everywhere. Then by degrees, in the silurian period, the tops of the mountains began to appear, the islands emerged, then disappeared in partial deluges, reappeared, became settled, formed continents, till at length the earth became geographically arranged, as we see in the present day. The solid had wrested from the liquid thirty-seven million six hundred and fifty-seven square miles, equal to twelve billion nine hundred and sixty millions of acres.
The shape of continents allows us to divide the waters into five great portions: the Arctic or Frozen Ocean, the Antarctic or Frozen Ocean, the Indian, the Atlantic, and the Pacific Oceans.

The Pacific Ocean extends from north to south between the two polar circles, and from east to west between Asia and America, over an extent of 145 degrees of longitude. It is the quietest of seas; its currents are broad and slow, it has medium tides, and abundant rain. Such was the ocean that my fate destined me first to travel over under these strange conditions.
“Sir,” said Captain Nemo, “we will, if you please, take our bearings and fix the starting-point of this voyage. It is a quarter to twelve; I will go up again to the surface.”

The Captain pressed an electric clock three times. The pumps began to drive the water from the tanks; the needle of the manometer marked by a different pressure the ascent of the _Nautilus_, then it stopped.
“We have arrived,” said the Captain.
I went to the central staircase which opened on to the platform, clambered up the iron steps, and found myself on the upper part of the _Nautilus_.

The platform was only three feet out of water. The front and back of the _Nautilus_ was of that spindle-shape which caused it justly to be compared to a cigar. I noticed that its iron plates, slightly overlaying each other, resembled the shell which clothes the bodies of our large terrestrial reptiles. It explained to me how natural it was, in spite of all glasses, that this boat should have been taken for a marine animal.

Toward the middle of the platform the long-boat, half buried in the hull of the vessel, formed a slight excrescence. Fore and aft rose two cages of medium height with inclined sides, and partly closed by thick lenticular glasses; one destined for the steersman who directed the _Nautilus_, the other containing a brilliant lantern to give light on the road.

The sea was beautiful, the sky pure. Scarcely could the long vehicle feel the broad undulations of the ocean. A light breeze from the east rippled the surface of the waters. The horizon, free from fog, made observation easy. Nothing was in sight. Not a quicksand, not an island. A vast desert.

Captain Nemo, by the help of his sextant, took the altitude of the sun, which ought also to give the latitude. He waited for some moments till its disc touched the horizon. Whilst taking observations not a muscle moved, the instrument could not have been more motionless in a hand of marble.
Captain Nemo took the Sun’s altitude
“Twelve o’clock, sir,” said he. “When you like——”
I cast a last look upon the sea, slightly yellowed by the Japanese coast, and descended to the saloon.

“And now, sir, I leave you to your studies,” added the Captain; “our course is E.N.E., our depth is twenty-six fathoms. Here are maps on a large scale by which you may follow it. The saloon is at your disposal, and with your permission, I will retire.” Captain Nemo bowed, and I remained alone, lost in thoughts all bearing on the commander of the _Nautilus_.

For a whole hour was I deep in these reflections, seeking to pierce this mystery so interesting to me. Then my eyes fell upon the vast planisphere spread upon the table, and I placed my finger on the very spot where the given latitude and longitude crossed.

The sea has its large rivers like the continents. They are special currents known by their temperature and their colour. The most remarkable of these is known by the name of the Gulf Stream. Science has decided on the globe the direction of five principal currents: one in the North Atlantic, a second in the South, a third in the North Pacific, a fourth in the South, and a fifth in the Southern Indian Ocean. It is even probable that a sixth current existed at one time or another in the Northern Indian Ocean, when the Caspian and Aral Seas formed but one vast sheet of water.

At this point indicated on the planisphere one of these currents was rolling, the Kuro-Scivo of the Japanese, the Black River, which, leaving the Gulf of Bengal, where it is warmed by the perpendicular rays of a tropical sun, crosses the Straits of Malacca along the coast of Asia, turns into the North Pacific to the Aleutian Islands, carrying with it trunks of camphor-trees and other indigenous productions, and edging the waves of the ocean with the pure indigo of its warm water. It was this current that the _Nautilus_ was to follow. I followed it with my eye; saw it lose itself in the vastness of the Pacific, and felt myself drawn with it, when Ned Land and Conseil appeared at the door of the saloon.
My two brave companions remained petrified at the sight of the wonders spread before them.
“Where are we, where are we?” exclaimed the Canadian. “In the museum at Quebec?”
“My friends,” I answered, making a sign for them to enter, “you are not in Canada, but on board the _Nautilus_, fifty yards below the level of the sea.”
“But, M. Aronnax,” said Ned Land, “can you tell me how many men there are on board? Ten, twenty, fifty, a hundred?”

“I cannot answer you, Mr. Land; it is better to abandon for a time all idea of seizing the _Nautilus_ or escaping from it. This ship is a masterpiece of modern industry, and I should be sorry not to have seen it. Many people would accept the situation forced upon us, if only to move amongst such wonders. So be quiet and let us try and see what passes around us.”
“See!” exclaimed the harpooner, “but we can see nothing in this iron prison! We are walking—we are sailing—blindly.”
Ned Land had scarcely pronounced these words when all was suddenly darkness. The luminous ceiling was gone, and so rapidly that my eyes received a painful impression.

We remained mute, not stirring, and not knowing what surprise awaited us, whether agreeable or disagreeable. A sliding noise was heard: one would have said that panels were working at the sides of the _Nautilus_.
“It is the end of the end!” said Ned Land.

Suddenly light broke at each side of the saloon, through two oblong openings. The liquid mass appeared vividly lit up by the electric gleam. Two crystal plates separated us from the sea. At first I trembled at the thought that this frail partition might break, but strong bands of copper bound them, giving an almost infinite power of resistance.

The sea was distinctly visible for a mile all round the _Nautilus_. What a spectacle! What pen can describe it? Who could paint the effects of the light through those transparent sheets of water, and the softness of the successive graduations from the lower to the superior strata of the ocean?

We know the transparency of the sea and that its clearness is far beyond that of rock-water. The mineral and organic substances which it holds in suspension heightens its transparency. In certain parts of the ocean at the Antilles, under seventy-five fathoms of water, can be seen with surprising clearness a bed of sand. The penetrating power of the solar rays does not seem to cease for a depth of one hundred and fifty fathoms. But in this middle fluid travelled over by the _Nautilus_, the electric brightness was produced even in the bosom of the waves. It was no longer luminous water, but liquid light.

On each side a window opened into this unexplored abyss. The obscurity of the saloon showed to advantage the brightness outside, and we looked out as if this pure crystal had been the glass of an immense aquarium.
“You wished to see, friend Ned; well, you see now.”
“Curious! curious!” muttered the Canadian, who, forgetting his ill-temper, seemed to submit to some irresistible attraction; “and one would come further than this to admire such a sight!”
“Ah!” thought I to myself, “I understand the life of this man; he has made a world apart for himself, in which he treasures all his greatest wonders.”

For two whole hours an aquatic army escorted the _Nautilus_. During their games, their bounds, while rivalling each other in beauty, brightness, and velocity, I distinguished the green labre; the banded mullet, marked by a double line of black; the round-tailed goby, of a white colour, with violet spots on the back; the Japanese scombrus, a beautiful mackerel of those seas, with a blue body and silvery head; the brilliant azurors, whose name alone defies description; some banded spares, with variegated fins of blue and yellow; the woodcocks of the seas, some specimens of which attain a yard in length; Japanese salamanders, spider lampreys, serpents six feet long, with eyes small and lively, and a huge mouth bristling with teeth; with many other species.

Our imagination was kept at its height, interjections followed quickly on each other. Ned named the fish, and Conseil classed them. I was in ecstasies with the vivacity of their movements and the beauty of their forms. Never had it been given to me to surprise these animals, alive and at liberty, in their natural element. I will not mention all the varieties which passed before my dazzled eyes, all the collection of the seas of China and Japan. These fish, more numerous than the birds of the air, came, attracted, no doubt, by the brilliant focus of the electric light.

Suddenly there was daylight in the saloon, the iron panels closed again, and the enchanting vision disappeared. But for a long time I dreamt on till my eyes fell on the instruments hanging on the partition. The compass still showed the course to be N.N.E., the manometer indicated a pressure of five atmospheres, equivalent to a depth of twenty-five fathoms, and the electric log gave a speed of fifteen miles an hour. I expected Captain Nemo, but he did not appear. The clock marked the hour of five.

Ned Land and Conseil returned to their cabin, and I retired to my chamber. My dinner was ready. It was composed of turtle soup made of the most delicate hawksbills, of a surmullet served with puff paste (the liver of which, prepared by itself, was most delicious), and fillets of the emperor-holocanthus, the savour of which seemed to me superior even to salmon.

I passed the evening reading, writing, and thinking. Then sleep overpowered me, and I stretched myself on my couch of zostera, and slept profoundly, whilst the _Nautilus_ was gliding rapidly through the current of the Black River.
translated_paragraphs: 据估计，地球表面为水覆盖的部分有八千多万英亩。这团水体共有二十二亿五千万立方英里，若凝成一个球，直径有六十里格，重量则达三百亿亿吨。要弄清这些大数，须知道一百亿亿与十亿之比，正如十亿与一之比。换句话说，一百亿亿里面有多少个十亿，就同十亿里面有多少个一相等。这团水的总量，约合地球上所有河流四万年流出的水。
在地质史的各时期中，火成时期接续着水成时期。最初，大洋统治一切。随后在志留纪，山顶慢慢露出来，岛屿浮现，又在局部洪水中没去，再度显露，渐渐稳定，形成大陆。到后来，地球才有了我们今天看到的地理布局。固体从液体手里夺下了三千七百万零六百五十七平方英里，相当于一百二十九亿六千万英亩。
按照大陆的形状，我们可以把水域分成五大部分：北冰洋，即北方的冰冻洋；南冰洋，即南方的冰冻洋；还有印度洋、大西洋和太平洋。
太平洋南北伸展于两条极圈之间，东西横跨亚洲与美洲之间的一百四十五个经度。它是各海洋中最平静的，洋流宽而缓，潮汐适中，雨量充沛。命运安排我在这样奇异的处境下旅行，头一程穿过的便是这片海洋。
“先生，”尼摩船长说，“如果您愿意，我们就来测定方位，确定这趟航行的出发点。现在差一刻十二点，我要重新浮到海面。”
船长在电动报时装置上按了三下。泵开始往外排压载舱里的水。压力计的指针借着压力的改变，标示出“鹦鹉螺号”在上升，最后停住了。
“我们到了。”船长说。
我走到通往平台的中央梯井，攀上铁梯，来到“鹦鹉螺号”的顶部。
平台只高出水面三英尺。“鹦鹉螺号”的前后两端都收作纺锤形，看上去的确像支雪茄。我注意到，船身上的铁板一块略覆着下一块，活像陆上大型爬行动物包裹身体的甲壳。这就难怪人们用尽了各式望远镜，仍会把这艘船认成海洋生物了。
平台中部，那条小艇半嵌在船壳里，微微隆起。前、后各有一座不算高的罩室，侧壁倾斜，部分嵌着厚厚的透镜状玻璃。一座供操纵“鹦鹉螺号”的舵手使用，另一座装有明亮的大灯，为航路照明。
海面美丽，天空澄净。这条长长的船几乎感觉不到辽阔洋面的缓缓起伏。一阵轻柔的东风吹皱海水。地平线上没有雾，做观测十分方便。目力所及，一无所有。没有一片流沙浅滩，没有一个岛。一望无涯的荒原。
尼摩船长用六分仪测量太阳高度，据此也该能得出纬度。他等候了片刻，让日轮的影像触到地平线。测量时他的肌肉没有一丝颤动，那仪器仿佛握在一只大理石雕成的手里，再稳不过。
图注　尼摩船长测量太阳高度
“十二点，先生，”他说，“您什么时候愿意，就请——”
我向海上最后望了一眼，海面因靠近日本海岸，略略泛黄。然后我下到客厅里。
“现在，先生，任您自行研究吧，”船长又说，“我们航向东东北，深度二十六英寻。这些大比例尺海图可供您跟踪航路。客厅听凭您使用。请容我告退。”尼摩船长向我一鞠躬。我独自留在屋里，满脑子思绪，全围绕着“鹦鹉螺号”的这位主人。
足足一个钟头，我深深陷在这些念头里，想把这令我如此着迷的谜窥破。随后我眼光落到摊在桌上的巨幅世界平面图上，把手指点在所给纬度和经度交会的那一点。
大海也跟大陆一样，有自己的大河。那是一些特别的洋流，凭其温度和颜色便能辨认。最著名的一支叫墨西哥湾流。科学已经弄清地球上五大洋流的走向：一支在北大西洋，一支在南大西洋，第三支在北太平洋，第四支在南太平洋，第五支在南印度洋。甚至很可能，早年里海与咸海连成一片浩大水面之时，北印度洋还曾有过第六支。

在平面图上标出的这个位置，就奔流着其中的一支。日本人称它黑潮，也就是“黑色的河”。它离开孟加拉湾，在那里受着热带太阳的直射而变暖，随后沿亚洲海岸穿过马六甲海峡，折入北太平洋，流向阿留申群岛。它携来樟树的树干和其他本地出产，又以暖水纯净的靛青给海浪镶上了一道边。“鹦鹉螺号”即将顺着这条洋流前进。我用眼睛追着它，看它消失在太平洋的茫茫无际之间，自己也像给吸着跟了去。就在这时，尼德·兰德和康塞尔出现在客厅门口。
我那两位勇敢的同伴一见眼前陈列的奇观，双双僵在了那里。
“我们在哪儿？我们这是在哪儿？”加拿大人叫道，“魁北克的博物馆吗？”
“朋友们，”我招手示意他们进来，回答道，“你们不在加拿大。这里是‘鹦鹉螺号’船上，在海面以下五十码。”
“可是，阿龙纳斯先生，”尼德·兰德问，“您能告诉我，这船上一共有多少人？十个，二十个，五十个，还是一百个？”
“兰德先生，这我答不上。咱们最好暂且放下夺取‘鹦鹉螺号’或者逃离它的种种念头。这条船是近代工业的杰作。我若没有见过它，会很遗憾。光为了有机会行走在这样的奇景之间，很多人就甘愿接受强加给我们的处境。请先静一静吧，咱们尽量看看周围正在发生些什么。”
“看！”叉手叫道，“在这所铁牢里可看得见什么？咱们在摸黑走路，摸黑行船！”
尼德·兰德的话还没说完，忽然一切都黑了。原先发光的天花板消失得这样快，刺激得我的眼睛一阵刺痛。
我们默默站着，动也不动，不知等着我们的，是个喜欢的惊奇，还是个不喜欢的。随即响起滑动的声音，仿佛“鹦鹉螺号”两边的护板在移动。
“这下真正完到底了！”尼德·兰德说。
忽然，亮光从客厅两侧的两个狭长开口透进来。海水已被电光照得通明。隔在我们同大海之间的是两块水晶玻璃。我起初一想到这单薄的屏障可能碎裂，便不禁战栗。可是它们被坚固的铜框紧紧箍住，有几乎无穷的抵抗力。
“鹦鹉螺号”周围一英里内，海水清晰可见。这是怎样的景象啊！哪一支笔能写得出？光线透过那层层透明的海水时变幻万端，从深处到高处，各层之间的色调柔和渐变，又有谁画得尽！
我们知道海水透明，它的清澈程度远胜山石间的泉水。其中悬浮的矿物和有机物使它更加透亮。在安的列斯群岛的一些海域，可以清晰得惊人地看见七十五英寻水下的沙床。太阳光线似乎一直到一百五十英寻深处都还有些穿透力。可是“鹦鹉螺号”如今行驶的水层中，电光就发自波浪的怀抱本身。眼前再不是发光的水，而是流动的光了。
我们左右各有一扇窗朝向这未经人探察的深渊。客厅里的昏暗越发衬托出外面的光明。我们向外望，仿佛这纯净的水晶就是一座无边水族馆的玻璃。
“尼德朋友，你方才想看看。好，这下看见了吧。”
“奇啊！真奇！”加拿大人咕哝道。他已把坏脾气忘光了，仿佛受到一种无法抗拒的力量吸引。“为看这样的景色，多走更远的路也值得！”
“啊！”我暗想，“我懂得这人的生活了。他给自己另造了一个世界，把他最珍爱的种种奇迹都藏在里头。”

整整两小时，一支水族大军护送着“鹦鹉螺号”。看它们嬉戏、跃动，在姿态、光彩和速度上一争高下，我辨出了绿色的隆头鱼，两道黑纹标在身上的带纹鲻，通体雪白而背上散布紫点的圆尾虾虎鱼，日本海域一种美丽的鲭鱼，鱼体湛蓝，头部银亮。还有辉煌的蓝光鱼，单是它那名字便已经难以形容；几种体有条纹的鲷鱼，鳍上黄蓝斑斓；人称“海山鹬”的鱼，有的长到一码；日本的蝾螈，以及蛛形七鳃鳗，那蛇形的躯体长达六英尺，生着灵动的小眼和一张布满牙齿的巨口。此外还有许多别的物种。
我们的想象始终在最高处，一句句惊叹紧接着脱口而出。尼德给鱼报名字，康塞尔给它们分门别类。我为它们动作的灵活、体形的美而出神。以前我哪有机会在这些动物天然栖居的环境中，窥见它们这样活泼、这样自在的模样！所有从我眩目的眼前游过的生物，中国海和日本海的全套家当，我不打算逐一列来。鱼比天空的飞鸟更为稠密，显然是叫那一团辉煌的电光吸引过来的。
忽然，客厅里又亮如白昼，铁制护板重新合拢，令人着迷的景象消失了。然而我恍惚了很久，目光才落到隔舱壁上的仪器。罗盘仍指示航向北东北，压力计显示五个大气压，相当于二十五英寻深，电动计程仪报出每小时十五英里的航速。我等着尼摩船长，他却没有露面。钟上已经五点。
尼德·兰德和康塞尔回自己的舱室了，我也回到卧房。晚餐已经备好：用最嫩的玳瑁作的龟汤，一条配着酥皮的红鲻鱼（鱼肝另做，尤其鲜美），还有几片皇帝刺盖鱼，我觉得味道甚至胜过鲑鱼。
我读书、写字、沉思，度过了这一个晚上。睡意终于压倒了我，我在鳗草铺成的卧榻上伸直身子，沉沉入睡。“鹦鹉螺号”还在那条黑色河流中飞速滑行。

sections.title_zh: 上部 / 第14章　一张请柬
sections.title_en: PART ONE / CHAPTER XIV — A NOTE OF INVITATION
source_paragraphs: The next day was the 9th of November. I awoke after a long sleep of twelve hours. Conseil came, according to custom, to know “how I had passed the night,” and to offer his services. He had left his friend the Canadian sleeping like a man who had never done anything else all his life. I let the worthy fellow chatter as he pleased, without caring to answer him. I was pre-occupied by the absence of the Captain during our sitting of the day before, and hoping to see him to-day.
As soon as I was dressed I went into the saloon. It was deserted.

I plunged into the study of the shell treasures hidden behind the glasses. I revelled also in great herbals filled with the rarest marine plants, which, although dried up, retained their lovely colours. Amongst these precious hydrophytes I remarked some vorticellæ, pavonariæ, delicate ceramies with scarlet tints, some fan-shaped agari, and some natabuli like flat mushrooms, which at one time used to be classed as zoophytes; in short, a perfect series of algæ.
The whole day passed without my being honoured by a visit from Captain Nemo. The panels of the saloon did not open. Perhaps they did not wish us to tire of these beautiful things.
The course of the _Nautilus_ was E.N.E., her speed twelve knots, the depth below the surface between twenty-five and thirty fathoms.

The next day, 10th of November, the same desertion, the same solitude. I did not see one of the ship’s crew: Ned and Conseil spent the greater part of the day with me. They were astonished at the inexplicable absence of the Captain. Was this singular man ill?—had he altered his intentions with regard to us?

After all, as Conseil said, we enjoyed perfect liberty, we were delicately and abundantly fed. Our host kept to his terms of the treaty. We could not complain, and, indeed, the singularity of our fate reserved such wonderful compensation for us, that we had no right to accuse it as yet.
That day I commenced the journal of these adventures which has enabled me to relate them with more scrupulous exactitude and minute detail. I wrote it on paper made from the zostera marina.

11th November, early in the morning. The fresh air spreading over the interior of the _Nautilus_ told me that we had come to the surface of the ocean to renew our supply of oxygen. I directed my steps to the central staircase, and mounted the platform.

It was six o’clock, the weather was cloudy, the sea grey but calm. Scarcely a billow. Captain Nemo, whom I hoped to meet, would he be there? I saw no one but the steersman imprisoned in his glass cage. Seated upon the projection formed by the hull of the pinnace, I inhaled the salt breeze with delight.

By degrees the fog disappeared under the action of the sun’s rays, the radiant orb rose from behind the eastern horizon. The sea flamed under its glance like a train of gunpowder. The clouds scattered in the heights were coloured with lively tints of beautiful shades, and numerous “mare’s tails,” which betokened wind for that day. But what was wind to this _Nautilus_ which tempests could not frighten!

I was admiring this joyous rising of the sun, so gay, and so lifegiving, when I heard steps approaching the platform. I was prepared to salute Captain Nemo, but it was his second (whom I had already seen on the Captain’s first visit) who appeared. He advanced on the platform, not seeming to see me. With his powerful glass to his eye he scanned every point of the horizon with great attention. This examination over, he approached the panel and pronounced a sentence in exactly these terms. I have remembered it, for every morning it was repeated under exactly the same conditions. It was thus worded—
“Nautron respoc lorni virch.”
What it meant I could not say.
These words pronounced, the second descended. I thought that the _Nautilus_ was about to return to its submarine navigation. I regained the panel and returned to my chamber.
Five days sped thus, without any change in our situation. Every morning I mounted the platform. The same phrase was pronounced by the same individual. But Captain Nemo did not appear.

I had made up my mind that I should never see him again, when, on the 16th November, on returning to my room with Ned and Conseil, I found upon my table a note addressed to me. I opened it impatiently. It was written in a bold, clear hand, the characters rather pointed, recalling the German type. The note was worded as follows—
16th of _November_, 1867.
TO PROFESSOR ARONNAX, On board the _Nautilus_.

Captain Nemo invites Professor Aronnax to a hunting-party, which will take place to-morrow morning in the forests of the island of Crespo. He hopes that nothing will prevent the Professor from being present, and he will with pleasure see him joined by his companions.
CAPTAIN NEMO, Commander of the _Nautilus_.
“A hunt!” exclaimed Ned.
“And in the forests of the island of Crespo!” added Conseil.
“Oh! then the gentleman is going on _terra firma?_” replied Ned Land.
“That seems to me to be clearly indicated,” said I, reading the letter once more.
“Well, we must accept,” said the Canadian. “But once more on dry ground, we shall know what to do. Indeed, I shall not be sorry to eat a piece of fresh venison.”
Without seeking to reconcile what was contradictory between Captain Nemo’s manifest aversion to islands and continents, and his invitation to hunt in a forest, I contented myself with replying—
“Let us first see where the island of Crespo is.”

I consulted the planisphere, and in 32° 40′ north lat. and 157° 50′ west long., I found a small island, recognised in 1801 by Captain Crespo, and marked in the ancient Spanish maps as Rocca de la Plata, the meaning of which is “The Silver Rock.” We were then about eighteen hundred miles from our starting-point, and the course of the _Nautilus_, a little changed, was bringing it back towards the south-east.
I showed this little rock lost in the midst of the North Pacific to my companions.
“If Captain Nemo does sometimes go on dry ground,” said I, “he at least chooses desert islands.”
Ned Land shrugged his shoulders without speaking, and Conseil and he left me.
After supper, which was served by the steward mute and impassive, I went to bed, not without some anxiety.
The next morning, the 17th of November, on awakening, I felt that the _Nautilus_ was perfectly still. I dressed quickly and entered the saloon.

Captain Nemo was there, waiting for me. He rose, bowed, and asked me if it was convenient for me to accompany him. As he made no allusion to his absence during the last eight days, I did not mention it, and simply answered that my companions and myself were ready to follow him.
We entered the dining-room, where breakfast was served.

“M. Aronnax,” said the Captain, “pray, share my breakfast without ceremony; we will chat as we eat. For though I promised you a walk in the forest, I did not undertake to find hotels there. So breakfast as a man who will most likely not have his dinner till very late.”

I did honour to the repast. It was composed of several kinds of fish, and slices of holothuridæ (excellent zoophytes), and different sorts of sea-weed. Our drink consisted of pure water, to which the Captain added some drops of a fermented liquor, extracted by the Kamschatcha method from a sea-weed known under the name of _Rhodomenia palmata_. Captain Nemo ate at first without saying a word. Then he began—
“Sir, when I proposed to you to hunt in my submarine forest of Crespo, you evidently thought me mad. Sir, you should never judge lightly of any man.”
“But Captain, believe me——”
“Be kind enough to listen, and you will then see whether you have any cause to accuse me of folly and contradiction.”
“I listen.”

“You know as well as I do, Professor, that man can live under water, providing he carries with him a sufficient supply of breathable air. In submarine works, the workman, clad in an impervious dress, with his head in a metal helmet, receives air from above by means of forcing pumps and regulators.”
“That is a diving apparatus,” said I.

“Just so, but under these conditions the man is not at liberty; he is attached to the pump which sends him air through an india-rubber tube, and if we were obliged to be thus held to the _Nautilus_, we could not go far.”
“And the means of getting free?” I asked.

“It is to use the Rouquayrol apparatus, invented by two of your own countrymen, which I have brought to perfection for my own use, and which will allow you to risk yourself under these new physiological conditions without any organ whatever suffering. It consists of a reservoir of thick iron plates, in which I store the air under a pressure of fifty atmospheres. This reservoir is fixed on the back by means of braces, like a soldier’s knapsack. Its upper part forms a box in which the air is kept by means of a bellows, and therefore cannot escape unless at its normal tension. In the Rouquayrol apparatus such as we use, two india-rubber pipes leave this box and join a sort of tent which holds the nose and mouth; one is to introduce fresh air, the other to let out the foul, and the tongue closes one or the other according to the wants of the respirator. But I, in encountering great pressures at the bottom of the sea, was obliged to shut my head, like that of a diver in a ball of copper; and it is to this ball of copper that the two pipes, the inspirator and the expirator, open.”
“Perfectly, Captain Nemo; but the air that you carry with you must soon be used; when it only contains fifteen per cent. of oxygen it is no longer fit to breathe.”

“Right! but I told you, M. Aronnax, that the pumps of the _Nautilus_ allow me to store the air under considerable pressure, and on these conditions the reservoir of the apparatus can furnish breathable air for nine or ten hours.”
“I have no further objections to make,” I answered; “I will only ask you one thing, Captain—how can you light your road at the bottom of the sea?”

“With the Ruhmkorff apparatus, M. Aronnax; one is carried on the back, the other is fastened to the waist. It is composed of a Bunsen pile, which I do not work with bichromate of potash, but with sodium. A wire is introduced which collects the electricity produced, and directs it towards a particularly made lantern. In this lantern is a spiral glass which contains a small quantity of carbonic gas. When the apparatus is at work this gas becomes luminous, giving out a white and continuous light. Thus provided, I can breathe and I can see.”

“Captain Nemo, to all my objections you make such crushing answers, that I dare no longer doubt. But if I am forced to admit the Rouquayrol and Ruhmkorff apparatus, I must be allowed some reservations with regard to the gun I am to carry.”
“But it is not a gun for powder,” answered the Captain.
“Then it is an air-gun.”
“Doubtless! How would you have me manufacture gunpowder on board, without either saltpetre, sulphur, or charcoal?”
“Besides,” I added, “to fire under water in a medium eight hundred and fifty-five times denser than the air, we must conquer very considerable resistance.”

“That would be no difficulty. There exist guns, according to Fulton, perfected in England by Philip Coles and Burley, in France by Furcy, and in Italy by Landi, which are furnished with a peculiar system of closing, which can fire under these conditions. But I repeat, having no powder, I use air under great pressure, which the pumps of the _Nautilus_ furnish abundantly.”
“But this air must be rapidly used?”

“Well, have I not my Rouquayrol reservoir, which can furnish it at need? A tap is all that is required. Besides, M. Aronnax, you must see yourself that, during our submarine hunt, we can spend but little air and but few balls.”
“But it seems to me that in this twilight, and in the midst of this fluid, which is very dense compared with the atmosphere, shots could not go far, nor easily prove mortal.”
“Sir, on the contrary, with this gun every blow is mortal; and however lightly the animal is touched, it falls as if struck by a thunderbolt.”
“Why?”

“Because the balls sent by this gun are not ordinary balls, but little cases of glass (invented by Leniebroek, an Austrian chemist), of which I have a large supply. These glass cases are covered with a case of steel, and weighted with a pellet of lead; they are real Leyden bottles, into which the electricity is forced to a very high tension. With the slightest shock they are discharged, and the animal, however strong it may be, falls dead. I must tell you that these cases are size number four, and that the charge for an ordinary gun would be ten.”
“I will argue no longer,” I replied, rising from the table; “I have nothing left me but to take my gun. At all events, I will go where you go.”

Captain Nemo then led me aft; and in passing before Ned’s and Conseil’s cabin, I called my two companions, who followed immediately. We then came to a kind of cell near the machinery-room, in which we were to put on our walking-dress.
translated_paragraphs: 次日是十一月九日。我一觉睡了十二个钟头才醒。康塞尔照例进来问“先生夜里过得可好”，随时听我使唤。他把那位加拿大朋友留在舱里，那人睡得真香，仿佛这一生别的什么也没干过，专门就会睡觉。我由着好心的康塞尔随意絮叨，无心回答。昨天我们坐在客厅里时，船长一直没有来，这件事占据着我的心思。我盼望今天能见到他。
穿好衣服，我马上去了客厅。里头空无一人。
我一头扎进玻璃罩后那些贝壳珍宝的研究里。我还沉醉于一册册大型植物标本集，里面满是最稀有的海洋植物，虽经干制，美丽的色泽依然保留着。在这些珍贵的水生标本中，我认出了钟形虫、羽鳃类、染着鲜绯色的精巧仙菜藻，还有扇形的石芝珊瑚，以及像扁蘑菇的杯状生物；有些过去曾归入所谓植形动物。总之，这里有一整套丰富的海藻标本。
整整一天过去，尼摩船长始终没有赏脸来访。客厅两边的护板也没有打开。或许他们是不愿我们把那些美景看腻。
“鹦鹉螺号”航向东东北，航速十二节，在距海面二十五至三十英寻之间的深度前进。
第二天，十一月十日，还是同样的冷清，同样的孤寂。我没看见一个船员。尼德和康塞尔陪我过了大半天。他们也对船长这无从解释的缺席惊奇不已。这个奇人是病了吗？还是改变了打算，不愿照先前的办法待我们了？
然而正如康塞尔所说，我们享有充分的行动自由，吃得精美又充足。主人信守了同我们定下的条件。我们无从抱怨。说来这奇特的命运给了我们那么美妙的补偿，至少到当时，我们还没有理由怨它。
那天，我开始为此番奇遇写日记。正因有了它，我今天才能这样一丝不苟、详尽如实地叙述。我把日记写在用海生鳗草造的纸上。
十一月十一日，清晨。新鲜空气在“鹦鹉螺号”内部散开，叫我知道，我们又浮上洋面补充氧气了。我朝中央阶梯走去，登上了平台。
当时六点，天色阴沉，大海灰暗却平静，几乎不见浪头。我盼望遇见的尼摩船长，会在这里吗？除了一名关在玻璃罩室中的舵手，我没看见别人。我坐在小艇嵌入船壳所形成的凸起上，欢欢喜喜地吸着带咸味的海风。
太阳的光线渐渐驱走浓雾，那明亮的圆轮从东方地平线后升起。海面经它一望，像点着一条火药线，顿时燃烧起来。散落在高处的云团全染上了明快而美丽的色调，天边还有许多“马尾云”，预告这天将起风。可是连风暴都吓不倒“鹦鹉螺号”，一点风对它算什么！
我正欣赏这轮欢欣上升的太阳，它是多么轻快，又给万物带来多少生机。忽然，通往平台的方向响起了脚步。我准备向尼摩船长致意，出现的却是他的副手，也就是船长头一次来见我们时在旁的那个人。他迈上平台，仿佛没有看见我，把一架高倍望远镜举到眼前，极仔细地扫过地平线各个方向。看完，他走到舱口，说了一句话，一字不差是下面这样。我之所以记得，是因为往后的每一天清晨，他都在一模一样的情形下说同样的话。他说的是：
“Nautron respoc lorni virch。”
这句话什么意思，我说不上。
说了这句话，副手便下去了。我想“鹦鹉螺号”大概快要恢复水下航行，便也走到舱口，回到自己房间。
就这样五天过去了，我们的处境毫无变化。每天早上我都上平台，同一个人都说同一句话。可尼摩船长始终不露面。
我已打定主意，以为从今再也见不着他。谁知十一月十六日，我同尼德、康塞尔一道回房，在桌上看到一张写给我的便笺。我急切地打开。笔迹遒劲清楚，字形略尖，叫人联想到德文字体。便笺上这样写道：
一八六七年十一月十六日
致“鹦鹉螺号”上的阿龙纳斯教授
尼摩船长谨邀阿龙纳斯教授参加明日上午在克雷斯波岛森林举行的狩猎。敬望教授届时得以莅临。如蒙携伴同行，船长尤感欣悦。
“鹦鹉螺号”指挥官　尼摩船长
“打猎！”尼德惊叫起来。
“而且是在克雷斯波岛的森林里！”康塞尔跟上一句。
“啊！这位先生难道打算上旱地去吗？”尼德·兰德回答。
“信上应当写得很清楚。”我又读了一遍，答道。
“好，咱们一定得去，”加拿大人说，“一旦重新踏上干地，该干什么咱们心里有数。老实说，能吃一块新鲜鹿肉，我也不会难受。”
尼摩船长明明憎恶岛屿和大陆，却又邀我们去森林打猎，两件事分明抵触，我无意立刻把它们调和，只答了一句：
“先看看克雷斯波岛在哪儿吧。”
我查世界平面图，在北纬三十二度四十分、西经一百五十七度五十分找到一座小岛。一八〇一年，克雷斯波船长曾发现它，西班牙旧海图标作Rocca de la Plata，意思是“银岩”。当时我们离出发点约一千八百英里。“鹦鹉螺号”稍稍改向，又折回东南方去。
我把那块失落在北太平洋中央的小石岛指给同伴看。
“尼摩船长就算偶尔肯上陆地，”我说，“选的也总是荒岛。”
尼德·兰德耸耸肩，没有说话，跟康塞尔一道离开了我。
晚饭仍是那个不动声色、一字不出的侍役送来。吃过以后，我上床睡觉，心里未免有些忐忑。
次日，十一月十七日，我一醒便觉得“鹦鹉螺号”纹丝不动。我赶紧穿衣，走进客厅。
尼摩船长在那里等我。他起身，鞠躬，问我今日跟他同行可方便。过去八天他为何没有露面，他一字不提，我也就没有提起，只答我和同伴已准备好跟随他。
我们走进餐厅，早饭已备在桌上。
“阿龙纳斯先生，”船长说，“请随意跟我用饭，不必客气，咱们边吃边聊。我虽答应陪您到林子里去走走，可没包办在那里找到旅馆。因此这顿早饭，您可得像个也许要到很晚才能吃上正餐的人，好好吃饱。”
这顿饭我可没有辜负。席上有几种鱼，切成片的海参（味道绝好的植形动物），还有各式各样的海藻。喝的是清水，船长滴了几滴发酵的酒液在里面。这酒依堪察加的办法，取一种名叫掌状红皮藻的海藻酿成。尼摩船长开头埋头吃饭，一声不响，随后才开口：
“先生，我提议邀您到克雷斯波那片海底森林去狩猎时，您显然以为我发了疯。先生，评断他人，可千万不能轻率。”
“可是船长，请相信我——”
“请先听我说完，到时再看，您是否有理由责我愚蠢，说我前后矛盾。”
“我听着。”
“教授，您和我一样清楚，人只要随身带着足够的可供呼吸的空气，就能够在水下生活。从事水下工程的工人穿的是不透水的服装，脑袋罩在金属头盔里，借压力泵和调节器接收上面送下的空气。”
“那是潜水装置。”我说。
“完全正确。不过在这种条件下，人并不自由。他拴在一台泵上，由橡皮管给他送气。要是我们也必须这样拴在‘鹦鹉螺号’上，那就走不了多远。”
“怎样才能解脱这条牵绳？”我问。

“办法是用鲁凯罗尔装置。它是您两位同胞的发明，我为了自用又把它改进过。靠这装置，您可以在这些全新的生理条件下冒险，而不至于损伤任何器官。它有一个厚铁板制的储气罐，我在里面存入五十个大气压的空气。罐由肩带固定在背上，像士兵背的行囊。罐子上部有一个小室，靠风箱调节空气，使它只能在恢复正常压力时放出。在我们使用的鲁凯罗尔装置上，两根橡皮管从小室引出，连到一只罩住口鼻的面罩。一根导入新气，一根排出浊气，舌头按呼吸的需要轮流关闭其中一根。不过我在海底要遭遇很大的压力，不得不像潜水工那样，把头关进一个铜球里。于是这两根管子，一根吸气管、一根呼气管，就都通到铜球里面。”
“讲得明白，尼摩船长。可您随身携带的空气很快会用完。里面氧气只剩百分之十五时，可就不宜呼吸了。”
“对！不过阿龙纳斯先生，我说过，‘鹦鹉螺号’上的泵能以很大压力为我储存空气。具备这种条件，装置的储气罐便能连续九至十个钟头提供可供呼吸的空气。”
“这方面我没别的疑问了，”我回答，“只想再请教您一件事，船长，在海底怎样照亮您脚下的路？”
“用鲁姆科夫装置，阿龙纳斯先生。一套背在背上，另一套系在腰间。照明装置靠一组本生电池，在我这里，所用的是钠，并非重铬酸钾。一根导线汇集产生的电流，送往一盏特制的提灯。提灯内有一根螺旋形玻璃管，装着少量二氧化碳气体。装置运转时，气体发亮，放出连续的白光。有了这些装备，我便既能呼吸，又能看见。”
“尼摩船长，提一个疑问，您便给一个压倒性的解答，我实在不敢再怀疑了。不过就算我承认鲁凯罗尔和鲁姆科夫的装置高明，至于我所要带的枪，您总得容我保留几分疑问。”
“可它不是一支用火药的枪。”船长答道。
“那么，是气枪。”
“当然！在船上既没有硝石，又没有硫磺或木炭，您叫我怎样制造火药？”
“再说，”我补充，“要在水下开枪，介质的密度比空气大八百五十五倍，势必要克服相当大的阻力。”
“这不会成为困难。按富尔顿的构想造的枪，在英国经菲利普·科尔斯和伯利，在法国经菲尔西，在意大利经兰迪，各有改进。这些枪有一套特制的密闭机构，能在这样的条件下射击。不过我再说一次，我没有火药，用的是很高压力的空气，‘鹦鹉螺号’的泵能够充分供应。”
“可是这股空气一定很快就用完吧？”
“我不是有鲁凯罗尔储气罐吗？需要时它就可以供气，只消接一只阀门。何况阿龙纳斯先生，您自己也该看得出，在水下狩猎时，我们用不了多少空气，也用不了多少子弹。”
“可是依我看，在那样昏暗的光线里，又在比大气稠密得多的液体中间，子弹打不远，也不容易致命。”
“先生，正相反，用这把枪，弹弹都能致命。无论多么轻地碰上那动物，它都会像挨了霹雳一样，立刻倒下。”
“为什么？”
“因为从这种枪里射出的并非普通子弹，而是奥地利化学家莱尼布鲁克发明的小玻璃弹壳，我手头存着很多。这些玻璃壳外包钢层，另有一颗铅丸配重。它们是些真真正正的小莱顿瓶，里头蓄着电压极高的电。一受碰撞，即刻放电。那动物无论多强壮，登时丧命。我还得告诉您，这种弹壳是四号尺寸，普通枪所用的弹丸则是十号。”
“不再争辩了，”我离桌起身，答道，“除了拿起自己的枪，我再也没有别的事可做。无论如何，您上哪儿，我都跟着。”
尼摩船长领我往船尾去。经过尼德和康塞尔的舱室，我叫上这两位同伴，他们马上跟来。我们来到机舱附近一间小室。在这里，我们要换上出门散步的衣服了。

sections.title_zh: 上部 / 第15章　海底散步
sections.title_en: PART ONE / CHAPTER XV — A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
source_paragraphs: This cell was, to speak correctly, the arsenal and wardrobe of the _Nautilus_. A dozen diving apparatuses hung from the partition, waiting our use.
Ned Land, on seeing them, showed evident repugnance to dress himself in one.
“But, my worthy Ned, the forests of the Island of Crespo are nothing but submarine forests.”
“Good!” said the disappointed harpooner, who saw his dreams of fresh meat fade away. “And you, M. Aronnax, are you going to dress yourself in those clothes?”
“There is no alternative, Master Ned.”
“As you please, sir,” replied the harpooner, shrugging his shoulders; “but as for me, unless I am forced, I will never get into one.”
“No one will force you, Master Ned,” said Captain Nemo.
“Is Conseil going to risk it?” asked Ned.
“I follow my master wherever he goes,” replied Conseil.

At the Captain’s call two of the ship’s crew came to help us to dress in these heavy and impervious clothes, made of india-rubber without seam, and constructed expressly to resist considerable pressure. One would have thought it a suit of armour, both supple and resisting. This suit formed trousers and waistcoat. The trousers were finished off with thick boots, weighted with heavy leaden soles. The texture of the waistcoat was held together by bands of copper, which crossed the chest, protecting it from the great pressure of the water, and leaving the lungs free to act; the sleeves ended in gloves, which in no way restrained the movement of the hands. There was a vast difference noticeable between these consummate apparatuses and the old cork breastplates, jackets, and other contrivances in vogue during the eighteenth century.

Captain Nemo and one of his companions (a sort of Hercules, who must have possessed great strength), Conseil, and myself, were soon enveloped in the dresses. There remained nothing more to be done but to enclose our heads in the metal box. But before proceeding to this operation, I asked the Captain’s permission to examine the guns we were to carry.

One of the _Nautilus_ men gave me a simple gun, the butt end of which, made of steel, hollow in the centre, was rather large. It served as a reservoir for compressed air, which a valve, worked by a spring, allowed to escape into a metal tube. A box of projectiles, in a groove in the thickness of the butt end, contained about twenty of these electric balls, which, by means of a spring, were forced into the barrel of the gun. As soon as one shot was fired, another was ready.
“Captain Nemo,” said I, “this arm is perfect, and easily handled: I only ask to be allowed to try it. But how shall we gain the bottom of the sea?”
“At this moment, Professor, the _Nautilus_ is stranded in five fathoms, and we have nothing to do but to start.”
“But how shall we get off?”
“You shall see.”

Captain Nemo thrust his head into the helmet, Conseil and I did the same, not without hearing an ironical “Good sport!” from the Canadian. The upper part of our dress terminated in a copper collar upon which was screwed the metal helmet. Three holes, protected by thick glass, allowed us to see in all directions, by simply turning our head in the interior of the head-dress. As soon as it was in position, the Rouquayrol apparatus on our backs began to act; and, for my part, I could breathe with ease.

With the Ruhmkorff lamp hanging from my belt, and the gun in my hand, I was ready to set out. But to speak the truth, imprisoned in these heavy garments, and glued to the deck by my leaden soles, it was impossible for me to take a step.
I was ready to set out

But this state of things was provided for. I felt myself being pushed into a little room contiguous to the wardrobe-room. My companions followed, towed along in the same way. I heard a water-tight door, furnished with stopper-plates, close upon us, and we were wrapped in profound darkness.

After some minutes, a loud hissing was heard. I felt the cold mount from my feet to my chest. Evidently from some part of the vessel they had, by means of a tap, given entrance to the water, which was invading us, and with which the room was soon filled. A second door cut in the side of the _Nautilus_ then opened. We saw a faint light. In another instant our feet trod the bottom of the sea.

And now, how can I retrace the impression left upon me by that walk under the waters? Words are impotent to relate such wonders! Captain Nemo walked in front, his companion followed some steps behind. Conseil and I remained near each other, as if an exchange of words had been possible through our metallic cases. I no longer felt the weight of my clothing, or of my shoes, of my reservoir of air, or my thick helmet, in the midst of which my head rattled like an almond in its shell.

The light, which lit the soil thirty feet below the surface of the ocean, astonished me by its power. The solar rays shone through the watery mass easily, and dissipated all colour, and I clearly distinguished objects at a distance of a hundred and fifty yards. Beyond that the tints darkened into fine gradations of ultramarine, and faded into vague obscurity. Truly this water which surrounded me was but another air denser than the terrestrial atmosphere, but almost as transparent. Above me was the calm surface of the sea.

We were walking on fine, even sand, not wrinkled, as on a flat shore, which retains the impression of the billows. This dazzling carpet, really a reflector, repelled the rays of the sun with wonderful intensity, which accounted for the vibration which penetrated every atom of liquid. Shall I be believed when I say that, at the depth of thirty feet, I could see as if I was in broad daylight?

For a quarter of an hour I trod on this sand, sown with the impalpable dust of shells. The hull of the _Nautilus_, resembling a long shoal, disappeared by degrees; but its lantern, when darkness should overtake us in the waters, would help to guide us on board by its distinct rays.

Soon forms of objects outlined in the distance were discernible. I recognised magnificent rocks, hung with a tapestry of zoophytes of the most beautiful kind, and I was at first struck by the peculiar effect of this medium.

It was then ten in the morning; the rays of the sun struck the surface of the waves at rather an oblique angle, and at the touch of their light, decomposed by refraction as through a prism, flowers, rocks, plants, shells, and polypi were shaded at the edges by the seven solar colours. It was marvellous, a feast for the eyes, this complication of coloured tints, a perfect kaleidoscope of green, yellow, orange, violet, indigo, and blue; in one word, the whole palette of an enthusiastic colourist! Why could I not communicate to Conseil the lively sensations which were mounting to my brain, and rival him in expressions of admiration? For aught I knew, Captain Nemo and his companion might be able to exchange thoughts by means of signs previously agreed upon. So, for want of better, I talked to myself; I declaimed in the copper box which covered my head, thereby expending more air in vain words than was perhaps expedient.

Various kinds of isis, clusters of pure tuft-coral, prickly fungi, and anemones formed a brilliant garden of flowers, enamelled with porphitæ, decked with their collarettes of blue tentacles, sea-stars studding the sandy bottom, together with asterophytons like fine lace embroidered by the hands of naïads, whose festoons were waved by the gentle undulations caused by our walk. It was a real grief to me to crush under my feet the brilliant specimens of molluscs which strewed the ground by thousands, of hammer-heads, donaciae (veritable bounding shells), of staircases, and red helmet-shells, angel-wings, and many others produced by this inexhaustible ocean. But we were bound to walk, so we went on, whilst above our heads waved shoals of physalides leaving their tentacles to float in their train, medusæ whose umbrellas of opal or rose-pink, escalloped with a band of blue, sheltered us from the rays of the sun and fiery pelagiæ, which, in the darkness, would have strewn our path with phosphorescent light.

All these wonders I saw in the space of a quarter of a mile, scarcely stopping, and following Captain Nemo, who beckoned me on by signs. Soon the nature of the soil changed; to the sandy plain succeeded an extent of slimy mud, which the Americans call “ooze,” composed of equal parts of silicious and calcareous shells. We then travelled over a plain of sea-weed of wild and luxuriant vegetation. This sward was of close texture, and soft to the feet, and rivalled the softest carpet woven by the hand of man. But whilst verdure was spread at our feet, it did not abandon our heads. A light network of marine plants, of that inexhaustible family of sea-weeds of which more than two thousand kinds are known, grew on the surface of the water. I saw long ribbons of fucus floating, some globular, others tuberous; laurenciæ and cladostephi of most delicate foliage, and some rhodomeniæ palmatæ, resembling the fan of a cactus. I noticed that the green plants kept nearer the top of the sea, whilst the red were at a greater depth, leaving to the black or brown hydrophytes the care of forming gardens and parterres in the remote beds of the ocean.

We had quitted the _Nautilus_ about an hour and a half. It was near noon; I knew by the perpendicularity of the sun’s rays, which were no longer refracted. The magical colours disappeared by degrees, and the shades of emerald and sapphire were effaced. We walked with a regular step, which rang upon the ground with astonishing intensity; the slightest noise was transmitted with a quickness to which the ear is unaccustomed on the earth; indeed, water is a better conductor of sound than air, in the ratio of four to one. At this period the earth sloped downwards; the light took a uniform tint. We were at a depth of a hundred and five yards and twenty inches, undergoing a pressure of six atmospheres.

At this depth I could still see the rays of the sun, though feebly; to their intense brilliancy had succeeded a reddish twilight, the lowest state between day and night; but we could still see well enough; it was not necessary to resort to the Ruhmkorff apparatus as yet. At this moment Captain Nemo stopped; he waited till I joined him, and then pointed to an obscure mass, looming in the shadow, at a short distance.
“It is the forest of the Island of Crespo,” thought I;—and I was not mistaken.
translated_paragraphs: 这间小室，说确切些，是“鹦鹉螺号”的军械库兼衣帽间。隔舱壁上挂着一打潜水装具，等着我们取用。
尼德·兰德瞧见这些东西，显然极不愿意挑一套穿在自己身上。
“我亲爱的尼德，克雷斯波岛的森林，原来就是海底森林呀。”
“好嘛！”失望的叉手眼见鲜肉的美梦烟消云散，说道，“阿龙纳斯先生，您呢，也要套上这种衣服吗？”
“没有别的办法，尼德师傅。”
“那就随您的意吧，先生，”叉手耸耸肩答道，“至于我，除非有人强迫，我是绝不肯钻进去的。”
“没人会强迫您，尼德师傅。”尼摩船长说。
“康塞尔也要冒这个险吗？”尼德问。
“先生去哪里，我就跟到哪里。”康塞尔回答。

船长一声招呼，来了两名船员，帮我们穿上这些又重又不透水的衣服。衣服用整块无缝的橡胶做成，特意设计来抵御相当大的压力，看着就像一身又能屈伸、又很坚韧的甲胄。全套衣服包括裤子和上身背心。裤腿底下连着一双厚靴，鞋底用沉重的铅块压着。背心的材料靠铜条固定，铜条在胸前交叉，保护胸部免受巨大水压，让肺可以自由活动。衣袖末端连着手套，手指动作毫不受碍。与这些精良的装具相比，十八世纪一度时兴的软木护胸、背心和其他种种发明，差别可大得很。
尼摩船长和一个同伴——他形如大力士赫拉克勒斯，一定有极大的力气——加上康塞尔和我，不一会儿都叫潜水服包裹严实，只剩把脑袋也关进金属罩子这一道手续。不过在做这一步以前，我请船长准我仔细看看我们将带的枪。
一名“鹦鹉螺号”的船员递给我一支颇简单的枪，枪托是钢制的，个头较大，中间空心，正好充作压缩空气的储气罐。一个用弹簧操纵的阀门，能将空气释放进金属管。枪托的厚壁中开了个槽，嵌着弹匣，约装二十枚这样的电弹。弹簧将它们压进枪管，一发打出去，下一发已经待命了。
“尼摩船长，”我说，“这件武器无可挑剔，操作也简便，我恨不得马上试试。不过，咱们怎样走到海底去？”
“教授，此刻‘鹦鹉螺号’已在五英寻的水底坐稳。咱们只管动身就是。”
“可是怎样下船呢？”
“您马上就看到了。”
尼摩船长把头套进头盔。康塞尔和我也照办了，耳边不免还听见加拿大人挖苦地道一句“祝你们满载而归！”衣服的上端收在一个铜领圈上，金属头盔就在圈上旋紧。头盔开着三个由厚玻璃保护的视孔，只要把头在盔内转一转，各个方向都看得见。一切就位，背上的鲁凯罗尔装置便开始工作。就我自己而论，呼吸颇为轻松。
我腰间挂着鲁姆科夫灯，手里握着枪，已准备出发。可说实话，身子困在重装里，铅底靴又把脚钉在甲板上，我连一步也挪不动。
图注　我已准备出发
但这种情形早在预计之中。我觉得自己被人推进紧挨衣帽间的一间小室，同伴们也被一样拖着跟来。只听身后一扇装有密封压板的水密门关紧，我们便处在一片浓黑之中。
几分钟后，响起嘶嘶的声息。寒意从我的脚一路升至胸口。显然有人在船上某处拧开阀门，把水放了进来。海水淹向我们，很快就灌满舱室。接着，开在“鹦鹉螺号”船舷上的第二道门也打开了。我们望见一缕朦胧的亮光。再一瞬，我们的脚已经踏上了海底。
如今，我要怎样重现那趟海底散步留给我的印象？这样的奇景，言语根本无力传达！尼摩船长走在前面，他的同伴落后几步。康塞尔同我挨着走，仿佛隔着两副金属外壳，我们还能够说话。我已不觉得衣服沉，也不觉得靴子、储气罐或厚头盔是重负。头在头盔里晃荡，像一粒杏仁在果壳里轻摇。
在海面以下三十英尺深处，照亮海底的光线竟如此有力，实在使我惊讶。阳光轻易穿透整片水体，把水色冲淡。我能清楚地分辨一百五十码外的物体。再往远，色调便渐次深为一层层优美的群青，末了隐进模糊的幽暗。的确，包围我的这片海水，不过是另一种空气，比陆地的大气稠密，却几乎同样透明。上方就是宁静的海面。
我们走在细软平整的沙地上。这里不像平坦的岸滩那样留下波浪的印纹，没有一道褶皱。这张耀眼的地毯实是一面反光镜，以奇妙的强度反射太阳的光，难怪每一粒水都仿佛在颤动。我若说水深三十英尺处，眼前明亮如同大白天，各位肯信吗？
约有一刻钟，我都踩着这种细沙走，沙里撒着摸不出来的贝壳细粉。“鹦鹉螺号”的船体像一条长长的浅滩，渐渐隐去。不过待黑暗在水里赶上我们，它的灯仍会以清晰的光束领我们回到船上。
不久，远处的东西显出了轮廓。我认出是一片壮美的岩石，岩上悬垂着形态极美的植形动物，仿佛披着挂毯。我头一个注意到的，是这种水下环境造成的一种奇异效果。

当时是上午十点，阳光以相当倾斜的角度落到浪面。光线碰上水，像经过棱镜般折射分解，花朵、岩石、草木、贝壳和珊瑚虫的边缘都晕着日光的七色。种种颜色交融，简直是奇迹，是眼睛的盛宴，是一具把绿、黄、橙、紫、靛、蓝旋在一起的万花筒。一句话，是一位醉心于色彩的画家摊开的整副调色板！为什么我不能把涌向头脑的鲜活感受传给康塞尔，跟他比赛谁能说出更多赞美？说不定尼摩船长跟同伴倒能凭预先商定的手势互通心意。我没有更好的办法，就自言自语，在罩住脑袋的铜球里大声咏叹。为这番空话浪费掉的空气，大概比明智的分量多了些。

各式竹节珊瑚、成丛的素色枝珊瑚、带刺的石芝和海葵，合成一座美得耀眼的花园。蓝钮扣水母像点缀其间的珐琅饰物，每只都围着一圈蓝色的触手领。海星星星点点缀在沙底，还有筐蛇尾，精巧得像水中仙女绣出的花边。我们步履引来的轻微波动一推，那一道道垂花便轻轻飘摇。几千只美丽的软体动物撒满地面，踩碎了它们真叫我心疼：槌蛤、会弹跳的斧蛤、梯螺、红盔螺、天使翼海笋，以及那取之不尽的海洋所出的许多别种。可我们总得迈步，便继续前进。头顶上成群的僧帽水母悠悠荡荡，将触手放在后面漂着。水母的伞盖有的色如蛋白石，有的玫瑰粉，扇贝形的边缘镶着蓝带，为我们挡住阳光。还有火红的游水母，要在黑暗中，本可以一路用磷光把我们的去路洒亮。

这许多奇观，都是在短短四分之一英里路上看见的。我几乎没有停步，一路跟着打手势招我往前的尼摩船长。很快，脚底换了质地，沙原过去是一片黏软的泥浆，美国人把这种东西叫作“软泥”，由含硅和含钙的细小硬壳各半组成。随后我们走过一片野生海藻繁茂滋长的平野。海藻铺得绵密，踩上去柔软，足与人手织出的最柔软的地毯争胜。绿意不单铺陈在脚下，抬头也在。海面上生着一张轻盈的水草网，都属于品种无穷的海藻，已知的就有两千多种。我看见长带似的褐藻随水浮动，有的结着球囊，有的带着块状突起。还有枝叶极其细致的凹顶藻和枝毛藻，以及摊开来像仙人掌一瓣阔扇的掌状红皮藻。我留意到，绿色的水草靠近海面，红色水草住得较深，更遥远的海底深处，就留给黑色或褐色的水生植物去铺花坛、建花园了。
我们离开“鹦鹉螺号”约一个半钟头。太阳直直地照进水里，光线已不再斜折，我知道快到中午了。魔法似的色彩慢慢消失，翡翠与蓝宝石的色泽都褪了。我们踏着均匀的步子，脚下地面却响得出奇。任何细小的响动，都以陆地上人耳不惯的速度传来。的确，水传声比空气好，速度之比约为四比一。这时脚下渐渐向下倾斜，光线只余单一的色调。我们来到了深一百零五码又二十英寸的地方，承受着六个大气压。
在这个深度，我还能看见太阳光线，只是很弱了。原先夺目的明亮已换作一片微红的暮色，贴着白天同黑夜之间最低的一线。但仍然看得够清楚，还不用借助鲁姆科夫灯。恰在此刻，尼摩船长停下，等我走到他身边，伸手指向不远处一团在昏暗中隐隐浮现的东西。
“那便是克雷斯波岛的森林。”我暗想。我没有猜错。

sections.title_zh: 上部 / 第16章　水下森林
sections.title_en: PART ONE / CHAPTER XVI — A SUBMARINE FOREST
source_paragraphs: We had at last arrived on the borders of this forest, doubtless one of the finest of Captain Nemo’s immense domains. He looked upon it as his own, and considered he had the same right over it that the first men had in the first days of the world. And, indeed, who would have disputed with him the possession of this submarine property? What other hardier pioneer would come, hatchet in hand, to cut down the dark copses?
This forest was composed of large tree-plants; and the moment we penetrated under its vast arcades, I was struck by the singular position of their branches—a position I had not yet observed.

Not a herb which carpeted the ground, not a branch which clothed the trees, was either broken or bent, nor did they extend horizontally; all stretched up to the surface of the ocean. Not a filament, not a ribbon, however thin they might be, but kept as straight as a rod of iron. The fuci and llianas grew in rigid perpendicular lines, due to the density of the element which had produced them. Motionless, yet when bent to one side by the hand, they directly resumed their former position. Truly it was the region of perpendicularity!

I soon accustomed myself to this fantastic position, as well as to the comparative darkness which surrounded us. The soil of the forest seemed covered with sharp blocks, difficult to avoid. The submarine flora struck me as being very perfect, and richer even than it would have been in the arctic or tropical zones, where these productions are not so plentiful. But for some minutes I involuntarily confounded the genera, taking zoophytes for hydrophytes, animals for plants; and who would not have been mistaken? The fauna and the flora are too closely allied in this submarine world.

These plants are self-propagated, and the principle of their existence is in the water, which upholds and nourishes them. The greater number, instead of leaves, shot forth blades of capricious shapes, comprised within a scale of colours,—pink, carmine, green, olive, fawn, and brown. I saw there (but not dried up, as our specimens of the _Nautilus_ are) pavonari spread like a fan, as if to catch the breeze; scarlet ceramies, whose laminaries extended their edible shoots of fern-shaped nereocysti, which grow to a height of fifteen feet; clusters of acetabuli, whose stems increase in size upwards; and numbers of other marine plants, all devoid of flowers!
“Curious anomaly, fantastic element!” said an ingenious naturalist, “in which the animal kingdom blossoms, and the vegetable does not!”

Under these numerous shrubs (as large as trees of the temperate zone), and under their damp shadow, were massed together real bushes of living flowers, hedges of zoophytes, on which blossomed some zebrameandrines, with crooked grooves, some yellow caryophylliæ; and, to complete the allusion, the fish-flies flew from branch to branch like a swarm of humming-birds, whilst yellow lepisacomthi, with bristling jaws, dactylopteri, and monocentrides rose at our feet like a flight of snipes.
In about an hour Captain Nemo gave the signal to halt. I, for my part, was not sorry, and we stretched ourselves under an arbour of alariæ, the long thin blades of which stood up like arrows.

This short rest seemed delicious to me; there was nothing wanting but the charm of conversation; but, impossible to speak, impossible to answer, I only put my great copper head to Conseil’s. I saw the worthy fellow’s eyes glistening with delight, and to show his satisfaction, he shook himself in his breastplate of air in the most comical way in the world.

After four hours of this walking I was surprised not to find myself dreadfully hungry. How to account for this state of the stomach I could not tell. But instead I felt an insurmountable desire to sleep, which happens to all divers. And my eyes soon closed behind the thick glasses, and I fell into a heavy slumber, which the movement alone had prevented before. Captain Nemo and his robust companion, stretched in the clear crystal, set us the example.

How long I remained buried in this drowsiness I cannot judge; but, when I woke, the sun seemed sinking towards the horizon. Captain Nemo had already risen, and I was beginning to stretch my limbs, when an unexpected apparition brought me briskly to my feet.

A few steps off, a monstrous sea-spider, about thirty-eight inches high, was watching me with squinting eyes, ready to spring upon me. Though my diver’s dress was thick enough to defend me from the bite of this animal, I could not help shuddering with horror. Conseil and the sailor of the _Nautilus_ awoke at this moment. Captain Nemo pointed out the hideous crustacean, which a blow from the butt end of the gun knocked over, and I saw the horrible claws of the monster writhe in terrible convulsions. This accident reminded me that other animals more to be feared might haunt these obscure depths, against whose attacks my diving-dress would not protect me. I had never thought of it before, but I now resolved to be upon my guard. Indeed, I thought that this halt would mark the termination of our walk; but I was mistaken, for, instead of returning to the _Nautilus_, Captain Nemo continued his bold excursion. The ground was still on the incline, its declivity seemed to be getting greater, and to be leading us to greater depths. It must have been about three o’clock when we reached a narrow valley, between high perpendicular walls, situated about seventy-five fathoms deep. Thanks to the perfection of our apparatus, we were forty-five fathoms below the limit which nature seems to have imposed on man as to his submarine excursions.

I say seventy-five fathoms, though I had no instrument by which to judge the distance. But I knew that even in the clearest waters the solar rays could not penetrate further. And accordingly the darkness deepened. At ten paces not an object was visible. I was groping my way, when I suddenly saw a brilliant white light. Captain Nemo had just put his electric apparatus into use; his companion did the same, and Conseil and I followed their example. By turning a screw I established a communication between the wire and the spiral glass, and the sea, lit by our four lanterns, was illuminated for a circle of thirty-six yards.

Captain Nemo was still plunging into the dark depths of the forest, whose trees were getting scarcer at every step. I noticed that vegetable life disappeared sooner than animal life. The medusæ had already abandoned the arid soil, from which a great number of animals, zoophytes, articulata, molluscs, and fishes, still obtained sustenance.

As we walked, I thought the light of our Ruhmkorff apparatus could not fail to draw some inhabitant from its dark couch. But if they did approach us, they at least kept at a respectful distance from the hunters. Several times I saw Captain Nemo stop, put his gun to his shoulder, and after some moments drop it and walk on. At last, after about four hours, this marvellous excursion came to an end. A wall of superb rocks, in an imposing mass, rose before us, a heap of gigantic blocks, an enormous, steep granite shore, forming dark grottos, but which presented no practicable slope; it was the prop of the Island of Crespo. It was the earth! Captain Nemo stopped suddenly. A gesture of his brought us all to a halt, and, however desirous I might be to scale the wall, I was obliged to stop. Here ended Captain Nemo’s domains. And he would not go beyond them. Further on was a portion of the globe he might not trample upon.

The return began. Captain Nemo had returned to the head of his little band, directing their course without hesitation. I thought we were not following the same road to return to the _Nautilus_. The new road was very steep, and consequently very painful. We approached the surface of the sea rapidly. But this return to the upper strata was not so sudden as to cause relief from the pressure too rapidly, which might have produced serious disorder in our organisation, and brought on internal lesions, so fatal to divers. Very soon light reappeared and grew, and the sun being low on the horizon, the refraction edged the different objects with a spectral ring. At ten yards and a half deep, we walked amidst a shoal of little fishes of all kinds, more numerous than the birds of the air, and also more agile; but no aquatic game worthy of a shot had as yet met our gaze, when at that moment I saw the Captain shoulder his gun quickly, and follow a moving object into the shrubs. He fired;—I heard a slight hissing, and a creature fell stunned at some distance from us. It was a magnificent sea-otter, an enhydrus, the only exclusively marine quadruped. This otter was five feet long, and must have been very valuable. Its skin, chestnut-brown above and silvery underneath, would have made one of those beautiful furs so sought after in the Russian and Chinese markets; the fineness and the lustre of its coat would certainly fetch £80. I admired this curious mammal, with its rounded head ornamented with short ears, its round eyes, and white whiskers like those of a cat, with webbed feet and nails, and tufted tail. This precious animal, hunted and tracked by fishermen, has now become very rare, and taken refuge chiefly in the northern parts of the Pacific, or probably its race would soon become extinct.

Captain Nemo’s companion took the beast, threw it over his shoulder, and we continued our journey. For one hour a plain of sand lay stretched before us. Sometimes it rose to within two yards and some inches of the surface of the water. I then saw our image clearly reflected, drawn inversely, and above us appeared an identical group reflecting our movements and our actions; in a word, like us in every point, except that they walked with their heads downward and their feet in the air.

Another effect I noticed, which was the passage of thick clouds which formed and vanished rapidly; but on reflection I understood that these seeming clouds were due to the varying thickness of the reeds at the bottom, and I could even see the fleecy foam which their broken tops multiplied on the water, and the shadows of large birds passing above our heads, whose rapid flight I could discern on the surface of the sea.

On this occasion, I was witness to one of the finest gun-shots which ever made the nerves of a hunter thrill. A large bird of great breadth of wing, clearly visible, approached, hovering over us. Captain Nemo’s companion shouldered his gun and fired, when it was only a few yards above the waves. The creature fell stunned, and the force of its fall brought it within the reach of the dexterous hunter’s grasp. It was an albatross of the finest kind.

Our march had not been interrupted by this incident. For two hours we followed these sandy plains, then fields of algæ very disagreeable to cross. Candidly, I could do no more when I saw a glimmer of light, which, for a half mile, broke the darkness of the waters. It was the lantern of the _Nautilus_. Before twenty minutes were over we should be on board, and I should be able to breathe with ease, for it seemed that my reservoir supplied air very deficient in oxygen. But I did not reckon on an accidental meeting, which delayed our arrival for some time.

I had remained some steps behind, when I presently saw Captain Nemo coming hurriedly towards me. With his strong hand he bent me to the ground, his companion doing the same to Conseil. At first I knew not what to think of this sudden attack, but I was soon reassured by seeing the Captain lie down beside me, and remain immovable.
I was stretched on the ground, just under the shelter of a bush of algæ, when, raising my head, I saw some enormous mass, casting phosphorescent gleams, pass blusteringly by.

My blood froze in my veins as I recognised two formidable sharks which threatened us. It was a couple of tintoreas, terrible creatures, with enormous tails and a dull glassy stare, the phosphorescent matter ejected from holes pierced around the muzzle. Monstrous brutes! which would crush a whole man in their iron jaws. I did not know whether Conseil stopped to classify them; for my part, I noticed their silver bellies, and their huge mouths bristling with teeth, from a very unscientific point of view, and more as a possible victim than as a naturalist.

Happily the voracious creatures do not see well. They passed without seeing us, brushing us with their brownish fins, and we escaped by a miracle from a danger certainly greater than meeting a tiger full-face in the forest. Half an hour after, guided by the electric light, we reached the _Nautilus_. The outside door had been left open, and Captain Nemo closed it as soon as we had entered the first cell. He then pressed a knob. I heard the pumps working in the midst of the vessel, I felt the water sinking from around me, and in a few moments the cell was entirely empty. The inside door then opened, and we entered the vestry.

There our diving-dress was taken off, not without some trouble; and, fairly worn out from want of food and sleep. I returned to my room, in great wonder at this surprising excursion at the bottom of the sea.
translated_paragraphs: 我们终于走到这片森林边缘。在尼摩船长的辽阔领地中，这无疑算得上最美的地方之一。他视森林为己有，相信自己对它享有的权利，同世界之初的先民享有的权利一样。说实话，谁会跑来跟他争这份海底产业？哪个更加勇敢的开拓者会手执斧头，来砍这些幽暗的树丛？
森林由树木般高大的水生植物组成。刚迈进那些巨大的拱廊，我就觉得它们枝条的姿态稀奇，先前没见过这样的。
地面的每一根草，树身的每一根枝，既无折曲，又无倾斜，也没有一枝一叶横向伸展，全都挺直了朝着海面。再细的一根丝，一条带，都像铁杆一样笔直。褐藻和藤蔓都沿着硬直的垂线生长，这是养育它们的水体的密度所致。静静不动，你要是用手扳向一边，它们立刻又回到原姿势。这里真是一个竖直的国度！
不久，我就像习惯四周较为幽暗的光线那样，习惯了这些奇异的姿态。森林的地面像铺满尖锐的石块，很难避开。这里的水下植物群显得十分完备，甚至比北极和热带的还丰富，那两处海里的草木并不这样繁多。有几分钟我不由自主地把属类搞混，将植形动物认成水草，将动物认成植物。可谁能不错认？在海底世界里，动物与植物挨得也太近了。
这些水草自行繁殖，水支撑并滋养着它们，也是它们生命的根本所在。多数没有寻常的叶片，抽出的长叶形态变化无穷，粉红、胭脂、翠绿、橄榄绿、浅褐和深褐，各有色阶。我看见扇面般张开的羽鳃，仿佛要兜住清风。这回见到的是活的，不像“鹦鹉螺号”的干标本。还有绯红的仙菜藻，长着可食嫩梢的海带和蕨状的牛尾藻，最高可达十五英尺；成丛的伞藻，梗越往上越粗；还有数不尽的别样海洋植物，全都没有花！
“多奇异的反常，多神妙的环境！”有位机敏的博物学家说过，“在这里，开花的是动物界，植物界反而不开花！”
无数这样的灌木长得像温带的乔木一样高。在它们潮湿的浓荫下，一丛丛活花结成真正的花灌木，植形动物排起篱笆，开着沟纹盘曲、带斑马纹的脑珊瑚，和黄黄的石竹珊瑚。那幻象还不止如此。蝇鱼像蜂鸟成群，在枝头之间飞来飞去。黄身而颌边竖刺的鱼、飞角鱼和松球鱼，从我们脚下刷地窜起，俨然一群受惊飞起的沙锥鸟。
走了约一小时，尼摩船长示意停步。对我来说，歇一歇倒也称心。我们在一蓬翼藻构成的凉亭下躺倒，翼藻狭长的叶片箭一般直指上方。
这会儿小歇，叫我觉得无比惬意，只缺一样，就是不能谈天。既不能开口，又不能答话，我便只能拿自己那颗大铜脑袋去挨挨康塞尔的铜脑袋。我看见这老实人的双眼因欢喜而发亮。为了表示称心，他穿着鼓满空气的胸甲晃动起身子，那模样真是天底下再滑稽不过。
这样走了四个钟头，肚子竟不觉得特别饿，我有些奇怪。我解释不了胃何以如此。代替饥饿而来的，是一股抵抗不住的睡意，潜水的人都会有这样的经历。隔着厚厚的玻璃，我的双眼不久就合上了，陷入沉沉酣睡，先前全凭着一路行走才没睡去。尼摩船长同他那健壮的伙伴早已横卧在水晶般清澈的水里，先给我们做了榜样。
我究竟沉睡了多久，自己无从判断，反正醒来时，太阳似乎已在向地平线落去。尼摩船长早已站起。我正要舒展四肢，没料到眼前出现个东西，把我一下子惊得跳起来。

离我几步远，一只高约三十八英寸的巨大海蜘蛛正斜着眼盯住我，作势要扑来。我的潜水服虽厚得足以抵御它的叮咬，我仍害怕得打了个寒噤。康塞尔和“鹦鹉螺号”的水手也在这时醒来。尼摩船长指一指这只丑恶的甲壳动物。枪托一击便将它翻倒，我看见那怪物吓人的爪子抽搐着扭成一团。这次小小的意外提醒我，这些幽暗深处可能还潜藏着比它更可怕的动物，潜水服也防不住它们的袭击。我先前从没想到这一点，如今打定主意要当心。我原以为休息以后便要结束这次散步，却弄错了。尼摩船长没有返回“鹦鹉螺号”，仍要继续他的大胆旅行。地面还是向下倾斜，坡势好像愈来愈陡，引我们往更深的地方走。到了两道高高的直壁之间一条狭谷时，想来已是三点左右。那儿位于七十五英寻深处。多亏了装备精良，我们已比大自然好像给人类海底出行划定的界限，还要多下去四十五英寻。
我说七十五英寻，手头其实没有测深仪器。不过我知道，即使在最清澈的水中，阳光能穿过的深度也到此为止。四周的确越来越黑了。十步以外，什么都看不见。我正摸索着往前，面前忽然亮起耀眼的白光。原来尼摩船长刚打开了电灯。他的同伴照做，康塞尔和我也跟着办。我一拧螺钮，导线便同螺旋形玻璃管接通了。四盏提灯一道发亮，海水中方圆三十六码都被照亮。
尼摩船长仍往森林的幽暗深处走，树木每一步都更稀少。我留意到植物的生命比动物更早消失。连水母也已离开了这片荒地，而许多别的动物，植形动物、分节动物、软体动物和鱼，仍能在这里取得养分。

我边走边想，鲁姆科夫灯这样明亮，怎会不把一两个居民从幽暗的卧处吸引出来？但即使它们来到近旁，也始终同猎手们保持着恭敬的距离。我好几次看到尼摩船长停下，把枪托举到肩上，过一会儿却又放下枪继续走。终于，约四小时后，这趟奇异的旅程到了尽头。面前耸着一堵雄伟的岩壁。巨石堆叠成壮观的整体，陡峭宽大的花岗岩岸凿出黑沉沉的洞窟，却没有一道能走上去的斜坡。这是托起克雷斯波岛的根基。这就是陆地！尼摩船长猛然停步，一打手势，我们便全停下了。尽管我很想攀上那道岩墙，也只能止步。尼摩船长的领地到此为止，他不肯越界。再朝前一步，就是地球上他不愿涉足的那一部分。

我们开始往回走。尼摩船长重新走在小队前面，辨起方向毫不迟疑。我觉得我们返回“鹦鹉螺号”走的不是原路。这条新路十分陡峭，走起来也就十分吃力。我们很快接近水面，却不至于返回上层太快，造成压力骤减。突然减压可能使身体出现严重紊乱，造成潜水人往往致命的内伤。天光不久又重新出现，越来越亮。太阳已在地平线上低垂，光线一折，种种物体的边缘都被镶上一圈彩晕。到了十码半深处，我们行走在一群形形色色的小鱼中间，数量比飞鸟多，动作也比它们敏捷。可值得开上一枪的水中猎物还没露面。忽然我看见船长飞快地举枪抵肩，枪口跟着一个移动的东西没入灌木。他扣下扳机。我只听见轻轻的一声咝响，离我们不远就有个生物应声昏倒。那是一只漂亮的海獭，唯一全在海里生活的四足兽。这只海獭长五英尺，一定值不少钱。它背上栗褐，肚腹银白，一身皮毛正是俄国和中国市场上争相求购的那种好裘皮。光凭毛的细密和光泽，就准卖得到八十英镑。我欣赏着这头有趣的哺乳动物。圆圆的头上点着两只短耳朵，圆眼，猫一样的白胡须，脚趾间有蹼，趾端有爪，尾上毛绒绒的。渔人捕猎追踪这种贵重动物，如今海獭已十分罕见，多半退避到北太平洋，否则恐怕不久整个族类便要灭绝。
尼摩船长的同伴揪起猎物，往肩上一扔，我们继续前行。有一小时之久，前面铺着一片沙地平原。有些地方地面升得离水面只剩两码又几英寸。那时我清楚看见我们的身影倒映在上方，完全相同的一群人，重复着我们的动作、我们的姿态，样样相同，只是他们行走时脑袋朝下，双脚冲着上空。
我还留意到另一种景象，一团团厚云迅速形成，又迅速消散。想了想才明白，这些看似云团的东西，原来是底下苇草的疏密变化造成的。我甚至还能看见折断的顶部在水面上激起絮状泡沫，又能看见大鸟从我们头顶飞过的影子，透过海面辨出它们迅疾的飞行。
就在这时候，我目睹了足以使任何猎手浑身激动的一发好枪。一只双翼展开极宽的大鸟清清楚楚地盘旋飞近。“鹦鹉螺号”上那位水手举枪抵肩，在它离浪尖不过几码时开了火。大鸟被击昏，一头坠下，跌落的冲力把它送到了这位身手灵巧的猎人手里。那是一只品相极好的信天翁。
这桩事没耽搁脚步。我们沿沙原又走了两个小时，随后穿过几片很难行走的海藻田。老实说，我已经再也走不动，恰好望见一道微光，照破了半英里的黑水。是“鹦鹉螺号”的灯！不到二十分钟我们就能上船，我也能重新舒舒服服呼吸。眼下我的储气罐送来的空气，仿佛已经相当缺氧。可我没有料到，一场偶然的相遇会将抵达的时刻又推迟一阵。
我落在后面几步，忽见尼摩船长匆匆朝我走来，用一只有力的大手将我按倒在地。他的同伴也对康塞尔这样做。起初我不明白怎么会突遭袭击，接着见船长也在我身边躺下，一动不动，才放了心。
我伸开身子趴在地上，刚好藏在一丛海藻底下。一抬头，我看见一大团庞然黑影放着磷光，气势汹汹地掠过。
我认出了威胁我们的，是两条可怕的鲨鱼，血都凝住了。这是一对大青鲨，凶相可怖，尾巴巨大，呆板的眼珠像玻璃，吻部周围密布的小孔里还放出磷光。好一对凶兽！那副铁钳般的颌骨，能把整个人都碾碎。我不知道康塞尔有没有停下来给它们分类。至于我，对着它们银色的肚皮和布满尖牙的巨口，持的可不是怎么科学的眼光。我当时是个险遭吞食的人，远远胜过一个博物学家。
幸亏那些贪食的东西目力不佳。它们没看见我们，褐色的鱼鳍擦过我们就游走了。我们奇迹般逃过的危险，分明比在林中迎面撞见一头老虎更甚。半小时以后，循着电光的指引，我们回到了“鹦鹉螺号”。外门原是敞着的，我们刚进第一间小舱，尼摩船长就把它关严。他摁了一颗按钮，我听见船中部的泵开始工作，觉得身旁的水渐渐退下，转眼间小舱已经排空。内门随之打开，我们走进了更衣室。
在那里，别人颇费了些力气才替我们脱掉潜水服。我又饿又困，彻底累坏了，回到自己的房间。这次惊奇的海底远足，仍叫我久久出神。

sections.title_zh: 上部 / 第17章　在太平洋下四千里格
sections.title_en: PART ONE / CHAPTER XVII — FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
