“Have you no need of my services, sir?”
“No, my friend. What is Ned Land doing?”
“If you will excuse me, sir,” answered Conseil, “friend Ned is busy making a kangaroo-pie which will be a marvel.”

I remained alone and went to bed, but slept indifferently. I heard the noise of the savages, who stamped on the platform, uttering deafening cries. The night passed thus, without disturbing the ordinary repose of the crew. The presence of these cannibals affected them no more than the soldiers of a masked battery care for the ants that crawl over its front.

At six in the morning I rose. The hatches had not been opened. The inner air was not renewed, but the reservoirs, filled ready for any emergency, were now resorted to, and discharged several cubic feet of oxygen into the exhausted atmosphere of the _Nautilus_.
I worked in my room till noon, without having seen Captain Nemo, even for an instant. On board no preparations for departure were visible.

I waited still some time, then went into the large saloon. The clock marked half-past two. In ten minutes it would be high-tide: and, if Captain Nemo had not made a rash promise, the _Nautilus_ would be immediately detached. If not, many months would pass ere she could leave her bed of coral.
However, some warning vibrations began to be felt in the vessel. I heard the keel grating against the rough calcareous bottom of the coral reef.
At five-and-twenty minutes to three, Captain Nemo appeared in the saloon.
“We are going to start,” said he.
“Ah!” replied I.
“I have given the order to open the hatches.”
“And the Papuans?”
“The Papuans?” answered Captain Nemo, slightly shrugging his shoulders.
“Will they not come inside the _Nautilus?_”
“How?”
“Only by leaping over the hatches you have opened.”
“M. Aronnax,” quietly answered Captain Nemo, “they will not enter the hatches of the _Nautilus_ in that way, even if they were open.”
I looked at the Captain.
“You do not understand?” said he.
“Hardly.”
“Well, come and you will see.”

I directed my steps towards the central staircase. There Ned Land and Conseil were slyly watching some of the ship’s crew, who were opening the hatches, while cries of rage and fearful vociferations resounded outside.

The port lids were pulled down outside. Twenty horrible faces appeared. But the first native who placed his hand on the stair-rail, struck from behind by some invisible force, I know not what, fled, uttering the most fearful cries and making the wildest contortions.
Ten of his companions followed him. They met with the same fate.
Conseil was in ecstasy. Ned Land, carried away by his violent instincts, rushed on to the staircase. But the moment he seized the rail with both hands, he, in his turn, was overthrown.
“I am struck by a thunderbolt,” cried he, with an oath.

This explained all. It was no rail; but a metallic cable charged with electricity from the deck communicating with the platform. Whoever touched it felt a powerful shock—and this shock would have been mortal if Captain Nemo had discharged into the conductor the whole force of the current. It might truly be said that between his assailants and himself he had stretched a network of electricity which none could pass with impunity.
Meanwhile, the exasperated Papuans had beaten a retreat paralysed with terror. As for us, half laughing, we consoled and rubbed the unfortunate Ned Land, who swore like one possessed.

But at this moment the _Nautilus_, raised by the last waves of the tide, quitted her coral bed exactly at the fortieth minute fixed by the Captain. Her screw swept the waters slowly and majestically. Her speed increased gradually, and, sailing on the surface of the ocean, she quitted safe and sound the dangerous passes of the Straits of Torres.
translated_paragraphs: 我们没有起身，一齐望向林边。我那只正要把食物送进嘴的手停在半空，尼德·兰德的那只手倒把该办的事办完了。
“石头是不会从天上掉下来的，”康塞尔说，“要是从天上掉下来，它们就配叫陨石了。”
第二块石头瞄得很准，把康塞尔手里一只鲜香的鸽腿打落，更给他这番议论添了分量。我们三个一齐站起，将枪抵上肩膀，准备还击任何进攻。
“是猿猴吗？”尼德·兰德叫道。
“差一点儿——是野人。”
“回小艇去！”我说着，匆匆往海边奔。
的确有必要退走了。在我们右手遮住天际的一片树林边缘，出现了二十来个岛民，拿着弓和投石索，离我们勉强一百步。
小艇系在距我们约六十英尺的地方。岛民们逼上来，步子倒不跑，却做着敌对的手势。石头和箭雨点似的落下。
尼德·兰德舍不得丢下补给，尽管危险迫近，他一边带着野猪，一边带着袋鼠，居然跑得还挺快。两分钟后我们便到了岸边。将食物和武器装艇，推艇下海，安好桨，只是一眨眼的事。没划出两链远，就有百来个岛民叫喊着、挥手顿足，蹚进齐腰的水中。我注视着“鹦鹉螺号”，想看看他们的出现会不会引几个船员到平台上来。并没有。那具庞大的机器停在不远处，空无一人。
二十分钟后，我们上了船。舱口开着。我们把小艇系牢，进入“鹦鹉螺号”内部。
我走下客厅，那里传来几个和弦。尼摩船长正在里面，俯身对着管风琴，沉醉在音乐的狂喜里。
“船长！”
他没听见。
“船长！”我轻触他的手，又唤了一声。
他一震，转过身来，说道：“啊，是您，教授！那么，狩猎顺利吗？采集植物也有收获吗？”
“是的，船长。可不幸的是，我们还招来一大群两足动物。他们就在近处，实在令我不安。”
“什么两足动物？”
“野人。”
“野人！”他带着讽意重复道，“这么说，教授，您踏上别人的土地，遇见了所谓野人，自己倒大感惊奇？野人！世上哪里没有？再说，您嘴里这些‘野人’，当真比别的人坏吗？”
“可是船长——”
“您数到了多少个？”
“至少一百。”
“阿龙纳斯先生，”尼摩船长把手指放回管风琴的音栓上，回答道，“便是全巴布亚的居民都聚到这段岸上，‘鹦鹉螺号’也不必怕他们的攻击。”

船长的手指随即在键盘上流动起来。我注意到他只碰黑键，弹出的旋律因此带着鲜明的苏格兰意味。过不多时，他又忘了我在这里，独自陷入遐想，我没有去打扰。我重新登上平台，夜幕已经降临。在这低纬度地带，太阳落得快，几乎没有暮色的过渡。我只能依稀望见小岛，但海滩上点起的许多火堆，足可见岛民并没有离开的打算。我独自待了几个钟头，有时想想岛民，倒并不怕他们，因为船长那不可动摇的信心会传染；有时又忘记了他们，转而欣赏热带的壮丽夜色。我的思念随那些黄道上的星辰飞向法国，再过几个钟头，它们便会照耀在那里。月亮正亮在天顶的众星之间。
一夜过去，平安无事。岛民们看到海湾里搁着一头怪物，大概也有些害怕。舱口一直敞着，谁想进入“鹦鹉螺号”内部，原是很容易的。
一月八日清晨六点，我又登上平台。天光初现，雾气正在消散。小岛渐渐显露出来，先是岸，再是高处的山峰。

岛民们还在那里，人数比前一天更众，约有五六百个。有人趁着低潮走上礁面，距“鹦鹉螺号”不足两链。我能清楚分辨他们的外貌。他们确是巴布亚人，体格矫健，身材雄健，额头高而开阔，五官大而不显扁平，一口白牙。卷曲的头发微微泛红，衬着乌黑发亮的身体，让人想起努比亚人。耳垂穿了孔，拉长了，挂着一串串骨饰。多数人不穿衣服。我看到几个女子从胯部到膝头穿着一圈向外蓬开的草裙，用植物纤维的腰带束着。有些首领在颈上挂了月牙饰物和红白玻璃珠串。几乎人人都有弓、箭和盾，肩上还背一只网袋，装着圆石，好用投石索娴熟地抛出。一个离“鹦鹉螺号”较近的首领正在细细察看它。他也许是一位地位很高的“马多”，因为他披着香蕉叶编的席衣，边缘剪成锯齿，又缀有鲜艳的颜色。
他就在近处，我要开枪，轻而易举便能把人放倒。不过我想，还是等真有敌对行动再说。欧洲人同他们称作野人的人相遇，该做的是敏捷防卫，不能先行攻击。
低潮时，岛民们在“鹦鹉螺号”附近往来，没有惹事。我听他们常常重复“阿赛”一词。从手势看，应是在邀我上岸。这份邀请我谢绝了。
于是那天小艇没有离船，这很叫兰德师傅扫兴。他没法把自己的口粮补足了。

这位多才多艺的加拿大人便把时间花在料理从岛上带回来的肉食上。至于岛民，上午十一点左右，潮水上涨，珊瑚礁尖开始重新没入水下，他们就退回岸边去了。可我看得见，岸边聚的人已增加许多。也许从邻岛赶来，很可能甚至从巴布亚赶来。不过我始终没见到一条本地独木舟。闲来无事，我便想在这片美丽清澈的海水里拖一网。底下明明可见成群的贝壳、植形动物和海生植物。何况如果尼摩船长说话算数，明天能重浮外海，这就是“鹦鹉螺号”在此停留的最后一天。
我于是叫来康塞尔，他给我拿了一具轻便的小拖具，很像采牡蛎用的那种。动手吧！我们不间断地捞了两小时，却没见着什么珍品。拖网上满是迈达斯耳螺、竖琴螺、川蜷之类，尤其有几只槌蛤，比我见过的哪一只都漂亮。我们还捞到几只海蛞蝓、几只珠母贝、十二只小海龟，后者留下来送进船上食品储藏室。
偏在我最不抱指望的时候，我摸到了一件奇物，也可以说是一件极少遇到的天然畸形。康塞尔正在起网，网里装着各色寻常贝壳，忽见我手臂迅速探进网中，拿出一枚螺壳，又听见我喊了一声。
“先生，怎么了？”他惊奇地问，“是先生被咬着了吗？”
“不，孩子。不过为了这个发现，我就是拿一根指头来换也甘心。”
“什么发现？”
“这枚螺壳。”我举起战利品给他看。
“不过是一枚斑纹榧螺，榧螺属，栉鳃目，腹足纲，软体动物类。”
“对，康塞尔。可是别的从右向左旋绕，这枚榧螺却是从左向右旋的。”
“有这种事？”
“是的，孩子，这是一枚左旋螺。”
螺壳几乎全是右旋，例外极少。要是偶然长出向左的螺纹，鉴赏家便甘愿拿跟它等重的黄金来换。
我和康塞尔专心欣赏这件珍宝。我正在心里盘算，这可要给博物馆的收藏增添光彩，偏有个岛民掷出的石头不巧击中康塞尔手里的珍物，将它打碎。我绝望地叫了一声！康塞尔提枪瞄准，在十码外，一个岛民正扬着投石索。我本想拦他，枪却已打响，击断了那人臂上由护身符串成的镯子。
图注　康塞尔一把抓起他的枪
“康塞尔！”我大喊，“康塞尔！”
“怎么，先生！先生没看见，那个食人者已经先动手了吗？”
“一枚螺壳抵不上一个人的命。”我说。
“啊，这个混账！”康塞尔叫道，“我倒宁愿他打碎的是我的肩膀！”

康塞尔是认真的，我却不赞同他。再说，几分钟以来情形有了变化，我们都没留意。约二十条独木舟围住了“鹦鹉螺号”。每一条都从整根树干凿出，又狭又长，极适于快行。旁边系着长竹竿浮在水上，借来保持平衡。划船的好手们半裸着身子。我不免有些不安地看他们渐渐迫近。这些巴布亚人显然早跟欧洲人打过交道，认得他们的船。可是停在水湾中的这个铁圆筒，既没有桅杆，也没有烟囱，他们能把它当作什么？多半不是什么好东西，所以开头还保持着相当远的距离。可见它始终不动，他们渐渐壮了胆，想跟它混熟一些。偏偏眼下得避免的，就是这种亲近。我们的武器没有声响，对于这些不大惧怕无声威势的岛民，作用想来有限。闪电若不带雷声，人们不会太怕它，虽然危险实在是电光带来的，不是那声响。
这时独木舟又向“鹦鹉螺号”靠近，一阵箭雨落在船身上。
我下到客厅，却没见到人。我大着胆子敲了敲那扇通往船长卧舱的门。“进来。”里面答道。
我进了门，发现尼摩船长正沉浸在关于未知数x和其他变量的代数推算之中。
“打扰您了。”我礼貌地说。
“这倒是真的，阿龙纳斯先生，”船长答道，“不过我想，您要见我，必定有紧要的原因？”
“十分紧要。岛民们划独木舟把我们围住了。再过几分钟，势必有好几百人向我们发动进攻。”
“啊！”尼摩船长安安静静地说，“他们乘独木舟来了？”
“是的，先生。”
“好，先生，那就只须关闭舱口。”
“正是，我来就是想告诉您——”
“再简单不过的事。”尼摩船长说。他按下一颗电钮，将一道命令传给船员。
“全办妥了，先生，”过了片刻，他说，“小艇已就位，舱口已关闭。您总不至于担心，这些先生能撞开连贵舰炮弹都无可奈何的船壁吧？”
“不，船长。不过仍有一项危险。”
“是哪一项，先生？”
“明天约莫这个时候，我们势必要打开舱口，给‘鹦鹉螺号’换气。假如到那时巴布亚人已占着平台，我可看不出您怎么拦得住他们进来。”
“那么，先生，您以为他们会登船？”
“我确信如此。”
“好，先生，那就让他们来吧。我看不出有何理由阻拦。说到底，这些巴布亚人也是些可怜的人。我不愿意他们里面任何一个不幸者，因我来访此岛便丢了性命。”
说到这里，我正想告退，尼摩船长却留住我，请我在他身旁坐下。他兴致盎然地询问我们上岸的见闻、打猎的情形，对于攫住加拿大人的那股想吃肉的渴望，却似乎怎么也不理解。随后我们谈及各种话题。尼摩船长没有比平常更愿意谈自己的事，人倒和蔼了许多。
闲谈间，说到“鹦鹉螺号”眼下的处境，正好在这道海峡里迪蒙·迪维尔曾经险些遇难的地方搁浅。他就此说起：
“这位迪维尔，是你们的一位伟大海员，”船长对我说，“是你们最聪明的航海家之一，法国人的库克船长。可怜的科学家，曾经迎战南极的冰山、大洋洲的珊瑚礁、太平洋的食人者，末了却凄惨地死在铁路列车中！这位精力过人的人，要是在生命的最后片刻还能思索，您猜，最后占据他心头的会是什么？”
尼摩船长这么说着，仿佛动了感情。他的感动也使我对他添了几分好感。随后我们手拿海图，重温这位法国航海家的行程，他环绕世界的几次航行，两度在南极一带停留，由此发现阿德莱德地和路易－菲利普地，以及他如何测定大洋洲主要岛屿的水文方位。
“你们的迪维尔在海面上办到的，”尼摩船长说，“我在海底也一一办到了，做起来比他更轻松，也更彻底。‘星盘号’和‘热忱号’无时无刻不在飓风中颠簸，哪里比得上‘鹦鹉螺号’这处清静的工作之所。它在海水中央，真正做得到纹丝不动。
“明天，”船长一边起身一边加上一句，“明天下午两点四十分，‘鹦鹉螺号’就会浮起，毫发无损地离开托雷斯海峡。”
尼摩船长简短说过这几句，微微欠身。这是示意我可以去了。我便回了自己的房间。
我在房里见到康塞尔，他想知道我这回见船长，结果如何。
“孩子，”我说，“我装作深信巴布亚人对他的‘鹦鹉螺号’构成了威胁，船长的答复就很挖苦。我只跟你说一句，信任他，安心去睡。”
“先生没有别的事吩咐吗？”
“没有，朋友。尼德·兰德在做什么？”
“恕我说一句，先生，”康塞尔回答，“尼德朋友正忙着做一张袋鼠肉馅饼，成了一定是件珍品。”
我独自留下，就寝，却睡得不怎么样。岛民在平台上跺脚，发出震耳的呼喊，我听得清清楚楚。一夜这样过去，并没打扰船员们惯常的安眠。这些被称作食人者的人站在头顶之上，他们一点不在意，如同隐蔽炮台的兵士不在意沿胸墙爬过的蚂蚁。
我清早六点起身。舱口还没打开，里面的空气没有换过，不过储气罐为了应急本已灌满，此时便启用，向“鹦鹉螺号”渐渐污浊的空气中释放了好几立方英尺的氧气。
我在房间里工作到正午，一次也没见到尼摩船长。船上看不出有任何出发的准备。
我又等了一会儿才去大客厅。钟面指着两点半。十分钟以后，潮将涨到最高。如果尼摩船长不曾轻率许诺，“鹦鹉螺号”立刻就该脱困。否则，要脱离这张珊瑚床，不知还得过多少个月。
不过船里已开始有预告性的微微颤动传来。我听见龙骨在珊瑚礁粗糙的石灰质表面上磨擦作响。
差二十五分三点时，尼摩船长出现在客厅。
“我们就要动身了。”他说。
“啊！”我答道。
“我已经下令打开舱口。”
“那么巴布亚人呢？”
“巴布亚人？”尼摩船长略耸了一下肩膀。
“他们不会闯进‘鹦鹉螺号’吗？”
“怎样闯？”
“从您打开的舱口跳进来就行。”
“阿龙纳斯先生，”尼摩船长镇定地答道，“即便舱口开着，他们也不能那样进入‘鹦鹉螺号’。”
我望着船长。
“您还不明白？”他问。
“不大明白。”
“好，来亲眼看看吧。”
我走向中央阶梯。尼德·兰德和康塞尔正偷偷观察着几名船员打开舱口。外头则响彻了愤怒的呼啸和吓人的叫嚷。
舱盖向外翻开，露出二十张面目狰狞的脸。可是头一个把手搭上楼梯扶栏的岛民，仿佛突然从背后挨了一股无形力量的一击，究竟是什么我还说不上，便发出凄厉至极的叫声，整个身子剧烈扭曲着逃走了。
十个同伴跟在他后头，遭遇了同样的命运。
康塞尔看得出神。尼德·兰德的冲动又占了上风，直冲向楼梯。可他双手刚一抓住扶栏，这回便轮到他摔个仰面朝天。
“我叫雷劈了！”他狠狠骂了一句，叫道。
一切都有了解释。那不是寻常扶栏，而是一条通向平台的金属缆索，船内已经给它通上电流。谁碰到它，都会受到强烈的电击。倘若尼摩船长把全部电流都放进这导体，电击就足以致命。确实可以说，他在来犯者与自己之间张起了一面电网，谁想闯过都要吃苦头。
这当儿，原先怒气冲冲的巴布亚人已经吓得手脚发僵，纷纷退走了。我们则半笑着安慰不幸的尼德·兰德，帮他揉搓挨了电击的地方。他还在发疯似的骂个不停。
可就在此刻，涨潮的最后几道波浪托起了“鹦鹉螺号”。分针恰好指到船长算定的四十分，它便脱离了珊瑚的卧床。螺旋桨缓慢而威严地划开海水，速度渐渐加快，船在洋面上行驶，平安无恙地穿出了托雷斯海峡的危险水道。

sections.title_en: PART ONE / CHAPTER XXII — “ÆGRI SOMNIA”
source_paragraphs: The following day 10th January, the _Nautilus_ continued her course between two seas, but with such remarkable speed that I could not estimate it at less than thirty-five miles an hour. The rapidity of her screw was such that I could neither follow nor count its revolutions. When I reflected that this marvellous electric agent, after having afforded motion, heat, and light to the _Nautilus_, still protected her from outward attack, and transformed her into an ark of safety which no profane hand might touch without being thunderstricken, my admiration was unbounded, and from the structure it extended to the engineer who had called it into existence.

Our course was directed to the west, and on the 11th of January we doubled Cape Wessel, situation in 135° long. and 10° north lat., which forms the east point of the Gulf of Carpentaria. The reefs were still numerous, but more equalised, and marked on the chart with extreme precision. The _Nautilus_ easily avoided the breakers of Money to port and the Victoria reefs to starboard, placed at 130° long. and on the 10th parallel, which we strictly followed.
On the 13th of January, Captain Nemo arrived in the Sea of Timor, and recognised the island of that name in 122° long.

From this point the direction of the _Nautilus_ inclined towards the south-west. Her head was set for the Indian Ocean. Where would the fancy of Captain Nemo carry us next? Would he return to the coast of Asia or would he approach again the shores of Europe? Improbable conjectures both, to a man who fled from inhabited continents. Then would he descend to the south? Was he going to double the Cape of Good Hope, then Cape Horn, and finally go as far as the Antarctic pole? Would he come back at last to the Pacific, where his _Nautilus_ could sail free and independently? Time would show.

After having skirted the sands of Cartier, of Hibernia, Seringapatam, and Scott, last efforts of the solid against the liquid element, on the 14th of January we lost sight of land altogether. The speed of the _Nautilus_ was considerably abated, and with irregular course she sometimes swam in the bosom of the waters, sometimes floated on their surface.

During this period of the voyage, Captain Nemo made some interesting experiments on the varied temperature of the sea, in different beds. Under ordinary conditions these observations are made by means of rather complicated instruments, and with somewhat doubtful results, by means of thermometrical sounding-leads, the glasses often breaking under the pressure of the water, or an apparatus grounded on the variations of the resistance of metals to the electric currents. Results so obtained could not be correctly calculated. On the contrary, Captain Nemo went himself to test the temperature in the depths of the sea, and his thermometer, placed in communication with the different sheets of water, gave him the required degree immediately and accurately.

It was thus that, either by overloading her reservoirs or by descending obliquely by means of her inclined planes, the _Nautilus_ successively attained the depth of three, four, five, seven, nine, and ten thousand yards, and the definite result of this experience was that the sea preserved an average temperature of four degrees and a half at a depth of five thousand fathoms under all latitudes.

On the 16th of January, the _Nautilus_ seemed becalmed only a few yards beneath the surface of the waves. Her electric apparatus remained inactive and her motionless screw left her to drift at the mercy of the currents. I supposed that the crew was occupied with interior repairs, rendered necessary by the violence of the mechanical movements of the machine.

My companions and I then witnessed a curious spectacle. The hatches of the saloon were open, and, as the beacon light of the _Nautilus_ was not in action, a dim obscurity reigned in the midst of the waters. I observed the state of the sea, under these conditions, and the largest fish appeared to me no more than scarcely defined shadows, when the _Nautilus_ found herself suddenly transported into full light. I thought at first that the beacon had been lighted, and was casting its electric radiance into the liquid mass. I was mistaken, and after a rapid survey perceived my error.

The _Nautilus_ floated in the midst of a phosphorescent bed which, in this obscurity, became quite dazzling. It was produced by myriads of luminous animalculae, whose brilliancy was increased as they glided over the metallic hull of the vessel. I was surprised by lightning in the midst of these luminous sheets, as though they had been rivulets of lead melted in an ardent furnace or metallic masses brought to a white heat, so that, by force of contrast, certain portions of light appeared to cast a shade in the midst of the general ignition, from which all shade seemed banished. No; this was not the calm irradiation of our ordinary lightning. There was unusual life and vigour: this was truly living light!

In reality, it was an infinite agglomeration of coloured infusoria, of veritable globules of jelly, provided with a threadlike tentacle, and of which as many as twenty-five thousand have been counted in less than two cubic half-inches of water.

During several hours the _Nautilus_ floated in these brilliant waves, and our admiration increased as we watched the marine monsters disporting themselves like salamanders. I saw there in the midst of this fire that burns not the swift and elegant porpoise (the indefatigable clown of the ocean), and some swordfish ten feet long, those prophetic heralds of the hurricane whose formidable sword would now and then strike the glass of the saloon. Then appeared the smaller fish, the balista, the leaping mackerel, wolf-thorn-tails, and a hundred others which striped the luminous atmosphere as they swam. This dazzling spectacle was enchanting! Perhaps some atmospheric condition increased the intensity of this phenomenon. Perhaps some storm agitated the surface of the waves. But at this depth of some yards, the _Nautilus_ was unmoved by its fury and reposed peacefully in still water.

So we progressed, incessantly charmed by some new marvel. The days passed rapidly away, and I took no account of them. Ned, according to habit, tried to vary the diet on board. Like snails, we were fixed to our shells, and I declare it is easy to lead a snail’s life.
Thus this life seemed easy and natural, and we thought no longer of the life we led on land; but something happened to recall us to the strangeness of our situation.

On the 18th of January, the _Nautilus_ was in 105° long. and 15° S. lat. The weather was threatening, the sea rough and rolling. There was a strong east wind. The barometer, which had been going down for some days, foreboded a coming storm. I went up on to the platform just as the second lieutenant was taking the measure of the horary angles, and waited, according to habit till the daily phrase was said. But on this day it was exchanged for another phrase not less incomprehensible. Almost directly, I saw Captain Nemo appear with a glass, looking towards the horizon.

For some minutes he was immovable, without taking his eye off the point of observation. Then he lowered his glass and exchanged a few words with his lieutenant. The latter seemed to be a victim to some emotion that he tried in vain to repress. Captain Nemo, having more command over himself, was cool. He seemed, too, to be making some objections to which the lieutenant replied by formal assurances. At least I concluded so by the difference of their tones and gestures. For myself, I had looked carefully in the direction indicated without seeing anything. The sky and water were lost in the clear line of the horizon.

However, Captain Nemo walked from one end of the platform to the other, without looking at me, perhaps without seeing me. His step was firm, but less regular than usual. He stopped sometimes, crossed his arms, and observed the sea. What could he be looking for on that immense expanse?
The _Nautilus_ was then some hundreds of miles from the nearest coast.

The lieutenant had taken up the glass and examined the horizon steadfastly, going and coming, stamping his foot and showing more nervous agitation than his superior officer. Besides, this mystery must necessarily be solved, and before long; for, upon an order from Captain Nemo, the engine, increasing its propelling power, made the screw turn more rapidly.

Just then the lieutenant drew the Captain’s attention again. The latter stopped walking and directed his glass towards the place indicated. He looked long. I felt very much puzzled, and descended to the drawing-room, and took out an excellent telescope that I generally used. Then, leaning on the cage of the watch-light that jutted out from the front of the platform, set myself to look over all the line of the sky and sea.
But my eye was no sooner applied to the glass than it was quickly snatched out of my hands.

I turned round. Captain Nemo was before me, but I did not know him. His face was transfigured. His eyes flashed sullenly; his teeth were set; his stiff body, clenched fists, and head shrunk between his shoulders, betrayed the violent agitation that pervaded his whole frame. He did not move. My glass, fallen from his hands, had rolled at his feet.

Had I unwittingly provoked this fit of anger? Did this incomprehensible person imagine that I had discovered some forbidden secret? No; I was not the object of this hatred, for he was not looking at me; his eye was steadily fixed upon the impenetrable point of the horizon. At last Captain Nemo recovered himself. His agitation subsided. He addressed some words in a foreign language to his lieutenant, then turned to me. “M. Aronnax,” he said, in rather an imperious tone, “I require you to keep one of the conditions that bind you to me.”
“What is it, Captain?”
“You must be confined, with your companions, until I think fit to release you.”
“You are the master,” I replied, looking steadily at him. “But may I ask you one question?”
“None, sir.”

There was no resisting this imperious command, it would have been useless. I went down to the cabin occupied by Ned Land and Conseil, and told them the Captain’s determination. You may judge how this communication was received by the Canadian.
But there was not time for altercation. Four of the crew waited at the door, and conducted us to that cell where we had passed our first night on board the _Nautilus_.
Ned Land would have remonstrated, but the door was shut upon him.
“Will master tell me what this means?” asked Conseil.
I told my companions what had passed. They were as much astonished as I, and equally at a loss how to account for it.

Meanwhile, I was absorbed in my own reflections, and could think of nothing but the strange fear depicted in the Captain’s countenance. I was utterly at a loss to account for it, when my cogitations were disturbed by these words from Ned Land:
“Hallo! breakfast is ready.”
And indeed the table was laid. Evidently Captain Nemo had given this order at the same time that he had hastened the speed of the _Nautilus_.
“Will master permit me to make a recommendation?” asked Conseil.
“Yes, my boy.”
“Well, it is that master breakfasts. It is prudent, for we do not know what may happen.”
“You are right, Conseil.”
“Unfortunately,” said Ned Land, “they have only given us the ship’s fare.”
“Friend Ned,” asked Conseil, “what would you have said if the breakfast had been entirely forgotten?”
This argument cut short the harpooner’s recriminations.
We sat down to table. The meal was eaten in silence.

Just then the luminous globe that lighted the cell went out, and left us in total darkness. Ned Land was soon asleep, and what astonished me was that Conseil went off into a heavy slumber. I was thinking what could have caused his irresistible drowsiness, when I felt my brain becoming stupefied. In spite of my efforts to keep my eyes open, they would close. A painful suspicion seized me. Evidently soporific substances had been mixed with the food we had just taken. Imprisonment was not enough to conceal Captain Nemo’s projects from us, sleep was more necessary. I then heard the panels shut. The undulations of the sea, which caused a slight rolling motion, ceased. Had the _Nautilus_ quitted the surface of the ocean? Had it gone back to the motionless bed of water? I tried to resist sleep. It was impossible. My breathing grew weak. I felt a mortal cold freeze my stiffened and half-paralysed limbs. My eyelids, like leaden caps, fell over my eyes. I could not raise them; a morbid sleep, full of hallucinations, bereft me of my being. Then the visions disappeared, and left me in complete insensibility.
translated_paragraphs: 次日，一月十日，“鹦鹉螺号”继续在水层之间穿行，速度非凡，依我估计，不会低于每小时三十五英里。螺旋桨旋转之快，我的眼睛既跟不上，也数不清。每想到电这种奇妙的动力，在给“鹦鹉螺号”供了推动力、热和光以后，竟还能防范外部的侵袭，把它变成一艘安全方舟，哪只妄加冒犯的手一碰就要受雷击，我的钦佩便无止境。赞叹既从这项造物而起，也自然转向了使它得以诞生的工程师。
航向往西。一月十一日，我们绕过韦塞尔角，位置是经度一百三十五度、北纬十度，构成卡奔塔利亚湾的东端。礁石仍然很多，不过分布较为整齐，海图上标示得极为精确。“鹦鹉螺号”轻易避开左舷莫尼礁的碎浪和右舷维多利亚礁。这些礁位于经度一百三十度、第十纬线上，而我们始终贴着这一纬线航行。
一月十三日，尼摩船长驶入帝汶海，在经度一百二十二度处辨出了同名的帝汶岛。
从这里起，“鹦鹉螺号”的航向渐渐转往西南。船首朝着印度洋。尼摩船长的兴致接下来又会带我们往哪里去？他要回到亚洲海岸吗？还是会重新接近欧洲的岸边？对一个愿意逃开有人居住的大陆的人而言，这两种猜想都不大可信。那么他要继续南下？他是否打算绕过好望角，再绕过合恩角，末了一直驶到南极？还是终将回到“鹦鹉螺号”能够自由自在航行的太平洋来？只有时间会告诉我们。
我们依次擦过卡蒂埃、海伯尼亚、塞林加帕坦和斯科特的几道沙洲。这是固体对无边水域所作的最后几次抗争。一月十四日，陆地终于从视野里完全消失。“鹦鹉螺号”的速度大大减缓，航线也不再固定，时而游在水的怀抱里，时而漂在水面上。
这段航程中，尼摩船长针对海洋不同水层的温度变化，作过一些有趣的实验。在通常条件下，人们得借助相当复杂的仪器来做这种观测，结果又颇可疑。要么用附温度计的测深铅锤，可玻璃常被水压挤碎，要么依靠利用金属电阻变化制成的仪器，所得读数难以准确推算。尼摩船长则不然。他亲自潜入深海测温。他的温度计和不同的水层直接接触，所求温度便立即准确可得。
就这样，“鹦鹉螺号”或是给储水舱多加些水，或是依靠倾斜舵板斜斜往下，陆续抵达三千、四千、五千、七千、九千及一万码深处。这一次试验得出了明确的结果：不拘什么纬度，海面下五千英寻处，海水的平均温度一律保持在四度半。
一月十六日，“鹦鹉螺号”似乎像遇到无风天的帆船一样停住了，距浪面不过几码。电力装置没有工作，螺旋桨一动不动，任船被洋流推着漂去。我猜船员们正在内部检修。机器运转得那样激烈，想来也到了该检修的时候。
这时，我和同伴们看见了一个奇特的景象。客厅两舷的护板已经打开，但“鹦鹉螺号”的探照灯没有点亮，海水中只有昏昏暗暗的一片。我正在这种条件下观察海况，连最大的鱼也只像些轮廓不清的影子。忽然，“鹦鹉螺号”整个进了明光之中。起初我以为探照灯已亮，正把电光投进水里。可我错了。迅速扫视一遍，就看出了先前的误判。

“鹦鹉螺号”漂浮在一层磷光之间，那光在暗处亮得耀眼。这是亿万个能发光的微小生物共同造成的。它们擦着金属船壳滑过时，光亮越加强烈。我又惊见这层层亮水中闪出电光一般的明灭，像灼热熔炉里流淌着一条条铅液的小溪，又像整块金属加热到白炽。明暗对比之强，使某些也是明亮的部分看起来竟似投下阴影，而在这片全面的燃烧之中，本该连一星阴影都没有的。不，这不是我们通常所见那种安稳的照耀。这里有不寻常的生命，有活力。这是真正活着的光！
实质上，这是无穷无尽、带着色彩的微生物的集合。一个个小球宛如胶冻，带一根丝线般的触手。在两小块边长半英寸的方水体所合的体积以内，就曾数出多达两万五千个。

好几个钟头，“鹦鹉螺号”都漂浮在这些辉煌的波浪之中。看着海洋巨物像传说中生在火里的火蜥蜴那般嬉游，我们愈加赞叹。在这不灼人的火焰里，我看见体态优雅而迅捷的鼠海豚，大海中不知疲倦的小丑；又看见几条十英尺长的箭鱼，那些预告飓风到来的先驱，用可怕的长剑不时敲上客厅的玻璃。随后，各种小鱼出现了：鳞鲀、飞跃的鲭鱼、带刺尾的鱼，还可再数出一百种，它们游过时，在发光的环境里划出一道道纹路。多么令人神往的耀眼奇观！或许当时的某种大气状况加深了现象的强度，也许海面正有风暴搅弄波浪。可是在这水下几码的深处，“鹦鹉螺号”不为风浪的怒气所动，在安静的水中安然休息。
就这样，我们不断前进，不断被新的奇迹吸引。日子飞快过去，我也不再计数。尼德照旧设法给船上的伙食换换花样。我们像蜗牛，紧紧附在自己的壳上。我敢说，当一只蜗牛，日子倒也好过。
这样的生活渐渐显得轻松而自然，我们已不再惦念岸上的生活。可是发生了一件事，使我们重新想起自己处境的古怪。
一月十八日，“鹦鹉螺号”在经度一百零五度、南纬十五度处。天气不祥，海浪粗暴翻滚，强劲的东风不停地吹。气压计接连几天往下降，预示一场风暴将至。我登上平台时，副手正在测量时角。我照习惯等他把每日那句话说完。可这次换了一句，同样听不懂。几乎立刻，我就看见尼摩船长带着望远镜出现，朝地平线张望。
他纹丝不动地站了几分钟，眼睛始终不离观察的目标。随后他放低望远镜，同副手交换几句话。副手仿佛受着某种情绪的摆布，尽力压制也压不住。尼摩船长比他更能作自己的主，面上仍冷静。他好像提出了几个异议，副手则用郑重的保证作答。至少从两人声调、手势的差别，我作了这样的推论。至于我自己，已经细细朝他们指的方向望过，什么也没看见。天和水在那道清晰的地平线上合而为一。
这时尼摩船长从平台这头走到那头，始终没有望我，或许压根没看见我。他的脚步有力，却不如平日均匀。他有时站住，双臂一交，观察海洋。那样广大的水面上，他究竟在寻找什么？
“鹦鹉螺号”当时离最近的海岸也有几百英里。
副手重新拿起望远镜，专注地察看地平线，走来走去，不时顿足，比上级更显出紧张不安。无论如何，这个谜必定会解开，而且想来不久。因为尼摩船长一声号令，机器加大了推进的功率，让螺旋桨转得更快了。
恰在此时，副手又向船长指出了什么。船长不再踱步，将望远镜转向所指之处。他看了很久。我满心疑惑，下到客厅取了平日惯用的一架上好望远镜。随后我倚着平台前端突出的探照灯罩室，打算把海天交接的整条线仔细看一遍。
可是我才把眼睛凑上镜筒，望远镜已被人一把夺去。
我转身一看。尼摩船长就在面前，却不像我认识的那个人了。他的面容全变了。双眼阴郁地冒火，牙关紧咬。僵直的身体、紧握的拳头、缩进双肩的脑袋，都泄露出穿遍全身的剧烈激动。他一下也没动。我的望远镜从他手中跌落，滚到了脚边。
我是不是无意中惹恼了他？这个不可理解的人是否以为我看破了什么不该知道的秘密？不，那道恨意并非冲着我来的，因为他并没有望我。他的目光始终牢牢钉在地平线上那个我看不透的点上。尼摩船长最终恢复了自制，激动平息，用我听不懂的语言对副手说了几句话，又转向我。“阿龙纳斯先生，”他的口气相当专横，“我要您履行当初同我讲定的条件之一。”
“是哪一条，船长？”
“您必须和同伴一道接受禁闭，直到我认为适合释放你们为止。”
“您是此地的主人，”我直视着他，答道，“不过容我问一句，可以吗？”
“一句也不行，先生。”
这样的命令不容反抗，反抗也无用。我下到尼德·兰德和康塞尔住的舱室，把船长的决定告诉了他们。加拿大人是怎样接下这消息的，各位不难想见。
可没有时间争执。门外有四名船员等着，把我们带到刚上“鹦鹉螺号”头一夜待过的那间囚室。
尼德·兰德正要抗议，门已经当着他的面关上了。
“先生肯告诉我，这是什么意思吗？”康塞尔问。
我把发生的事告诉两个同伴。他们跟我一样惊奇，也一样摸不着头脑，找不到解释。
我陷入自己的思索中，除了船长脸上那种奇异的恐惧，别的什么都想不到。始终猜不出原因。尼德·兰德的一句话打断了我的沉思。
“嚯！早饭已经上桌啦。”
桌子果然已经摆好。尼摩船长显然是在催促“鹦鹉螺号”加速时，一并下达了这道命令。
“先生准不准我进一言？”康塞尔问。
“说吧，孩子。”
“那么，我劝先生吃早饭。这样做审慎些，因为往后会有什么事，咱们不知道。”
“有道理，康塞尔。”
“可惜，”尼德·兰德说，“他们只给咱们送了船上的伙食。”
“尼德朋友，”康塞尔问，“要是他们干脆忘了早饭，你又该怎么说？”
这个道理一出来，叉手的抱怨也就到头了。
我们在桌边坐下。这顿饭吃得一声不响。

就在这时，给囚室照明的发光圆球熄灭了，四周一片漆黑。尼德·兰德很快睡着。让我惊讶的是，康塞尔竟也一下子陷入沉睡。我正在想什么会使他产生这样无法抗拒的倦意，自己的脑筋也开始迟钝。任我怎么努力想睁着眼，眼皮就是要合拢。一个痛苦的疑心攫住了我。显然，才吃下去的食物里混进了催眠的药物。要把尼摩船长的计划瞒过我们，光把人关起来还不够，更要我们睡着。随即我听见舱口关上了。先前海水起伏使船体略有横摇，此刻横摇也停止了。“鹦鹉螺号”已经离开洋面了吗？难道它回到了平静不动的水层？我想抵抗睡意。办不到。我的呼吸变得微弱，一股致命的寒意冻住了已经僵硬、麻痹了半边的四肢。眼皮像两扇铅盖，落下来合在眼睛上方。我再也抬不起它们。病态的睡眠夹带着层层幻象，将我的自我意识夺去。最后，幻象也散了，只剩下全然的无知无觉。

sections.title_zh: 上部 / 第23章　珊瑚王国
sections.title_en: PART ONE / CHAPTER XXIII — THE CORAL KINGDOM
source_paragraphs: The next day I woke with my head singularly clear. To my great surprise, I was in my own room. My companions, no doubt, had been reinstated in their cabin, without having perceived it any more than I. Of what had passed during the night they were as ignorant as I was, and to penetrate this mystery I only reckoned upon the chances of the future.

I then thought of quitting my room. Was I free again or a prisoner? Quite free. I opened the door, went to the half-deck, went up the central stairs. The panels, shut the evening before, were open. I went on to the platform.

Ned Land and Conseil waited there for me. I questioned them; they knew nothing. Lost in a heavy sleep in which they had been totally unconscious, they had been astonished at finding themselves in their cabin.
As for the _Nautilus_, it seemed quiet and mysterious as ever. It floated on the surface of the waves at a moderate pace. Nothing seemed changed on board.
The second lieutenant then came on to the platform, and gave the usual order below.
As for Captain Nemo, he did not appear.
Of the people on board, I only saw the impassive steward, who served me with his usual dumb regularity.

About two o’clock, I was in the drawing-room, busied in arranging my notes, when the Captain opened the door and appeared. I bowed. He made a slight inclination in return, without speaking. I resumed my work, hoping that he would perhaps give me some explanation of the events of the preceding night. He made none. I looked at him. He seemed fatigued; his heavy eyes had not been refreshed by sleep; his face looked very sorrowful. He walked to and fro, sat down and got up again, took a chance book, put it down, consulted his instruments without taking his habitual notes, and seemed restless and uneasy. At last, he came up to me, and said:
“Are you a doctor, M. Aronnax?”
I so little expected such a question that I stared some time at him without answering.
“Are you a doctor?” he repeated. “Several of your colleagues have studied medicine.”
“Well,” said I, “I am a doctor and resident surgeon to the hospital. I practised several years before entering the museum.”
“Very well, sir.”
My answer had evidently satisfied the Captain. But, not knowing what he would say next, I waited for other questions, reserving my answers according to circumstances.
“M. Aronnax, will you consent to prescribe for one of my men?” he asked.
“Is he ill?”
“Yes.”
“I am ready to follow you.”
“Come, then.”

I own my heart beat, I do not know why. I saw certain connection between the illness of one of the crew and the events of the day before; and this mystery interested me at least as much as the sick man.
Captain Nemo conducted me to the poop of the _Nautilus_, and took me into a cabin situated near the sailors’ quarters.
There, on a bed, lay a man about forty years of age, with a resolute expression of countenance, a true type of an Anglo-Saxon.

I leant over him. He was not only ill, he was wounded. His head, swathed in bandages covered with blood, lay on a pillow. I undid the bandages, and the wounded man looked at me with his large eyes and gave no sign of pain as I did it. It was a horrible wound. The skull, shattered by some deadly weapon, left the brain exposed, which was much injured. Clots of blood had formed in the bruised and broken mass, in colour like the dregs of wine.

There was both contusion and suffusion of the brain. His breathing was slow, and some spasmodic movements of the muscles agitated his face. I felt his pulse. It was intermittent. The extremities of the body were growing cold already, and I saw death must inevitably ensue. After dressing the unfortunate man’s wounds, I readjusted the bandages on his head, and turned to Captain Nemo.
“What caused this wound?” I asked.
“What does it signify?” he replied, evasively. “A shock has broken one of the levers of the engine, which struck myself. But your opinion as to his state?”
I hesitated before giving it.
“You may speak,” said the Captain. “This man does not understand French.”
I gave a last look at the wounded man.
“He will be dead in two hours.”
“Can nothing save him?”
“Nothing.”
Captain Nemo’s hand contracted, and some tears glistened in his eyes, which I thought incapable of shedding any.

For some moments I still watched the dying man, whose life ebbed slowly. His pallor increased under the electric light that was shed over his death-bed. I looked at his intelligent forehead, furrowed with premature wrinkles, produced probably by misfortune and sorrow. I tried to learn the secret of his life from the last words that escaped his lips.
“You can go now, M. Aronnax,” said the Captain.

I left him in the dying man’s cabin, and returned to my room much affected by this scene. During the whole day, I was haunted by uncomfortable suspicions, and at night I slept badly, and between my broken dreams I fancied I heard distant sighs like the notes of a funeral psalm. Were they the prayers of the dead, murmured in that language that I could not understand?
The next morning I went on to the bridge. Captain Nemo was there before me. As soon as he perceived me he came to me.
“Professor, will it be convenient to you to make a submarine excursion to-day?”
“With my companions?” I asked.
“If they like.”
“We obey your orders, Captain.”
“Will you be so good then as to put on your cork jackets?”

It was not a question of dead or dying. I rejoined Ned Land and Conseil, and told them of Captain Nemo’s proposition. Conseil hastened to accept it, and this time the Canadian seemed quite willing to follow our example.

It was eight o’clock in the morning. At half-past eight we were equipped for this new excursion, and provided with two contrivances for light and breathing. The double door was open; and, accompanied by Captain Nemo, who was followed by a dozen of the crew, we set foot, at a depth of about thirty feet, on the solid bottom on which the _Nautilus_ rested.

A slight declivity ended in an uneven bottom, at fifteen fathoms depth. This bottom differed entirely from the one I had visited on my first excursion under the waters of the Pacific Ocean. Here, there was no fine sand, no submarine prairies, no sea-forest. I immediately recognised that marvellous region in which, on that day, the Captain did the honours to us. It was the coral kingdom.

The light produced a thousand charming varieties, playing in the midst of the branches that were so vividly coloured. I seemed to see the membraneous and cylindrical tubes tremble beneath the undulation of the waters. I was tempted to gather their fresh petals, ornamented with delicate tentacles, some just blown, the others budding, while a small fish, swimming swiftly, touched them slightly, like flights of birds. But if my hand approached these living flowers, these animated, sensitive plants, the whole colony took alarm. The white petals re-entered their red cases, the flowers faded as I looked, and the bush changed into a block of stony knobs.

Chance had thrown me just by the most precious specimens of the zoophyte. This coral was more valuable than that found in the Mediterranean, on the coasts of France, Italy and Barbary. Its tints justified the poetical names of “Flower of Blood,” and “Froth of Blood,” that trade has given to its most beautiful productions. Coral is sold for £20 per ounce; and in this place the watery beds would make the fortunes of a company of coral-divers. This precious matter, often confused with other polypi, formed then the inextricable plots called “macciota,” and on which I noticed several beautiful specimens of pink coral.

But soon the bushes contract, and the arborisations increase. Real petrified thickets, long joists of fantastic architecture, were disclosed before us. Captain Nemo placed himself under a dark gallery, where by a slight declivity we reached a depth of a hundred yards. The light from our lamps produced sometimes magical effects, following the rough outlines of the natural arches and pendants disposed like lustres, that were tipped with points of fire.

At last, after walking two hours, we had attained a depth of about three hundred yards, that is to say, the extreme limit on which coral begins to form. But there was no isolated bush, nor modest brushwood, at the bottom of lofty trees. It was an immense forest of large mineral vegetations, enormous petrified trees, united by garlands of elegant sea-bindweed, all adorned with clouds and reflections. We passed freely under their high branches, lost in the shade of the waves.

Captain Nemo had stopped. I and my companions halted, and, turning round, I saw his men were forming a semi-circle round their chief. Watching attentively, I observed that four of them carried on their shoulders an object of an oblong shape.

We occupied, in this place, the centre of a vast glade surrounded by the lofty foliage of the submarine forest. Our lamps threw over this place a sort of clear twilight that singularly elongated the shadows on the ground. At the end of the glade the darkness increased, and was only relieved by little sparks reflected by the points of coral.

Ned Land and Conseil were near me. We watched, and I thought I was going to witness a strange scene. On observing the ground, I saw that it was raised in certain places by slight excrescences encrusted with limy deposits, and disposed with a regularity that betrayed the hand of man.

In the midst of the glade, on a pedestal of rocks roughly piled up, stood a cross of coral that extended its long arms that one might have thought were made of petrified blood. Upon a sign from Captain Nemo one of the men advanced; and at some feet from the cross he began to dig a hole with a pickaxe that he took from his belt. I understood all! This glade was a cemetery, this hole a tomb, this oblong object the body of the man who had died in the night! The Captain and his men had come to bury their companion in this general resting-place, at the bottom of this inaccessible ocean!

The grave was being dug slowly; the fish fled on all sides while their retreat was being thus disturbed; I heard the strokes of the pickaxe, which sparkled when it hit upon some flint lost at the bottom of the waters. The hole was soon large and deep enough to receive the body. Then the bearers approached; the body, enveloped in a tissue of white linen, was lowered into the damp grave. Captain Nemo, with his arms crossed on his breast, and all the friends of him who had loved them, knelt in prayer.
All fell on their knees in an attitude of prayer

The grave was then filled in with the rubbish taken from the ground, which formed a slight mound. When this was done, Captain Nemo and his men rose; then, approaching the grave, they knelt again, and all extended their hands in sign of a last adieu. Then the funeral procession returned to the _Nautilus_, passing under the arches of the forest, in the midst of thickets, along the coral bushes, and still on the ascent. At last the light of the ship appeared, and its luminous track guided us to the _Nautilus_. At one o’clock we had returned.
As soon as I had changed my clothes I went up on to the platform, and, a prey to conflicting emotions, I sat down near the binnacle. Captain Nemo joined me. I rose and said to him:
“So, as I said he would, this man died in the night?”
“Yes, M. Aronnax.”
“And he rests now, near his companions, in the coral cemetery?”

“Yes, forgotten by all else, but not by us. We dug the grave, and the polypi undertake to seal our dead for eternity.” And, burying his face quickly in his hands, he tried in vain to suppress a sob. Then he added: “Our peaceful cemetery is there, some hundred feet below the surface of the waves.”
“Your dead sleep quietly, at least, Captain, out of the reach of sharks.”
“Yes, sir, of sharks and men,” gravely replied the Captain.
translated_paragraphs: 第二天醒来，我的头脑竟分外清楚。令我大为惊讶的是，我待在自己的房里。同伴们无疑也已被送回他们的舱室，跟我一样毫无知觉。夜里发生过什么，他们也同我同样一无所知。要窥破这个谜，我只能指望未来的机缘。
随后我想走出房间。我重新得了自由，还是个囚犯？原来完全自由。我推开门，走过中层甲板，沿中央阶梯往上。昨晚关严的舱口已经敞开。我登上平台。
尼德·兰德和康塞尔正在那里等我。我问他们，他们什么也不知道。一场昏沉的睡眠使他们全然失去知觉，醒来发现自己在舱里，两人都大吃一惊。
至于“鹦鹉螺号”，依然静谧而神秘，一如往常。它以适中的速度漂行在起伏的海面上。船中看不出什么改变。
副手接着上了平台，照常向下面发出那句口令。
尼摩船长却没有出现。
船上其他人，我只见到那个不动声色的侍役。他照旧准时，一言不发地服侍我。
大约两点，我正在客厅整理笔记，船长推门进来了。我向他鞠躬，他微微欠身还礼，没有开口。我继续工作，暗想他也许会把前一夜的事稍稍解释。他什么也没说。我望着他。他看去十分疲乏，沉重的双眼没有得到睡眠的滋养，脸上透出深重的哀伤。他踱来踱去，坐了又起，随手抽一本书，又放下；察看仪器，却没有照常记下读数，整个人不安而烦乱。最后，他走到我面前，说道：
“阿龙纳斯先生，您是医生吗？”
我怎样也想不到他会提这个问题，盯着他看了好一会儿都答不上话。
“您是医生吗？”他重复道，“您的同事中有好几位学过医。”
“不错，”我说，“我是医生，做过医院的住院外科医师。进博物馆以前，我行过几年医。”
“很好，先生。”
这回答显然使船长满意。但我还不知道他接着要讲什么，便等他来问，再看情形作答。
“阿龙纳斯先生，您愿意为我的一个人诊治吗？”他问。
“他病了吗？”
“是的。”
“我随时可以跟您去。”
“那么，来吧。”
我得承认，我的心跳得有些不稳，也不知为什么。我隐约感觉到，这名船员的病与前一天发生的事之间，有着某种联系。那个谜至少和这个病人一样，引起了我的兴趣。
尼摩船长领我走向“鹦鹉螺号”的船尾，进了靠近船员寝舱的一间小舱。
一张床上躺着一个约四十岁的汉子，脸上的线条透出坚毅，看去是典型的盎格鲁－撒克逊人。
我俯身看他。他不只是患病，而是受了伤。头上缠着满是血迹的绷带，枕在枕头上。我解开绷带。伤者用一双大眼睛望着我，等我揭完，也没流露半点疼痛。那是道可怕的伤口。头骨给某种凶狠的器物击碎，下面的脑组织露在外头，也已受到重创。伤处挫裂的组织中凝聚着血块，颜色如同沉淀的酒渣。
脑部既有挫伤，又有出血。他呼吸缓慢，脸上的肌肉不时痉挛地抽动。我诊了脉，搏动时断时续。他的四肢末端已经发冷，我看得出死亡无可避免。替这不幸的人处理好伤口、重新缠上头部的绷带后，我转向尼摩船长。
“伤是怎样造成的？”我问。
“这有什么要紧？”他含糊答道，“一阵撞击把机器上的一根杠杆折断，打到了我身上。不过他眼下的情形，您怎么看？”
我迟疑了一下，没立刻给出判断。
“您尽管说，”船长道，“这个人听不懂法语。”
我最后望了一眼伤者。
“他两小时之内就会死。”
“没有什么能救他吗？”
“没有。”
尼摩船长的手猛地攥紧，眼里闪着几滴泪光。我原以为那双眼睛根本不会流泪。
我又看着垂死的人待了片刻，他的生命正在缓缓退潮。电光照在临终的床前，他显得愈加苍白。我望着那片显出聪慧的额头，过早刻上的皱纹，想来是苦难与悲伤留下的。我试图从他双唇漏出的最后几句话里，听出他一生的秘密。
“阿龙纳斯先生，您现在可以走了。”船长说。
我把他留在垂死者的舱里，自己回房，深受刚才那一幕的触动。整整一天，我给种种叫人不安的猜测纠缠。夜里也没睡好，在断断续续的梦之间，似乎听见远处传来声声叹息，像葬礼圣诗的曲调。会不会是他们用我听不懂的语言，低声为死者做的祷告？
第二天早晨，我上了甲板。尼摩船长先于我到了那里。一瞧见我，他便走来。
“教授，今天您可方便再作一次海底旅行？”
“和我的同伴一起吗？”我问。
“只要他们乐意。”
“我们听您的吩咐，船长。”
“那么劳驾各位，穿好潜水衣。”
他一句也没提那个死去或将死的人。我去找尼德·兰德和康塞尔，把尼摩船长的提议告诉了他们。康塞尔马上答应。这一回，加拿大人也显得相当愿意跟随我们。
那时是上午八点。八点半，我们为这一程穿戴整齐，备好照明和呼吸两套装具。双层舱门打开了。我们由尼摩船长陪着，他身后还跟着十二名船员。我们踏进深约三十英尺的海水，脚下正是“鹦鹉螺号”停卧的坚实海床。
一道缓坡通往十五英寻深处凹凸不平的海底。这里与我头一次在太平洋下远足时走过的海床大不相同。没有细沙，没有海底草原，也没有海底森林。我立即认出了船长今日做东、领我们探访的奇境。这是珊瑚王国。
光线嬉游在浓艳的枝杈间，生出千般可爱的变化。水波摇曳中，我仿佛看见那些带膜的圆柱形细管也在发颤。新鲜的花瓣以细巧的触手装饰，有些刚刚开放，有些尚在含苞，令我忍不住想伸手采撷。一条小鱼迅速游过，轻轻擦着它们，像一群飞鸟掠过花枝。可我的手一靠近这些活着的花朵，这些能感觉、能活动的“植物”，整个群体便惊慌起来。白色花瓣缩回红色的小鞘，花在我眼前凋谢了，方才花团锦簇的灌木顷刻只剩一块布满石疙瘩的东西。
碰巧我身边就是这种植形动物最名贵的标本。这里的珊瑚比法国、意大利和巴巴里沿岸地中海中的珊瑚还贵重。那些艳美的色泽当得起商人送给上品的诗意名称：“血之花”，“血之沫”。珊瑚每盎司售价二十英镑。单单此处水下的珊瑚床，便足以使一整班潜水采珊瑚的人发财。这种珍贵之物时常同别的珊瑚虫混淆，在这里构成了盘根错节、名叫“马乔塔”的密丛。丛中我看见几株极美的粉红珊瑚。
很快，矮丛渐密，向树形伸展的高枝越来越多。真像一片石化的密林，一道道长梁，架成了奇幻的建筑，在我们面前展露。尼摩船长走进一道幽暗的长廊，我们沿缓坡降到一百码深处。灯光顺着天然拱门凹凸的轮廓游走，那些垂饰排开如同枝形吊灯，尖端全点着火星一般。有时，光的效果几乎像魔法。
走了两小时，我们终于到了约三百码深处，也就是珊瑚开始形成的深度极限。这里再也没有孤零零的枝丛，高树脚下也不再有低矮的灌木。满眼只是一片矿物巨木生长的大森林，棵棵是巨大的石化树木，树与树之间，以优美的海旋花藤编成的花环相连，周身饰着云影和反光。我们在波浪的阴翳里，在它们高高的枝下自在穿行。
尼摩船长停住了。我和同伴也停下，转身一看，他的手下正在他周围围成半圆。我细细一瞧，发现其中四个人肩上抬着一个长方形的物件。
我们所在的地方，是一大片林间空地的中央，周围环绕着海底森林高耸的枝叶。我们的灯在此处投下一种明净的暮光，地上的影子被拉得异样长。空地尽头更加幽暗，只有珊瑚尖端反射出的点点火星打破它。
尼德·兰德和康塞尔就在我身旁。我们望着，我感觉自己要见证一场奇异的仪式。仔细看地面，某些地方鼓起一些小小的土包，上面覆着石灰质的沉积物，排得颇有规律，显然有过人手的安排。
空地中央，几块石头粗略堆起一个台座，上面立着一座珊瑚十字架。长长的双臂向外伸展，几乎像用石化的鲜血做成。尼摩船长一个手势，一名船员走上前，在离十字架几英尺的地方，从腰带上取出十字镐，开始掘坑。我一下全明白了！这片空地是墓园，那土坑是坟穴，那长方形的物件正是夜里去世那个人的遗体！船长和船员们，是来这片人迹难到的大洋底下，把伙伴安葬在他们共同的安息地啊！
墓穴慢慢掘成。鱼儿清静的住处受了惊扰，四面逃散。我听得见一下下镐击的声音。镐尖碰到隐在海底的一块燧石，就迸出火花。很快，坑已挖得够大、够深，可以容纳遗体。抬着遗体的人走近，用白亚麻布包裹着的尸身被放进湿漉漉的墓穴。尼摩船长双臂交叠在胸前，跪地祈祷。死者生前爱过的那些朋友，也都跪了下来。
图注　众人都跪下祈祷
他们用挖出来的碎石泥土把坟穴填平，堆成一座微微隆起的小丘。办完，尼摩船长和船员们站起身来，又走到坟边，重新下跪。众人一同伸出双手，作最后一次诀别。随后送葬的行列踏上回“鹦鹉螺号”的路。他们穿过森林的拱廊，绕过密密的枝丛，沿珊瑚灌木不断往上走。最后，船上的灯出现了，它那条明亮的光路引我们回到“鹦鹉螺号”。归来时已是一点。
我一换好衣服，便登上平台。心里好几种情绪交相激荡，我便在罗经柜附近坐下。尼摩船长过来，我站起身对他说：
“那么，那个人果然像我所说的，在夜里去世了？”
“是的，阿龙纳斯先生。”
“他现在也挨着他的伙伴，安息在珊瑚墓园了？”
“是的。尽管别人都把他遗忘，我们却不会。坟是我们挖的，珊瑚虫会替我们永远封护死者。”他说着猛然把脸埋进双手，竭力想压下一声呜咽，却没能压住。随后又说：“我们宁静的墓园，就在那里，在浪下几百英尺的地方。”
“船长，您的死者至少睡得安稳，鲨鱼再也够不着他们了。”
“是的，先生。鲨鱼够不着，人也够不着。”船长庄重地答道。

sections.title_zh: 下部 / 第1章　印度洋
sections.title_en: PART TWO / CHAPTER I — THE INDIAN OCEAN
source_paragraphs: We now come to the second part of our journey under the sea. The first ended with the moving scene in the coral cemetery which left such a deep impression on my mind. Thus, in the midst of this great sea, Captain Nemo’s life was passing, even to his grave, which he had prepared in one of its deepest abysses. There, not one of the ocean’s monsters could trouble the last sleep of the crew of the _Nautilus_, of those friends riveted to each other in death as in life. “Nor any man, either,” had added the Captain. Still the same fierce, implacable defiance towards human society!
I could no longer content myself with the theory which satisfied Conseil.

That worthy fellow persisted in seeing in the Commander of the _Nautilus_ one of those unknown _savants_ who return mankind contempt for indifference. For him, he was a misunderstood genius who, tired of earth’s deceptions, had taken refuge in this inaccessible medium, where he might follow his instincts freely. To my mind, this explains but one side of Captain Nemo’s character. Indeed, the mystery of that last night during which we had been chained in prison, the sleep, and the precaution so violently taken by the Captain of snatching from my eyes the glass I had raised to sweep the horizon, the mortal wound of the man, due to an unaccountable shock of the _Nautilus_, all put me on a new track. No; Captain Nemo was not satisfied with shunning man. His formidable apparatus not only suited his instinct of freedom, but perhaps also the design of some terrible retaliation.
At this moment nothing is clear to me; I catch but a glimpse of light amidst all the darkness, and I must confine myself to writing as events shall dictate.

That day, the 24th of January, 1868, at noon, the second officer came to take the altitude of the sun. I mounted the platform, lit a cigar, and watched the operation. It seemed to me that the man did not understand French; for several times I made remarks in a loud voice, which must have drawn from him some involuntary sign of attention, if he had understood them; but he remained undisturbed and dumb.

As he was taking observations with the sextant, one of the sailors of the _Nautilus_ (the strong man who had accompanied us on our first submarine excursion to the Island of Crespo) came to clean the glasses of the lantern. I examined the fittings of the apparatus, the strength of which was increased a hundredfold by lenticular rings, placed similar to those in a lighthouse, and which projected their brilliance in a horizontal plane. The electric lamp was combined in such a way as to give its most powerful light. Indeed, it was produced in vacuo, which insured both its steadiness and its intensity. This vacuum economised the graphite points between which the luminous arc was developed—an important point of economy for Captain Nemo, who could not easily have replaced them; and under these conditions their waste was imperceptible. When the _Nautilus_ was ready to continue its submarine journey, I went down to the saloon. The panel was closed, and the course marked direct west.

We were furrowing the waters of the Indian Ocean, a vast liquid plain, with a surface of 1,200,000,000 of acres, and whose waters are so clear and transparent that any one leaning over them would turn giddy. The _Nautilus_ usually floated between fifty and a hundred fathoms deep. We went on so for some days. To any one but myself, who had a great love for the sea, the hours would have seemed long and monotonous; but the daily walks on the platform, when I steeped myself in the reviving air of the ocean, the sight of the rich waters through the windows of the saloon, the books in the library, the compiling of my memoirs, took up all my time, and left me not a moment of ennui or weariness.

For some days we saw a great number of aquatic birds, sea-mews or gulls. Some were cleverly killed and, prepared in a certain way, made very acceptable water-game. Amongst large-winged birds, carried a long distance from all lands and resting upon the waves from the fatigue of their flight, I saw some magnificent albatrosses, uttering discordant cries like the braying of an ass, and birds belonging to the family of the long-wings.
As to the fish, they always provoked our admiration when we surprised the secrets of their aquatic life through the open panels. I saw many kinds which I never before had a chance of observing.

I shall notice chiefly ostracions peculiar to the Red Sea, the Indian Ocean, and that part which washes the coast of tropical America. These fishes, like the tortoise, the armadillo, the sea-hedgehog, and the Crustacea, are protected by a breastplate which is neither chalky nor stony, but real bone. In some it takes the form of a solid triangle, in others of a solid quadrangle. Amongst the triangular I saw some an inch and a half in length, with wholesome flesh and a delicious flavour; they are brown at the tail, and yellow at the fins, and I recommend their introduction into fresh water, to which a certain number of sea-fish easily accustom themselves. I would also mention quadrangular ostracions, having on the back four large tubercles; some dotted over with white spots on the lower part of the body, and which may be tamed like birds; trigons provided with spikes formed by the lengthening of their bony shell, and which, from their strange gruntings, are called “seapigs”; also dromedaries with large humps in the shape of a cone, whose flesh is very tough and leathery.

I now borrow from the daily notes of Master Conseil. “Certain fish of the genus petrodon peculiar to those seas, with red backs and white chests, which are distinguished by three rows of longitudinal filaments; and some electrical, seven inches long, decked in the liveliest colours. Then, as specimens of other kinds, some ovoides, resembling an egg of a dark brown colour, marked with white bands, and without tails; diodons, real sea-porcupines, furnished with spikes, and capable of swelling in such a way as to look like cushions bristling with darts; hippocampi, common to every ocean; some pegasi with lengthened snouts, which their pectoral fins, being much elongated and formed in the shape of wings, allow, if not to fly, at least to shoot into the air; pigeon spatulae, with tails covered with many rings of shell; macrognathi with long jaws, an excellent fish, nine inches long, and bright with most agreeable colours; pale-coloured calliomores, with rugged heads; and plenty of chaetodons, with long and tubular muzzles, which kill insects by shooting them, as from an air-gun, with a single drop of water. These we may call the flycatchers of the seas.

“In the eighty-ninth genus of fishes, classed by Lacepede, belonging to the second lower class of bony, characterised by opercules and bronchial membranes, I remarked the scorpaena, the head of which is furnished with spikes, and which has but one dorsal fin; these creatures are covered, or not, with little shells, according to the sub-class to which they belong. The second sub-class gives us specimens of didactyles fourteen or fifteen inches in length, with yellow rays, and heads of a most fantastic appearance. As to the first sub-class, it gives several specimens of that singular looking fish appropriately called a ‘seafrog,’ with large head, sometimes pierced with holes, sometimes swollen with protuberances, bristling with spikes, and covered with tubercles; it has irregular and hideous horns; its body and tail are covered with callosities; its sting makes a dangerous wound; it is both repugnant and horrible to look at.”

From the 21st to the 23rd of January the _Nautilus_ went at the rate of two hundred and fifty leagues in twenty-four hours, being five hundred and forty miles, or twenty-two miles an hour. If we recognised so many different varieties of fish, it was because, attracted by the electric light, they tried to follow us; the greater part, however, were soon distanced by our speed, though some kept their place in the waters of the _Nautilus_ for a time. The morning of the 24th, in 12° 5′ S. lat., and 94° 33′ long., we observed Keeling Island, a coral formation, planted with magnificent cocos, and which had been visited by Mr. Darwin and Captain Fitzroy. The _Nautilus_ skirted the shores of this desert island for a little distance. Its nets brought up numerous specimens of polypi and curious shells of mollusca. Some precious productions of the species of delphinulae enriched the treasures of Captain Nemo, to which I added an astraea punctifera, a kind of parasite polypus often found fixed to a shell.
Soon Keeling Island disappeared from the horizon, and our course was directed to the north-west in the direction of the Indian Peninsula.

From Keeling Island our course was slower and more variable, often taking us into great depths. Several times they made use of the inclined planes, which certain internal levers placed obliquely to the waterline. In that way we went about two miles, but without ever obtaining the greatest depths of the Indian Sea, which soundings of seven thousand fathoms have never reached. As to the temperature of the lower strata, the thermometer invariably indicated 4° above zero. I only observed that in the upper regions the water was always colder in the high levels than at the surface of the sea.

On the 25th of January the ocean was entirely deserted; the _Nautilus_ passed the day on the surface, beating the waves with its powerful screw and making them rebound to a great height. Who under such circumstances would not have taken it for a gigantic cetacean? Three parts of this day I spent on the platform. I watched the sea. Nothing on the horizon, till about four o’clock a steamer running west on our counter. Her masts were visible for an instant, but she could not see the _Nautilus_, being too low in the water. I fancied this steamboat belonged to the P. O. Company, which runs from Ceylon to Sydney, touching at King George’s Point and Melbourne.
At five o’clock in the evening, before that fleeting twilight which binds night to day in tropical zones, Conseil and I were astonished by a curious spectacle.
It was a shoal of argonauts travelling along on the surface of the ocean. We could count several hundreds. They belonged to the tubercle kind which are peculiar to the Indian seas.

These graceful molluscs moved backwards by means of their locomotive tube, through which they propelled the water already drawn in. Of their eight tentacles, six were elongated, and stretched out floating on the water, whilst the other two, rolled up flat, were spread to the wing like a light sail. I saw their spiral-shaped and fluted shells, which Cuvier justly compares to an elegant skiff. A boat indeed! It bears the creature which secretes it without its adhering to it.

For nearly an hour the _Nautilus_ floated in the midst of this shoal of molluscs. Then I know not what sudden fright they took. But as if at a signal every sail was furled, the arms folded, the body drawn in, the shells turned over, changing their centre of gravity, and the whole fleet disappeared under the waves. Never did the ships of a squadron manœuvre with more unity.
At that moment night fell suddenly, and the reeds, scarcely raised by the breeze, lay peaceably under the sides of the _Nautilus_.

The next day, 26th of January, we cut the equator at the eighty-second meridian and entered the northern hemisphere. During the day a formidable troop of sharks accompanied us, terrible creatures, which multiply in these seas and make them very dangerous. They were “cestracio philippi” sharks, with brown backs and whitish bellies, armed with eleven rows of teeth—eyed sharks—their throat being marked with a large black spot surrounded with white like an eye. There were also some Isabella sharks, with rounded snouts marked with dark spots. These powerful creatures often hurled themselves at the windows of the saloon with such violence as to make us feel very insecure. At such times Ned Land was no longer master of himself. He wanted to go to the surface and harpoon the monsters, particularly certain smooth-hound sharks, whose mouth is studded with teeth like a mosaic; and large tiger-sharks nearly six yards long, the last named of which seemed to excite him more particularly. But the _Nautilus_, accelerating her speed, easily left the most rapid of them behind.

The 27th of January, at the entrance of the vast Bay of Bengal, we met repeatedly a forbidding spectacle, dead bodies floating on the surface of the water. They were the dead of the Indian villages, carried by the Ganges to the level of the sea, and which the vultures, the only undertakers of the country, had not been able to devour. But the sharks did not fail to help them at their funeral work.

About seven o’clock in the evening, the _Nautilus_, half-immersed, was sailing in a sea of milk. At first sight the ocean seemed lactified. Was it the effect of the lunar rays? No; for the moon, scarcely two days old, was still lying hidden under the horizon in the rays of the sun. The whole sky, though lit by the sidereal rays, seemed black by contrast with the whiteness of the waters.
Conseil could not believe his eyes, and questioned me as to the cause of this strange phenomenon. Happily I was able to answer him.
“It is called a milk sea,” I explained. “A large extent of white wavelets often to be seen on the coasts of Amboyna, and in these parts of the sea.”
“But, sir,” said Conseil, “can you tell me what causes such an effect? for I suppose the water is not really turned into milk.”

“No, my boy; and the whiteness which surprises you is caused only by the presence of myriads of infusoria, a sort of luminous little worm, gelatinous and without colour, of the thickness of a hair, and whose length is not more than seven-thousandths of an inch. These insects adhere to one another sometimes for several leagues.”
“Several leagues!” exclaimed Conseil.
“Yes, my boy; and you need not try to compute the number of these infusoria. You will not be able, for, if I am not mistaken, ships have floated on these milk seas for more than forty miles.”

Towards midnight the sea suddenly resumed its usual colour; but behind us, even to the limits of the horizon, the sky reflected the whitened waves, and for a long time seemed impregnated with the vague glimmerings of an aurora borealis.
translated_paragraphs: 现在，这趟海底旅行到了第二部。头一部收束于珊瑚墓园中那动人的一幕，它在我心里留下了极深的印象。原来，尼摩船长的一生就这样度在大海怀中，甚至连坟墓，也已备在海洋的一道深渊里。那里，没一头海怪能够惊扰“鹦鹉螺号”船员最后的长眠。这些朋友生前紧紧相依，死后也挨在一起。“人也够不着。”船长还加过这么一句。他对人类社会的抗拒，依旧那样强烈，那样不容化解！
那套足以叫康塞尔满意的解释，再也不能叫我满足。

这个好心人始终认定，“鹦鹉螺号”的指挥官是一位默默无闻的学者，世人以冷淡待他，他便以轻蔑作答。在康塞尔眼里，他是一个不被理解的天才，厌倦了陆地上的虚伪，遁入人迹难至的海底，好在那里自由地顺从天性。我看，这只能解释尼摩船长性格的一面。那天晚上我们被关进囚室，糊里糊涂地睡着；我举起望远镜，要扫视地平线，船长却如此粗暴地把镜筒从我眼前夺去；那名水手受了致命伤，据说“鹦鹉螺号”挨过一下难以解释的撞击。这一连串谜团已把我的思路引向别处。不，尼摩船长并不满足于躲避世人。他拥有的这台可怕的机器，不仅顺从他追求自由的天性，也许还服务于某一项可怕的复仇计划。
在眼下，还没有什么是我能看清的。重重黑暗中，我只依稀瞥见一点光亮。因此只好事情怎样发展，我便怎样往下写。
那天是一八六八年一月二十四日。正午，副手上来测量太阳高度。我也登上平台，点燃一支雪茄，观看他的操作。我觉得这人不懂法语。我好几次故意大声发表意见，倘若他听得懂，多半会不由自主流露出一点留心的痕迹。他却毫无反应，沉默如常。

他用六分仪做观测时，“鹦鹉螺号”的一名水手上来擦灯罩，正是头一次陪我们到克雷斯波岛海底远足的那个壮汉。我端详着灯的装置。一圈圈透镜的安放，类似灯塔，能把光力增强百倍，沿水平面投射出去。电灯各部分配合得巧妙，将光力发挥到最强。光是在真空中产生的，因此既稳定，又强烈。电弧在两枚石墨尖端之间形成，真空让尖端几乎不发生损耗。对于很难补充它们的尼摩船长，这是很要紧的一项节省。“鹦鹉螺号”准备继续水下航程时，我下到客厅。舱盖关好，航向显示正西。

我们正犁开印度洋的水面。这片浩瀚的液体平原，面积达十二亿英亩，海水清澈透明，谁从上面俯望，都会一阵目眩。“鹦鹉螺号”通常在五十至一百英寻深处行驶。我们就这样走了几天。若非像我这样热爱海洋的人，这样的时辰或许会显得漫长而单调。可每天出门在平台上漫步，让自己浸在使人振作的海风中，隔着客厅的窗子看富饶的水世界，读图书室的书，然后整理自己的旅行手记，已经占满了我的时间，连厌烦、疲倦的工夫都没给我留下一刻。
有几天，我们看见了成群的水鸟，多是海鸥。有人手法利落，打下几只，照一定的法子烹调，倒也是可口的野味。有些阔翼鸟已远离陆地，飞倦了，歇在海浪上。其中有几只信天翁，姿态非凡，叫声却很刺耳，活像驴叫。我还看见了几种长翼鸟。
至于那些鱼，每逢舷窗的遮板打开，我们得以窥见它们在水中生活的秘密，总要由衷赞叹。我看见的许多鱼，过去从来没有机会观察。

我特别要提到箱鲀。红海、印度洋和临近美洲热带沿岸的一带海域是它们特有的产地。像龟、犰狳、海胆和甲壳动物一样，它们披着护甲。那甲既非石灰，也非石质，而是真正的骨板。有些呈三角体，有些呈四角体。在三角形的当中，我看到几条长一英寸半，肉质健康，滋味鲜美。尾部是棕色，鳍是黄色。我还愿意提议，试着把它们引入淡水中，原有不少海鱼能轻易适应淡水。值得一提的还包括四角箱鲀，背部有四个大突起；有些下半身点着白斑，可以像鸟儿一样驯养；还有些三角箱鲀，长长的骨甲尖端形成了棘刺，因其发出奇异的呼噜声，被叫作“海猪”；又有背部带巨大圆锥形驼峰的，形似单峰驼，肉质却坚韧如皮革。

现在借用康塞尔师傅的逐日笔记。“有些是这一带特有的鲀类，背红胸白，身上有三列纵向细丝，很好辨认。还有些能发电的小鱼，长七英寸，颜色鲜艳得惊人。别的类型中，有一种椭圆鱼，活像一枚带白条纹的深褐色蛋，不见尾巴。还有刺鲀，真正的海豪猪，满身是刺，鼓起来时简直像一只插满短矢的靠垫。海马在各个大洋都能见到。海蛾鱼吻部长，胸鳍也特别长，形似双翼，纵不能真飞，至少能冲到水面之上。另有尾部裹着层层壳环的鸽形匙鱼、长颌的棘鳅，后者是很好的鱼，身长九英寸，满身闪着悦目的颜色；淡色的鼠衔鱼，头部粗糙不平；还有许多蝴蝶鱼，管状的长嘴可以射出一滴水，像用气枪那样，击毙昆虫。我们不妨称它们为海里的捕蝇能手。

“在拉塞佩德所分的第八十九个鱼属中，我留意到鲉鱼。它隶于硬骨鱼的第二小类，以具有鳃盖和鳃膜为特征。鲉鱼头部生刺，背鳍却只有一个。依所属亚类的不同，有的小鳞如甲，有的则不具这种覆片。第二亚类中可见双指鳍的鱼，长十四五英寸，鳍条黄色，头形极为奇异。第一亚类则给出了几件模样有趣的标本，叫它‘海蛙’十分贴切。头大，有时凹出小孔，有时鼓出种种凸块；刺竖着，结节遍布，还有形状不规则、十分难看的角。周身及尾部全是硬茧，带刺的部位扎伤了人相当危险。整个模样既叫人嫌恶，也叫人害怕。”

一月二十一日至二十三日，“鹦鹉螺号”每二十四小时航行二百五十里格，合五百四十英里，即每小时约二十二英里。我们能辨出这么多种鱼，是因为它们受到电灯吸引，试图随我们同行。大多数很快被我们的速度甩开，但也有些能在“鹦鹉螺号”的航迹中保持一阵。二十四日早晨，在南纬十二度五分、经度九十四度三十三分，我们望见了基林岛。这是座珊瑚岛，盛长壮丽的椰树，达尔文先生和菲茨罗伊船长都曾来访。“鹦鹉螺号”沿这座无人岛的岸边走了一小段。拖网捞起许多珊瑚虫标本和形状奇特的贝壳。有几件名贵的齿轮螺，为尼摩船长的珍藏增了色。我又添上一件点纹星珊瑚，是种常常附着在贝壳上的寄生珊瑚虫。
不久，基林岛从地平线上消失，我们朝西北方的印度半岛驶去。
离开基林岛以后，航速缓了，航路也多了变化，时常带我们去很深的水层。好几次船上动用倾斜舵板，由内部杠杆将它们相对于水线斜斜放下。借此我们下到过约两英里深处，但始终没达到印度洋的最深点。七千英寻的测深索也从来不曾触到那个底。至于深层温度，温度计一贯显示零上四度。我只注意到，即便在靠上的水层，只要略低于海面，水就比洋面上的冷。

一月二十五日，大洋上空空荡荡。“鹦鹉螺号”一整天浮在水面，用强大的螺旋桨拍打波浪，使浪花高高地飞起。在这种情形下，又有谁不会把它当成一头巨鲸呢？一天里有四分之三的时间我都待在平台上，望着海洋。地平线上什么也没有。约四点，才有一条向西行驶的轮船出现在我们的船尾方向。我只看见它的桅杆一霎。它可看不见“鹦鹉螺号”，我们的船露出水面太低了。我猜那条轮船属于半岛东方轮船公司，在锡兰和悉尼之间航行，中途停靠乔治王角和墨尔本。
傍晚五点，在热带那一缕将昼夜系在一起、转瞬即逝的暮光尚未来临之前，我和康塞尔都叫一种奇特的景象惊住了。
原来是一群船蛸，正贴着海面游过，数一数足有几百只。它们身上带着疣状突起，是印度洋特有的一类。
这些优雅的软体动物靠漏斗状喷水管，先把水吸进来，再将水向外喷出，身子便向后行进。八条腕中，六条伸长，浮在水面，另两条原本平卷着，这时张开来迎风，看着俨然一面轻帆。我看清它们螺旋形、带沟纹的壳，居维叶把这壳比作一叶雅致的小舟，再贴切不过。可不正是一条艇！它载着那只分泌出它的动物，那动物却不必黏在壳上。
“鹦鹉螺号”在这群软体动物中间浮行了将近一个钟头。也不知它们忽然受了什么惊吓，像是有令传下，每一面帆都卷起来，每一条腕都折回，身子也收拢。贝壳翻转，重心一换，整支舰队便消失在浪下。没有哪一队船能操演得如此齐整。
暮色就在这时骤然落下，水草几乎没被微风扬起，静静依傍在“鹦鹉螺号”两舷。

第二天是一月二十六日，我们在第八十二度经线上越过赤道，进入北半球。白天有一大队骇人的鲨鱼同我们相伴。这类可怕生物在这一带繁衍很多，使海面大增凶险。其中有菲利普港角鲨（Cestracio philippi），背褐腹白，长着十一排牙齿；还有带眼斑的鲨鱼，喉部一个大黑点镶着白边，形如眼睛；另有几条伊莎贝拉鲨，圆圆的吻部布着深色斑点。这些强有力的生物常向客厅的窗户猛撞，用力之大，真叫我们不敢觉得安稳。这时尼德·兰德就不再是自己的主人。他真想上浮出去，用捕鲸叉收拾这些怪物，尤其是那些星鲨，它们口内的牙排列得像镶嵌画，还有几条将近六码长的大虎鲨，数它们把他撩拨得最厉害。不过“鹦鹉螺号”只须加快一点速度，连游得最快的也能轻易甩在后头。
一月二十七日，在辽阔的孟加拉湾入口，我们好几次看见阴惨的景象，有死者的遗体漂在海面。那是印度村庄里的亡人，由恒河带到海洋。沿岸的秃鹫仿佛当地仅有的殡葬人，也没有将尸体啄尽。不过，鲨鱼绝不曾忘记来帮它们办这场丧事。
当晚七点左右，“鹦鹉螺号”半浸在水里，驶入了一片乳白色的海。乍看上去，简直是海水变作了乳汁。难道是月光的作用？不。新月才到第二天，早在太阳的余晖里隐没在地平线下。满天虽然有星芒照耀，在雪白的海水一衬之下，仿佛一片漆黑。
康塞尔不敢相信自己的眼睛，问我这个奇异现象由何而来。幸而我能够回答他。
“这叫乳海，”我解释说，“是连绵一大片白色的小波浪。在安汶岛海岸和我们所在的这些海面，经常可以遇见。”
“可是先生，”康塞尔说，“先生能否告诉我，是怎样出现了这样的光景？我想水并没真的变成乳汁吧。”
“没有，孩子。叫你惊奇的白色，无非是无数细微生物聚集而成。那是一类发光的小虫，身子胶质无色，粗细如发，长不超过千分之七英寸。这些小生物彼此依附，有时延绵好几里格。”
“几里格！”康塞尔叫道。
“是啊，孩子。也不必试着估算小虫的数目，你算不出来。据我所知，有些船只曾在这样的乳海上航行过四十多英里。”
午夜前后，大海忽然恢复了平常的颜色。可在我们身后，直到天际，天空还返照着发白的波浪。好长一阵，那里都像浸染着北极光朦胧的光辉。

sections.title_zh: 下部 / 第2章　尼摩船长的新提议
sections.title_en: PART TWO / CHAPTER II — A NOVEL PROPOSAL OF CAPTAIN NEMO’S
source_paragraphs: On the 28th of February, when at noon the _Nautilus_ came to the surface of the sea, in 9° 4′ N. lat., there was land in sight about eight miles to westward. The first thing I noticed was a range of mountains about two thousand feet high, the shapes of which were most capricious. On taking the bearings, I knew that we were nearing the island of Ceylon, the pearl which hangs from the lobe of the Indian Peninsula.
Captain Nemo and his second appeared at this moment. The Captain glanced at the map. Then turning to me, said:
“The Island of Ceylon, noted for its pearl-fisheries. Would you like to visit one of them, M. Aronnax?”
“Certainly, Captain.”

“Well, the thing is easy. Though, if we see the fisheries, we shall not see the fishermen. The annual exportation has not yet begun. Never mind, I will give orders to make for the Gulf of Manaar, where we shall arrive in the night.”
The Captain said something to his second, who immediately went out. Soon the _Nautilus_ returned to her native element, and the manometer showed that she was about thirty feet deep.
“Well, sir,” said Captain Nemo, “you and your companions shall visit the Bank of Manaar, and if by chance some fisherman should be there, we shall see him at work.”
“Agreed, Captain!”
“By the bye, M. Aronnax you are not afraid of sharks?”
“Sharks!” exclaimed I.
This question seemed a very hard one.
“Well?” continued Captain Nemo.
“I admit, Captain, that I am not yet very familiar with that kind of fish.”

“We are accustomed to them,” replied Captain Nemo, “and in time you will be too. However, we shall be armed, and on the road we may be able to hunt some of the tribe. It is interesting. So, till to-morrow, sir, and early.”
This said in a careless tone, Captain Nemo left the saloon. Now, if you were invited to hunt the bear in the mountains of Switzerland, what would you say?
“Very well! to-morrow we will go and hunt the bear.” If you were asked to hunt the lion in the plains of Atlas, or the tiger in the Indian jungles, what would you say?

“Ha! ha! it seems we are going to hunt the tiger or the lion!” But when you are invited to hunt the shark in its natural element, you would perhaps reflect before accepting the invitation. As for myself, I passed my hand over my forehead, on which stood large drops of cold perspiration. “Let us reflect,” said I, “and take our time. Hunting otters in submarine forests, as we did in the Island of Crespo, will pass; but going up and down at the bottom of the sea, where one is almost certain to meet sharks, is quite another thing! I know well that in certain countries, particularly in the Andaman Islands, the negroes never hesitate to attack them with a dagger in one hand and a running noose in the other; but I also know that few who affront those creatures ever return alive. However, I am not a negro, and if I were I think a little hesitation in this case would not be ill-timed.”
At this moment Conseil and the Canadian entered, quite composed, and even joyous. They knew not what awaited them.
“Faith, sir,” said Ned Land, “your Captain Nemo—the devil take him!—has just made us a very pleasant offer.”
“Ah!” said I, “you know?”

“If agreeable to you, sir,” interrupted Conseil, “the commander of the _Nautilus_ has invited us to visit the magnificent Ceylon fisheries to-morrow, in your company; he did it kindly, and behaved like a real gentleman.”
“He said nothing more?”
“Nothing more, sir, except that he had already spoken to you of this little walk.”
“Sir,” said Conseil, “would you give us some details of the pearl fishery?”
“As to the fishing itself,” I asked, “or the incidents, which?”
“On the fishing,” replied the Canadian; “before entering upon the ground, it is as well to know something about it.”
“Very well; sit down, my friends, and I will teach you.”
Ned and Conseil seated themselves on an ottoman, and the first thing the Canadian asked was:
“Sir, what is a pearl?”

“My worthy Ned,” I answered, “to the poet, a pearl is a tear of the sea; to the Orientals, it is a drop of dew solidified; to the ladies, it is a jewel of an oblong shape, of a brilliancy of mother-of-pearl substance, which they wear on their fingers, their necks, or their ears; for the chemist it is a mixture of phosphate and carbonate of lime, with a little gelatine; and lastly, for naturalists, it is simply a morbid secretion of the organ that produces the mother-of-pearl amongst certain bivalves.”
“Branch of molluscs,” said Conseil.

“Precisely so, my learned Conseil; and, amongst these testacea the earshell, the tridacnae, the turbots, in a word, all those which secrete mother-of-pearl, that is, the blue, bluish, violet, or white substance which lines the interior of their shells, are capable of producing pearls.”
“Mussels too?” asked the Canadian.
“Yes, mussels of certain waters in Scotland, Wales, Ireland, Saxony, Bohemia, and France.”
“Good! For the future I shall pay attention,” replied the Canadian.

“But,” I continued, “the particular mollusc which secretes the pearl is the pearl-oyster, the meleagrina margaritifera, that precious pintadine. The pearl is nothing but a nacreous formation, deposited in a globular form, either adhering to the oyster shell, or buried in the folds of the creature. On the shell it is fast; in the flesh it is loose; but always has for a kernel a small hard substance, may be a barren egg, may be a grain of sand, around which the pearly matter deposits itself year after year successively, and by thin concentric layers.”
“Are many pearls found in the same oyster?” asked Conseil.
“Yes, my boy. Some are a perfect casket. One oyster has been mentioned, though I allow myself to doubt it, as having contained no less than a hundred and fifty sharks.”
“A hundred and fifty sharks!” exclaimed Ned Land.
“Did I say sharks?” said I hurriedly. “I meant to say a hundred and fifty pearls. Sharks would not be sense.”
“Certainly not,” said Conseil; “but will you tell us now by what means they extract these pearls?”

“They proceed in various ways. When they adhere to the shell, the fishermen often pull them off with pincers; but the most common way is to lay the oysters on mats of the seaweed which covers the banks. Thus they die in the open air; and at the end of ten days they are in a forward state of decomposition. They are then plunged into large reservoirs of sea-water; then they are opened and washed.”
“The price of these pearls varies according to their size?” asked Conseil.

“Not only according to their size,” I answered, “but also according to their shape, their water (that is, their colour), and their lustre: that is, that bright and diapered sparkle which makes them so charming to the eye. The most beautiful are called virgin pearls, or paragons. They are formed alone in the tissue of the mollusc, are white, often opaque, and sometimes have the transparency of an opal; they are generally round or oval. The round are made into bracelets, the oval into pendants, and, being more precious, are sold singly. Those adhering to the shell of the oyster are more irregular in shape, and are sold by weight. Lastly, in a lower order are classed those small pearls known under the name of seed-pearls; they are sold by measure, and are especially used in embroidery for church ornaments.”
“But,” said Conseil, “is this pearl-fishery dangerous?”
“No,” I answered, quickly; “particularly if certain precautions are taken.”
“What does one risk in such a calling?” said Ned Land, “the swallowing of some mouthfuls of sea-water?”
“As you say, Ned. By the bye,” said I, trying to take Captain Nemo’s careless tone, “are you afraid of sharks, brave Ned?”
“I!” replied the Canadian; “a harpooner by profession? It is my trade to make light of them.”

“But,” said I, “it is not a question of fishing for them with an iron-swivel, hoisting them into the vessel, cutting off their tails with a blow of a chopper, ripping them up, and throwing their heart into the sea!”
“Then, it is a question of——”
“Precisely.”
“In the water?”
“In the water.”
“Faith, with a good harpoon! You know, sir, these sharks are ill-fashioned beasts. They turn on their bellies to seize you, and in that time——”
Ned Land had a way of saying “seize” which made my blood run cold.
“Well, and you, Conseil, what do you think of sharks?”
“Me!” said Conseil. “I will be frank, sir.”
“So much the better,” thought I.
“If you, sir, mean to face the sharks, I do not see why your faithful servant should not face them with you.”
translated_paragraphs: 二月二十八日正午，“鹦鹉螺号”在北纬九度四分处升上海面。向西约八英里，望得见陆地。我最先注意到一带约两千英尺高的山，轮廓千姿百态。测了方位，我才知道我们正在接近锡兰，那颗悬在印度半岛耳垂上的明珠。
尼摩船长和副手正在此时出现。船长瞥了眼地图，转向我，说：
“锡兰岛，以采珠场闻名。阿龙纳斯先生，您愿意去其中一处看看吗？”
“当然，船长。”
“那很容易。不过采珠场虽然看得见，采珠人却看不见。每年一度的采珠作业还没开始。不要紧，我会吩咐驶向马纳尔湾，夜里就能到。”
船长向副手吩咐了几句，副手立刻离开。没多久，“鹦鹉螺号”便回到了自己的老家水里，压力计显示水深约三十英尺。
“好了，先生，”尼摩船长说，“您和两位同伴都会到马纳尔珠滩上去。若凑巧有采珠人在场，我们还可看看他怎样工作。”
“一言为定，船长！”
“顺便问一句，阿龙纳斯先生，您不怕鲨鱼吧？”
“鲨鱼！”我叫道。
这问题好像颇难回答。
“怎么样？”尼摩船长接着问。
“说实话，船长，我跟这种鱼还没熟到什么地步。”
“我们已经跟它们混熟了，”尼摩船长说，“日后您也会习惯。不管怎样，我们会带武器。途中兴许还有机会猎上它们一两头。挺有趣的。那么，先生，明天见，要早起。”
尼摩船长满不在乎地说完便出了客厅。如今，要是有人邀您上瑞士的山里去猎熊，您会怎样回答？
“很好！明天我们去猎熊。”要是有人请您到阿特拉斯山的平原上去猎狮，或者到印度丛林里去猎虎，您又怎样说？

“哈！哈！这么说咱们要去猎虎或猎狮啦！”可要是人家请您到鲨鱼的本乡本土去猎鲨，您说不定就要先想一想，再接受邀请。我呢，伸手往额头上一抹，摸到的全是大颗冷汗。“容咱们想想，”我自语道，“慢慢想。像克雷斯波岛那回到海底森林猎水獭，还说得过去。但若是在海底上上下下地走，又几乎必定遇上鲨鱼，那就是另一回事了！我早就知道，在某些地方，尤其安达曼群岛，当地的黑人一手握匕首，一手持活套，敢毫不犹豫地进攻它们。可我也知道，敢正面跟这种东西较量，还能活着回来的极少。不管怎样，我不是当地的黑人。就算我是，我想此刻稍作踌躇，也没有什么不合时宜吧。”
就在这时，康塞尔和加拿大人进来了，神情不但从容，甚至还很快活。他们不晓得前面等着他们的是什么。
“说实话，先生，”尼德·兰德说，“您那位尼摩船长，让魔鬼带走他吧，刚刚倒给我们提了个很讨人喜欢的主意。”
“啊！”我说，“你们知道了？”
“先生若是同意，”康塞尔接话，“‘鹦鹉螺号’的指挥官邀我们明天陪先生一起，去拜访锡兰那些壮丽的采珠场。他态度和蔼，举止完全配得上一位绅士。”
“他没说别的了？”
“没有，先生，只说先前已经和先生谈过这次小小的散步。”
“先生，”康塞尔又说，“能不能给我们讲一讲采珠场的情形？”
“你想听采珠本身，”我问，“还是那些意外遭遇？”
“说采珠吧，”加拿大人答道，“到了那个地方以前，先了解几分总是好的。”
“好。朋友们，请坐，我来给你们讲。”
尼德和康塞尔在无靠背的软榻上坐定，加拿大人开口第一句便问：
“先生，珍珠是什么？”
“我亲爱的尼德，”我回答，“对诗人，它是大海的一滴眼泪；在东方人的想象里，它是凝住的一颗露珠；对女士们，它是颗长圆形、闪着珠母般光泽的宝石，可以戴在指上、颈间或耳畔；对化学家，它是磷酸钙、碳酸钙和少量胶质的混合物；最后，对博物学家，它不过是某些双壳贝体内分泌珠母层的器官，在异常状况下产生的分泌物。”
“软体动物门。”康塞尔说。
“正是，我博学的康塞尔。在这些有壳动物中，耳鲍、砗磲、蝾螺，一句话，凡能分泌珠母层，也就是衬在壳内的蓝色、淡蓝、紫色或白色物质的，都有可能产珍珠。”
“河蚌也行？”加拿大人问。
“是的。苏格兰、威尔士、爱尔兰、萨克森、波希米亚和法国某些水域里的蚌都能。”
“好！往后我得留神了。”加拿大人答道。
“不过，”我接着说，“专以分泌珍珠著称的软体动物，是珠母贝，学名Meleagrina margaritifera，就是那种珍贵的黑蝶贝。珍珠无非是珠母质结成球形，或附在贝壳内侧，或埋在贝体的褶皱间。附在壳上便牢牢固定，埋在肉里则可以自由取出。不过它总有个小小的硬核，可能是一颗未受精的卵，也可能是一粒沙。珠母质围绕它，年年沉积，添上一层又一层同心的薄膜。”
“一枚贝里面能找出很多颗珍珠吗？”康塞尔问。
“能，孩子。有的简直是座珠宝匣。有人说到过一枚贝，里面竟藏着不下一百五十条鲨鱼。不过请容我稍有怀疑。”
“一百五十条鲨鱼！”尼德·兰德叫道。
“我说的是鲨鱼吗？”我匆忙答道，“我要说的是一百五十颗珍珠。说成鲨鱼当然没有道理。”
“自然没有，”康塞尔说，“不过先生，能不能再告诉我们，他们用什么方法取出那些珍珠？”
“办法不只一种。珍珠若黏在壳上，采珠人常用钳子撬下来。不过最常见的办法，是把珍珠贝摊在珠滩遍地的海藻席上，让它们在空气中死去。过了十天，贝肉已经腐坏得相当厉害，便投入装满海水的大池，再开壳洗净。”
“珍珠的价格随个头大小而定？”康塞尔问。

“不仅看大小，”我答道，“还看形状，看水头，也就是它的色泽，还要看珠光，那是一层明亮而又微微带着细纹的闪光，最叫眼睛欢喜。顶美的称作处女珠，也叫绝品珠，单独结在贝体组织中，颜色洁白，多半不透明，偶尔也像蛋白石般半透。形状通常是圆形或卵圆形。圆珠拿来串手链，卵圆珠做坠子，因为更珍贵，往往一颗一颗出售。粘连在贝壳上的珍珠形状较不规则，论重量售卖。末一等是称为米珠的小珍珠，用量器计价，尤其适于绣制教堂的饰物。”
“可是，”康塞尔问，“采珠有危险吗？”
“没有，”我立刻答道，“尤其是采取了某些防备的时候。”
“干这行能有什么险可冒？”尼德·兰德说，“最多灌上几口海水？”
“就照你说的，尼德。顺便问一句，”我努力学尼摩船长那满不在乎的口气，“勇敢的尼德，你怕鲨鱼吗？”
“我！”加拿大人答道，“一个靠捕鲸叉吃饭的人？不把它们放在眼里就是我的行当。”
“可是，”我说，“这次可不比平常拿铁钩钓住，吊到船上，大砍刀一挥斩去尾巴，再剖开肚子，把心扔回海里！”
“那么，是要——”
“正是。”
“在水里？”
“在水里。”
“嗐！只要有把好叉子！先生，您知道，鲨鱼这畜生长得不大得法。它要咬住您，得先翻个身，把肚子转过来。趁这个当口——”
尼德·兰德偏会把“咬住”两个字说得叫我血都凉了。
“那么你呢，康塞尔，你对鲨鱼有什么想法？”
“我！”康塞尔说，“先生，我愿意照直说。”
“那就再好不过。”我暗想。
“先生若打算正面迎战鲨鱼，我实在看不出，为什么先生忠实的仆人不该陪先生一同面对。”

sections.title_zh: 下部 / 第3章　价值千万的珍珠
sections.title_en: PART TWO / CHAPTER III — A PEARL OF TEN MILLIONS
source_paragraphs: The next morning at four o’clock I was awakened by the steward whom Captain Nemo had placed at my service. I rose hurriedly, dressed, and went into the saloon.
Captain Nemo was awaiting me.
“M. Aronnax,” said he, “are you ready to start?”
“I am ready.”
“Then please to follow me.”
“And my companions, Captain?”
“They have been told and are waiting.”
“Are we not to put on our diver’s dresses?” asked I.

“Not yet. I have not allowed the _Nautilus_ to come too near this coast, and we are some distance from the Manaar Bank; but the boat is ready, and will take us to the exact point of disembarking, which will save us a long way. It carries our diving apparatus, which we will put on when we begin our submarine journey.”

Captain Nemo conducted me to the central staircase, which led on the platform. Ned and Conseil were already there, delighted at the idea of the “pleasure party” which was preparing. Five sailors from the _Nautilus_, with their oars, waited in the boat, which had been made fast against the side.

The night was still dark. Layers of clouds covered the sky, allowing but few stars to be seen. I looked on the side where the land lay, and saw nothing but a dark line enclosing three parts of the horizon, from south-west to north-west. The _Nautilus_, having returned during the night up the western coast of Ceylon, was now west of the bay, or rather gulf, formed by the mainland and the Island of Manaar. There, under the dark waters, stretched the pintadine bank, an inexhaustible field of pearls, the length of which is more than twenty miles.
Captain Nemo, Ned Land, Conseil, and I took our places in the stern of the boat. The master went to the tiller; his four companions leaned on their oars, the painter was cast off, and we sheered off.

The boat went towards the south; the oarsmen did not hurry. I noticed that their strokes, strong in the water, only followed each other every ten seconds, according to the method generally adopted in the navy. Whilst the craft was running by its own velocity, the liquid drops struck the dark depths of the waves crisply like spats of melted lead. A little billow, spreading wide, gave a slight roll to the boat, and some samphire reeds flapped before it.

We were silent. What was Captain Nemo thinking of? Perhaps of the land he was approaching, and which he found too near to him, contrary to the Canadian’s opinion, who thought it too far off. As to Conseil, he was merely there from curiosity.

About half-past five the first tints on the horizon showed the upper line of coast more distinctly. Flat enough in the east, it rose a little to the south. Five miles still lay between us, and it was indistinct owing to the mist on the water. At six o’clock it became suddenly daylight, with that rapidity peculiar to tropical regions, which know neither dawn nor twilight. The solar rays pierced the curtain of clouds, piled up on the eastern horizon, and the radiant orb rose rapidly. I saw land distinctly, with a few trees scattered here and there. The boat neared Manaar Island, which was rounded to the south. Captain Nemo rose from his seat and watched the sea.
At a sign from him the anchor was dropped, but the chain scarcely ran, for it was little more than a yard deep, and this spot was one of the highest points of the bank of pintadines.

“Here we are, M. Aronnax,” said Captain Nemo. “You see that enclosed bay? Here, in a month will be assembled the numerous fishing boats of the exporters, and these are the waters their divers will ransack so boldly. Happily, this bay is well situated for that kind of fishing. It is sheltered from the strongest winds; the sea is never very rough here, which makes it favourable for the diver’s work. We will now put on our dresses, and begin our walk.”

I did not answer, and, while watching the suspected waves, began with the help of the sailors to put on my heavy sea-dress. Captain Nemo and my companions were also dressing. None of the _Nautilus_ men were to accompany us on this new excursion.

Soon we were enveloped to the throat in india-rubber clothing; the air apparatus fixed to our backs by braces. As to the Ruhmkorff apparatus, there was no necessity for it. Before putting my head into the copper cap, I had asked the question of the Captain.

“They would be useless,” he replied. “We are going to no great depth, and the solar rays will be enough to light our walk. Besides, it would not be prudent to carry the electric light in these waters; its brilliancy might attract some of the dangerous inhabitants of the coast most inopportunely.”
As Captain Nemo pronounced these words, I turned to Conseil and Ned Land. But my two friends had already encased their heads in the metal cap, and they could neither hear nor answer.
One last question remained to ask of Captain Nemo.
“And our arms?” asked I; “our guns?”
“Guns! What for? Do not mountaineers attack the bear with a dagger in their hand, and is not steel surer than lead? Here is a strong blade; put it in your belt, and we start.”
I looked at my companions; they were armed like us, and, more than that, Ned Land was brandishing an enormous harpoon, which he had placed in the boat before leaving the _Nautilus_.

Then, following the Captain’s example, I allowed myself to be dressed in the heavy copper helmet, and our reservoirs of air were at once in activity. An instant after we were landed, one after the other, in about two yards of water upon an even sand. Captain Nemo made a sign with his hand, and we followed him by a gentle declivity till we disappeared under the waves.

Over our feet, like coveys of snipe in a bog, rose shoals of fish, of the genus monoptera, which have no other fins but their tail. I recognized the Javanese, a real serpent two and a half feet long, of a livid colour underneath, and which might easily be mistaken for a conger eel if it were not for the golden stripes on its side. In the genus stromateus, whose bodies are very flat and oval, I saw some of the most brilliant colours, carrying their dorsal fin like a scythe; an excellent eating fish, which, dried and pickled, is known by the name of Karawade; then some tranquebars, belonging to the genus apsiphoroides, whose body is covered with a shell cuirass of eight longitudinal plates.

The heightening sun lit the mass of waters more and more. The soil changed by degrees. To the fine sand succeeded a perfect causeway of boulders, covered with a carpet of molluscs and zoophytes. Amongst the specimens of these branches I noticed some placenae, with thin unequal shells, a kind of ostracion peculiar to the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean; some orange lucinae with rounded shells; rockfish three feet and a half long, which raised themselves under the waves like hands ready to seize one. There were also some panopyres, slightly luminous; and lastly, some oculines, like magnificent fans, forming one of the richest vegetations of these seas.

In the midst of these living plants, and under the arbours of the hydrophytes, were layers of clumsy articulates, particularly some raninae, whose carapace formed a slightly rounded triangle; and some horrible looking parthenopes.
At about seven o’clock we found ourselves at last surveying the oyster-banks on which the pearl-oysters are reproduced by millions.

Captain Nemo pointed with his hand to the enormous heap of oysters; and I could well understand that this mine was inexhaustible, for Nature’s creative power is far beyond man’s instinct of destruction. Ned Land, faithful to his instinct, hastened to fill a net which he carried by his side with some of the finest specimens. But we could not stop. We must follow the Captain, who seemed to guide himself by paths known only to himself. The ground was sensibly rising, and sometimes, on holding up my arm, it was above the surface of the sea. Then the level of the bank would sink capriciously. Often we rounded high rocks scarped into pyramids. In their dark fractures huge crustacea, perched upon their high claws like some war-machine, watched us with fixed eyes, and under our feet crawled various kinds of annelides.

At this moment there opened before us a large grotto dug in a picturesque heap of rocks and carpeted with all the thick warp of the submarine flora. At first it seemed very dark to me. The solar rays seemed to be extinguished by successive gradations, until its vague transparency became nothing more than drowned light. Captain Nemo entered; we followed. My eyes soon accustomed themselves to this relative state of darkness.
