I could distinguish the arches springing capriciously from natural pillars, standing broad upon their granite base, like the heavy columns of Tuscan architecture. Why had our incomprehensible guide led us to the bottom of this submarine crypt? I was soon to know. After descending a rather sharp declivity, our feet trod the bottom of a kind of circular pit. There Captain Nemo stopped, and with his hand indicated an object I had not yet perceived. It was an oyster of extraordinary dimensions, a gigantic tridacne, a goblet which could have contained a whole lake of holy-water, a basin the breadth of which was more than two yards and a half, and consequently larger than that ornamenting the saloon of the _Nautilus_. I approached this extraordinary mollusc. It adhered by its filaments to a table of granite, and there, isolated, it developed itself in the calm waters of the grotto. I estimated the weight of this tridacne at 600 lbs. Such an oyster would contain 30 lbs. of meat; and one must have the stomach of a Gargantua to demolish some dozens of them.

Captain Nemo was evidently acquainted with the existence of this bivalve, and seemed to have a particular motive in verifying the actual state of this tridacne. The shells were a little open; the Captain came near and put his dagger between to prevent them from closing; then with his hand he raised the membrane with its fringed edges, which formed a cloak for the creature. There, between the folded plaits, I saw a loose pearl, whose size equalled that of a coco-nut. Its globular shape, perfect clearness, and admirable lustre made it altogether a jewel of inestimable value. Carried away by my curiosity, I stretched out my hand to seize it, weigh it, and touch it; but the Captain stopped me, made a sign of refusal, and quickly withdrew his dagger, and the two shells closed suddenly. I then understood Captain Nemo’s intention. In leaving this pearl hidden in the mantle of the tridacne he was allowing it to grow slowly. Each year the secretions of the mollusc would add new concentric circles. I estimated its value at £500,000 at least.

After ten minutes Captain Nemo stopped suddenly. I thought he had halted previously to returning. No; by a gesture he bade us crouch beside him in a deep fracture of the rock, his hand pointed to one part of the liquid mass, which I watched attentively.

About five yards from me a shadow appeared, and sank to the ground. The disquieting idea of sharks shot through my mind, but I was mistaken; and once again it was not a monster of the ocean that we had anything to do with.

It was a man, a living man, an Indian, a fisherman, a poor devil who, I suppose, had come to glean before the harvest. I could see the bottom of his canoe anchored some feet above his head. He dived and went up successively. A stone held between his feet, cut in the shape of a sugar loaf, whilst a rope fastened him to his boat, helped him to descend more rapidly. This was all his apparatus. Reaching the bottom, about five yards deep, he went on his knees and filled his bag with oysters picked up at random. Then he went up, emptied it, pulled up his stone, and began the operation once more, which lasted thirty seconds.

The diver did not see us. The shadow of the rock hid us from sight. And how should this poor Indian ever dream that men, beings like himself, should be there under the water watching his movements and losing no detail of the fishing? Several times he went up in this way, and dived again. He did not carry away more than ten at each plunge, for he was obliged to pull them from the bank to which they adhered by means of their strong byssus. And how many of those oysters for which he risked his life had no pearl in them! I watched him closely; his manœuvres were regular; and for the space of half an hour no danger appeared to threaten him.

I was beginning to accustom myself to the sight of this interesting fishing, when suddenly, as the Indian was on the ground, I saw him make a gesture of terror, rise, and make a spring to return to the surface of the sea.

I understood his dread. A gigantic shadow appeared just above the unfortunate diver. It was a shark of enormous size advancing diagonally, his eyes on fire, and his jaws open. I was mute with horror and unable to move.
The voracious creature shot towards the Indian, who threw himself on one side to avoid the shark’s fins; but not its tail, for it struck his chest and stretched him on the ground.

This scene lasted but a few seconds: the shark returned, and, turning on his back, prepared himself for cutting the Indian in two, when I saw Captain Nemo rise suddenly, and then, dagger in hand, walk straight to the monster, ready to fight face to face with him. The very moment the shark was going to snap the unhappy fisherman in two, he perceived his new adversary, and, turning over, made straight towards him.

I can still see Captain Nemo’s position. Holding himself well together, he waited for the shark with admirable coolness; and, when it rushed at him, threw himself on one side with wonderful quickness, avoiding the shock, and burying his dagger deep into its side. But it was not all over. A terrible combat ensued.
A terrible combat began

The shark had seemed to roar, if I might say so. The blood rushed in torrents from its wound. The sea was dyed red, and through the opaque liquid I could distinguish nothing more. Nothing more until the moment when, like lightning, I saw the undaunted Captain hanging on to one of the creature’s fins, struggling, as it were, hand to hand with the monster, and dealing successive blows at his enemy, yet still unable to give a decisive one.
The shark’s struggles agitated the water with such fury that the rocking threatened to upset me.
I wanted to go to the Captain’s assistance, but, nailed to the spot with horror, I could not stir.

I saw the haggard eye; I saw the different phases of the fight. The Captain fell to the earth, upset by the enormous mass which leant upon him. The shark’s jaws opened wide, like a pair of factory shears, and it would have been all over with the Captain; but, quick as thought, harpoon in hand, Ned Land rushed towards the shark and struck it with its sharp point.

The waves were impregnated with a mass of blood. They rocked under the shark’s movements, which beat them with indescribable fury. Ned Land had not missed his aim. It was the monster’s death-rattle. Struck to the heart, it struggled in dreadful convulsions, the shock of which overthrew Conseil.

But Ned Land had disentangled the Captain, who, getting up without any wound, went straight to the Indian, quickly cut the cord which held him to his stone, took him in his arms, and, with a sharp blow of his heel, mounted to the surface.
We all three followed in a few seconds, saved by a miracle, and reached the fisherman’s boat.

Captain Nemo’s first care was to recall the unfortunate man to life again. I did not think he could succeed. I hoped so, for the poor creature’s immersion was not long; but the blow from the shark’s tail might have been his death-blow.

Happily, with the Captain’s and Conseil’s sharp friction, I saw consciousness return by degrees. He opened his eyes. What was his surprise, his terror even, at seeing four great copper heads leaning over him! And, above all, what must he have thought when Captain Nemo, drawing from the pocket of his dress a bag of pearls, placed it in his hand! This munificent charity from the man of the waters to the poor Cingalese was accepted with a trembling hand. His wondering eyes showed that he knew not to what super-human beings he owed both fortune and life.
At a sign from the Captain we regained the bank, and, following the road already traversed, came in about half an hour to the anchor which held the canoe of the _Nautilus_ to the earth.
Once on board, we each, with the help of the sailors, got rid of the heavy copper helmet.
Captain Nemo’s first word was to the Canadian.
“Thank you, Master Land,” said he.
“It was in revenge, Captain,” replied Ned Land. “I owed you that.”
A ghastly smile passed across the Captain’s lips, and that was all.
“To the _Nautilus_,” said he.

The boat flew over the waves. Some minutes after we met the shark’s dead body floating. By the black marking of the extremity of its fins, I recognised the terrible melanopteron of the Indian Seas, of the species of shark so properly called. It was more than twenty-five feet long; its enormous mouth occupied one-third of its body. It was an adult, as was known by its six rows of teeth placed in an isosceles triangle in the upper jaw.

Whilst I was contemplating this inert mass, a dozen of these voracious beasts appeared round the boat; and, without noticing us, threw themselves upon the dead body and fought with one another for the pieces.
At half-past eight we were again on board the _Nautilus_. There I reflected on the incidents which had taken place in our excursion to the Manaar Bank.

Two conclusions I must inevitably draw from it—one bearing upon the unparalleled courage of Captain Nemo, the other upon his devotion to a human being, a representative of that race from which he fled beneath the sea. Whatever he might say, this strange man had not yet succeeded in entirely crushing his heart.
When I made this observation to him, he answered in a slightly moved tone:
“That Indian, sir, is an inhabitant of an oppressed country; and I am still, and shall be, to my last breath, one of them!”
translated_paragraphs: 次日凌晨四点，尼摩船长派来服侍我的侍役把我唤醒。我匆匆起身穿衣，去了客厅。
尼摩船长正在等我。
“阿龙纳斯先生，”他说，“可以出发了吗？”
“准备好了。”
“那请跟我来。”
“船长，我的同伴呢？”
“已经通知，他们在等了。”
“我们不穿潜水服吗？”我问。
“现在还不穿。我没有让‘鹦鹉螺号’过分接近这段海岸。我们离马纳尔珠滩还有一段距离。不过小艇已经备好，它会把我们送到恰当的下水地点，省上好长一段路。潜水装具就在艇里，等要动身走海底那一程时再穿。”
尼摩船长领我走到通往平台的中央阶梯。尼德和康塞尔已到了，很为即将到来的这场“游乐”而高兴。“鹦鹉螺号”的五名水手带着桨，候在系于船舷的小艇里。
天色还完全是黑的。层层云幕遮住天空，只容几颗星透出。我朝陆地所在的方向望去，只见一道从西南延至西北的黑边，把那一方大半的天际围住。夜间“鹦鹉螺号”已折向北，沿锡兰西岸航行。现在它位于陆地同马纳尔岛围成的那个小湾——更确切说，那片海湾——的西方。在那里的暗水底下，珠母贝滩绵延超过二十英里，是采之不尽的珍珠田。
尼摩船长、尼德·兰德、康塞尔和我坐进艇尾。水手长掌舵，他的四位伙伴执桨就位。艇首索解开，我们轻轻离了船。
小艇往南走，桨手们不慌不忙。他们下桨有力，我留意数了数，两桨之间隔着十秒，正是海军惯用的划法。小艇借自身的冲力滑行时，桨叶滴下的水珠清脆地敲在黑幽幽的浪上，像飞溅的铅汁。一个小浪缓缓摊开，叫小艇轻轻一摇，几根海滨水草在艇前拍动。
大家都没说话。尼摩船长在想什么？也许想的是正在接近的陆地。他怕嫌岸太近，加拿大人却一心嫌岸太远。至于康塞尔，只为好奇，便坐在这里。
五点半左右，天际出现初光，海岸的上缘清楚了些。东面颇为平整，往南略见升高。离我们仍有五英里，又因水上笼着薄雾，看来还不真切。六点，天猛然大亮。只有既不大见黎明又不大见黄昏的热带地方，才有这种速度。太阳的光线穿过堆在东方地平线的云幕，光辉的日轮迅速上升。我清楚看见了陆地，几株树疏疏落落点在其间。小艇向马纳尔岛靠近，从南端绕了过去。尼摩船长从座位上站起，观察海面。
他一打手势，艇上便抛了锚。锚链几乎没有放下多少，因为水深才刚过一码。我们来到的，是珠母贝滩最高的地点之一。
“到了，阿龙纳斯先生，”尼摩船长说，“您看见那边四面围拢的小湾了吗？再过一个月，众多珠商的采珠船就会聚到这里。那班潜水人要大胆搜遍的正是这些海水。好在这个湾地势适合采珠。它避开了最烈的风，海面从来不太粗暴，对水下作业很有利。现在穿好衣服，开始散步吧。”
我没有回答，一面注视着那片使我疑虑的波浪，一面在水手的帮助下穿起沉重的潜水服。尼摩船长和同伴们也在穿衣。“鹦鹉螺号”的水手，这次没有一个跟我们走。
不久，橡胶衣一直将我们裹到脖子，储气装置也用肩带固定在背上。鲁姆科夫照明装置却用不着。在把脑袋塞进铜盔以前，我已问过船长。
“那些用不上，”他回答，“我们下得并不深，有阳光足够照亮道路。何况在这带水域携带电灯并不审慎。那灯光太亮，说不定会在极不合宜的时候，把沿岸某些危险的居民吸引来。”
尼摩船长说出这话时，我转头看康塞尔和尼德·兰德。可朋友们已经把头套进金属盔，既听不见，也无从回答。
我还有最后一个问题要问尼摩船长。
“那么武器呢？”我问，“我们的枪呢？”
“枪！拿来做什么？山民敢执一把短刀去攻熊，钢刀岂不是比铅弹可靠？给您一把坚牢的刀，插在腰带上，咱们走吧。”
我望望同伴。他俩同我们一样带了刀。此外，尼德·兰德手上还挥着一柄大得惊人的捕鲸叉，离开“鹦鹉螺号”之前，他已经把它藏到小艇里了。
我照船长的榜样，让人给我套上沉重的铜盔，储气罐立即运转起来。片刻之后，我们相继下艇，落在平整的沙底，水深约两码。尼摩船长用手一招，我们便跟着他走下一道缓坡，渐渐没入浪下。
脚边成群鱼惊起，像沼泽地里飞起一群群沙锥鸟。那是些单鳍鳝，除尾部以外别无鳍片。我认出了爪哇的一种，活像一条两英尺半长的蛇，腹部青白。若不是身侧有几道金纹，很容易认作康吉鳗。在身子扁平呈卵形的鲳鱼属里，我见到几尾颜色鲜艳的，背鳍像一把镰刀。此鱼滋味甚好，晒干腌过，便是人们叫作“卡拉瓦德”的食品。接着是几尾特兰奎巴尔的甲鱼形小鱼，八列纵长的骨板在身上构成一副甲壳。
太阳越升越高，照得整片海水越来越亮。地面也逐渐改变，细沙过后竟是一整道卵石铺成的路，覆盖着软体动物和植形动物的地毯。在这些类群里，我留意到窗贝，薄壳左右不等，属红海和印度洋特有的有壳生物；接着有橙黄、圆壳的满月蛤；还有身长三英尺半的岩栖鱼，在水下挺立起来，像几只随时准备把人抓住的手。另有微微发光的几样贝，以及眼珊瑚，像一把把华丽的扇子，构成这片洋面上最繁盛的“草木”之一。
在这些活的花木之间，在海草搭起的凉棚底下，一层层挤着笨重的节肢动物。特别有蛙蟹，头胸甲呈微圆的三角形；还有几只菱蟹，模样可实在吓人。
七点左右，我们终于来到那片珠母贝以百万计地繁衍的贝滩，亲眼端详它的全貌。

尼摩船长用手指着层层叠叠的贝。我能相信这座矿藏取之不尽，因为自然创造的力量原就远远超过人类毁坏的本能。尼德·兰德倒是忠实地依从自己的本能，赶忙挑几只最漂亮的，塞进腰边带的网袋。然而不能久留。我们得跟上船长，他走的仿佛都是自己才认得的路径。海床明显往上升高。有时我把胳膊一举，手就伸出水面了。随后珠滩又任性地低落下去。我们时时绕过一些被削成金字塔形的高礁。在礁石幽暗的裂隙中，巨型甲壳动物高踞在长爪上，像一台台战争机器，瞪着眼睛望我们。脚边则有种种环节动物在爬。

这时前方现出一座大洞窟，开在一堆形状别致的岩石中，地上披着海底水草织成的厚毯。我起初觉得洞里相当暗，阳光仿佛一层层熄去，那一丝朦胧的通透，到头只像溺在水里的光。尼摩船长进了洞，我们跟进去。眼睛很快适应了这相对的昏暗。我辨认出天然立柱上随势架起的道道拱券，柱脚宽阔，安在花岗岩基座上，像托斯卡纳建筑中那种厚重的圆柱。我们这不可捉摸的向导，为什么把我们领到水下地穴的深处？我很快便知道了。走下一道颇陡的坡，我们踏在一处圆形洼地底部。尼摩船长在这里停下，用手指出一样我此前没留意到的东西。那是一只大得出奇的贝，一只巨砗磲！这个杯子能装得下一整湖圣水，盆口超过两码半宽，比点缀“鹦鹉螺号”客厅的那只还大。我走近这只非凡的软体动物。它以足丝牢牢附在一块平坦的花岗岩上，孤零零地在洞中平静的海水里生长。我估计这只砗磲重六百磅。这样一个贝可有三十磅肉；要一口气吃掉几十个这样的家伙，非得有个巨人卡冈都亚的胃不可。

尼摩船长显然知道这只双壳贝，也似乎有特别的理由要查一查它眼下的情形。两片壳微微张着。船长走近，把匕首插在当中，不让它闭合。接着他伸手掀起边缘缀着流苏的薄膜，那是遮罩贝体的外套膜。就在膜的一层层褶皱间，躺着一颗脱离壳面的珍珠，个头足足抵得上一枚椰子。球形圆整，光色清洁无瑕，珠辉美妙，使它成为一件根本无法估价的珠宝。我被好奇心催着，伸手想拿它掂掂，摸上一摸。船长拦住我，打手势表示不许，随即抽去匕首。两扇贝壳忽地扣合。我这才明白尼摩船长的用意。他把珍珠继续留在砗磲的外套膜里，就是为叫它慢慢长大。软体动物每一年的分泌，都还会为它加上新的同心圆层。我估它的价值至少有五十万英镑。
走了十分钟，尼摩船长忽然停住。我原以为他在准备掉头。不，他打手势命我们贴着他蹲进岩石的一条深缝，一手指向水里的某处。我凝神望去。
离我约五码，一个影子出现，慢慢沉到底。我脑中掠过叫人不安的鲨鱼，可我又猜错了。这回我们打交道的，仍然并非海中的怪兽。
是一个人，一个活人！一个印度人，一个渔夫，一个可怜的穷人。我猜，他想赶在正式收获以前，捡些零星的收成。我看得见他的独木舟底，锚就下在他头顶几英尺处。他不断下潜，上浮。他用两脚夹住一块削成糖锥形的石头，另有一根绳子连着船，凭石重便能较快沉底。这就是他的全部装具。到了约五码深的海床，他双膝跪下，随手拾贝塞满袋子。随后上浮，倒空袋子，提起石块，再做一遍。整套动作，只有三十秒钟。
潜水人没看见我们。岩影遮住了我们的身形。这个可怜的印度人又怎会想到，水下还有人，同他一样的人，正默默看他的一举一动，采珠的每个细节都看得一清二楚？他这样上浮，又下潜，来来回回好几次。每次带走的贝不超过十个，因为它们用坚牢的足丝粘在滩上，非用力扯下不可。他冒着性命危险采的这些贝，究竟会有多少个压根没有珍珠啊！我专注地看着他。他的动作很有规律。半小时过去，并没有什么危险威胁到他。
我正看得渐渐习惯了这种有趣的采珠作业，忽然见印度人还在海床上便做了个惊恐的手势，立起身，猛地一蹬要逃回水面。
他的恐惧我立刻就明白了。一个巨大的黑影出现在那不幸的潜水人正上方。那是一头硕大无朋的鲨鱼，正斜着冲来，两眼像要喷火，双颌大张。我吓得既不能出声，又不能动。
贪食的怪物朝印度人疾射过去。他向一侧扑倒，侥幸避过鱼鳍，却没有避开鱼尾。大尾巴正击中胸口，把他撂倒在地。
这一幕只有几秒。鲨鱼去而复返，翻过身子，准备把印度人咬作两截。此时我看见尼摩船长猛地站起，手执匕首，竟直接迎向怪物，准备同它面对面搏斗。就在鲨鱼要一口咬断不幸的采珠人的瞬间，它看见了新的对手，翻个身，直奔船长而来。
我至今还看得见尼摩船长当时的身姿。他全身收紧站稳，以令人钦佩的冷静等着鲨鱼。它一扑下来，他向侧面一闪，快得出奇。避过迎头一冲的同时，匕首已深深扎入它侧腹。但事情远未结束。一场可怕的搏斗随之展开。
图注　一场可怕的搏斗开始了
要是可以这么形容，那鲨鱼仿佛咆哮起来。鲜血从伤口里成股涌出。大海染得通红，水不再透明，我什么也看不清了。直到一瞬如闪电，我才看见那毫不畏惧的船长抓住了鲨鱼的一面鳍，像跟怪物徒手相搏一般，一刀接一刀地捅着仇敌，却始终没能扎中决定胜负的要害。
鲨鱼挣扎得极其狂暴，水流被它搅荡，颠得我几乎立足不住。
我想上前帮船长，可是惊骇把我钉在原处，我一动也动不了。
我看清了那双惊骇的眼睛，看见搏斗中一个又一个不同的瞬间。船长倒在海床上，那具巨大的躯体压过来，把他掀翻了。鲨鱼双颌大张，像厂里一把巨剪。船长原本就要完了。不料尼德·兰德快得简直同念头一样，手执捕鲸叉朝鲨鱼冲去，将尖锐的叉锋狠狠刺下。
水中尽是浓血。鲨鱼扑打得凶狠难言，波浪随着它的挣动来回摇荡。尼德·兰德没有失手。那是怪物临死的挣扎。它已被刺中心脏，还在猛烈抽搐，震起的水浪竟将康塞尔掀倒。
可尼德·兰德已使船长脱了身。他站起，身上竟没有伤，径直奔向印度人，迅速割断系住石块的绳索，把人抱进怀里，脚后跟有力一蹬，便升向水面。
我们三个人几秒之后也跟上去。众人奇迹般脱险，到了渔夫的小艇边。
尼摩船长头一桩心事，是设法把这个不幸的人救醒。我不大认为他能成功，心里却又盼着如此。那可怜人在水下的时间并不算长，但鲨尾打来的那一下，可能已是致命伤。
幸而船长和康塞尔用力揉搓之下，我看见他渐渐恢复了知觉。他睁开双眼，瞧见四颗大铜脑袋全俯在他上方，想想他该有多惊异，甚至多么害怕！尤其是尼摩船长又从衣袋里取出一袋珍珠，塞到他的手上。那时他又能怎么想？来自海中人的这份慷慨馈赠，那贫穷的僧伽罗人用颤抖的手接住了。他惊异的眼神分明在说：生命和财富一并得还，自己却全不知道该感谢什么超凡的存在。
船长一打手势，我们便回到贝滩，沿来路往回走。约半小时后，已到将“鹦鹉螺号”的小艇系在海底的锚跟前。
一上艇，水手便帮我们一个个摘下沉重的铜盔。
尼摩船长的第一句话是说给加拿大人听的。
“谢谢您，兰德师傅。”他说。
“这是还您的人情，船长，”尼德·兰德答道，“我本来就欠您这一回。”
一丝惨淡的笑掠过船长嘴边，再没别的了。
“回‘鹦鹉螺号’。”他说。
小艇贴浪如飞。几分钟后，我们遇见死去鲨鱼漂浮的尸体。看它各鳍尖端的黑纹，我认出那就是印度洋可怕的黑鳍鲨，真正当得起鲨鱼这个名字的一种。它身长超过二十五英尺，巨口占去体长的三分之一。从上颌排成等腰三角形的六排牙齿，可以看出它已长成。
我还在观察这团一动不动的尸肉，小艇周围已出现十来条同样贪吃的怪兽。它们不理会我们，一齐扑向尸体，互相争抢撕下的碎块。
八点半，我们又回到“鹦鹉螺号”上。在那里，我思量着这趟马纳尔珠滩之行所发生的一件件事。
我势必从中得出两个结论。其一关乎尼摩船长无可比拟的勇气，其二关乎他对一个人的舍命相救。那人正是他遁入海底所要逃避的种族——人类——中的一个。任这个奇人怎样说，他到底还没有能够把自己的这颗心完全压死。
我把这番观察向他一提，他以略带激动的口气答道：
“先生，那个印度人是受压迫国家的人民。我自己也是他们中的一员。直到最后一口气，我永远是他们中的一员！”

sections.title_en: PART TWO / CHAPTER IV — THE RED SEA
source_paragraphs: In the course of the day of the 29th of January, the island of Ceylon disappeared under the horizon, and the _Nautilus_, at a speed of twenty miles an hour, slid into the labyrinth of canals which separate the Maldives from the Laccadives. It coasted even the Island of Kiltan, a land originally coraline, discovered by Vasco da Gama in 1499, and one of the nineteen principal islands of the Laccadive Archipelago, situated between 10° and 14° 30′ N. lat., and 69° 50′ 72″ E. long.
We had made 16,220 miles, or 7,500 (French) leagues from our starting-point in the Japanese Seas.

The next day (30th January), when the _Nautilus_ went to the surface of the ocean there was no land in sight. Its course was N.N.E., in the direction of the Sea of Oman, between Arabia and the Indian Peninsula, which serves as an outlet to the Persian Gulf. It was evidently a block without any possible egress. Where was Captain Nemo taking us to? I could not say. This, however, did not satisfy the Canadian, who that day came to me asking where we were going.
“We are going where our Captain’s fancy takes us, Master Ned.”
“His fancy cannot take us far, then,” said the Canadian. “The Persian Gulf has no outlet: and, if we do go in, it will not be long before we are out again.”
“Very well, then, we will come out again, Master Land; and if, after the Persian Gulf, the _Nautilus_ would like to visit the Red Sea, the Straits of Bab-el-mandeb are there to give us entrance.”

“I need not tell you, sir,” said Ned Land, “that the Red Sea is as much closed as the Gulf, as the Isthmus of Suez is not yet cut; and, if it was, a boat as mysterious as ours would not risk itself in a canal cut with sluices. And again, the Red Sea is not the road to take us back to Europe.”
“But I never said we were going back to Europe.”
“What do you suppose, then?”

“I suppose that, after visiting the curious coasts of Arabia and Egypt, the _Nautilus_ will go down the Indian Ocean again, perhaps cross the Channel of Mozambique, perhaps off the Mascarenhas, so as to gain the Cape of Good Hope.”
“And once at the Cape of Good Hope?” asked the Canadian, with peculiar emphasis.

“Well, we shall penetrate into that Atlantic which we do not yet know. Ah! friend Ned, you are getting tired of this journey under the sea; you are surfeited with the incessantly varying spectacle of submarine wonders. For my part, I shall be sorry to see the end of a voyage which it is given to so few men to make.”

For four days, till the 3rd of February, the _Nautilus_ scoured the Sea of Oman, at various speeds and at various depths. It seemed to go at random, as if hesitating as to which road it should follow, but we never passed the Tropic of Cancer.

In quitting this sea we sighted Muscat for an instant, one of the most important towns of the country of Oman. I admired its strange aspect, surrounded by black rocks upon which its white houses and forts stood in relief. I saw the rounded domes of its mosques, the elegant points of its minarets, its fresh and verdant terraces. But it was only a vision! The _Nautilus_ soon sank under the waves of that part of the sea.

We passed along the Arabian coast of Mahrah and Hadramaut, for a distance of six miles, its undulating line of mountains being occasionally relieved by some ancient ruin. The 5th of February we at last entered the Gulf of Aden, a perfect funnel introduced into the neck of Bab-el-mandeb, through which the Indian waters entered the Red Sea.

The 6th of February, the _Nautilus_ floated in sight of Aden, perched upon a promontory which a narrow isthmus joins to the mainland, a kind of inaccessible Gibraltar, the fortifications of which were rebuilt by the English after taking possession in 1839. I caught a glimpse of the octagon minarets of this town, which was at one time the richest commercial magazine on the coast.
I certainly thought that Captain Nemo, arrived at this point, would back out again; but I was mistaken, for he did no such thing, much to my surprise.
The next day, the 7th of February, we entered the Straits of Bab-el-mandeb, the name of which, in the Arab tongue, means The Gate of Tears.

To twenty miles in breadth, it is only thirty-two in length. And for the _Nautilus_, starting at full speed, the crossing was scarcely the work of an hour. But I saw nothing, not even the Island of Perim, with which the British Government has fortified the position of Aden. There were too many English or French steamers of the line of Suez to Bombay, Calcutta to Melbourne, and from Bourbon to the Mauritius, furrowing this narrow passage, for the _Nautilus_ to venture to show itself. So it remained prudently below. At last about noon, we were in the waters of the Red Sea.

I would not even seek to understand the caprice which had decided Captain Nemo upon entering the gulf. But I quite approved of the _Nautilus_ entering it. Its speed was lessened: sometimes it kept on the surface, sometimes it dived to avoid a vessel, and thus I was able to observe the upper and lower parts of this curious sea.

The 8th of February, from the first dawn of day, Mocha came in sight, now a ruined town, whose walls would fall at a gunshot, yet which shelters here and there some verdant date-trees; once an important city, containing six public markets, and twenty-six mosques, and whose walls, defended by fourteen forts, formed a girdle of two miles in circumference.

The _Nautilus_ then approached the African shore, where the depth of the sea was greater. There, between two waters clear as crystal, through the open panels we were allowed to contemplate the beautiful bushes of brilliant coral and large blocks of rock clothed with a splendid fur of green algæ and fuci. What an indescribable spectacle, and what variety of sites and landscapes along these sandbanks and volcanic islands which bound the Libyan coast! But where these shrubs appeared in all their beauty was on the eastern coast, which the _Nautilus_ soon gained. It was on the coast of Tehama, for there not only did this display of zoophytes flourish beneath the level of the sea, but they also formed picturesque interlacings which unfolded themselves about sixty feet above the surface, more capricious but less highly coloured than those whose freshness was kept up by the vital power of the waters.
What charming hours I passed thus at the window of the saloon! What new specimens of submarine flora and fauna did I admire under the brightness of our electric lantern!

The 9th of February the _Nautilus_ floated in the broadest part of the Red Sea, which is comprised between Souakin, on the west coast, and Komfidah, on the east coast, with a diameter of ninety miles.

That day at noon, after the bearings were taken, Captain Nemo mounted the platform, where I happened to be, and I was determined not to let him go down again without at least pressing him regarding his ulterior projects. As soon as he saw me he approached and graciously offered me a cigar.

“Well, sir, does this Red Sea please you? Have you sufficiently observed the wonders it covers, its fishes, its zoophytes, its parterres of sponges, and its forests of coral? Did you catch a glimpse of the towns on its borders?”
“Yes, Captain Nemo,” I replied; “and the _Nautilus_ is wonderfully fitted for such a study. Ah! it is an intelligent boat!”
“Yes, sir, intelligent and invulnerable. It fears neither the terrible tempests of the Red Sea, nor its currents, nor its sandbanks.”
“Certainly,” said I, “this sea is quoted as one of the worst, and in the time of the ancients, if I am not mistaken, its reputation was detestable.”

“Detestable, M. Aronnax. The Greek and Latin historians do not speak favourably of it, and Strabo says it is very dangerous during the Etesian winds and in the rainy season. The Arabian Edrisi portrays it under the name of the Gulf of Colzoum, and relates that vessels perished there in great numbers on the sandbanks and that no one would risk sailing in the night. It is, he pretends, a sea subject to fearful hurricanes, strewn with inhospitable islands, and ‘which offers nothing good either on its surface or in its depths.’”
“One may see,” I replied, “that these historians never sailed on board the _Nautilus_.”

“Just so,” replied the Captain, smiling; “and in that respect moderns are not more advanced than the ancients. It required many ages to find out the mechanical power of steam. Who knows if, in another hundred years, we may not see a second _Nautilus?_ Progress is slow, M. Aronnax.”
“It is true,” I answered; “your boat is at least a century before its time, perhaps an era. What a misfortune that the secret of such an invention should die with its inventor!”
Captain Nemo did not reply. After some minutes’ silence he continued:
“You were speaking of the opinions of ancient historians upon the dangerous navigation of the Red Sea.”
“It is true,” said I; “but were not their fears exaggerated?”

“Yes and no, M. Aronnax,” replied Captain Nemo, who seemed to know the Red Sea by heart. “That which is no longer dangerous for a modern vessel, well rigged, strongly built, and master of its own course, thanks to obedient steam, offered all sorts of perils to the ships of the ancients. Picture to yourself those first navigators venturing in ships made of planks sewn with the cords of the palmtree, saturated with the grease of the seadog, and covered with powdered resin! They had not even instruments wherewith to take their bearings, and they went by guess amongst currents of which they scarcely knew anything. Under such conditions shipwrecks were, and must have been, numerous. But in our time, steamers running between Suez and the South Seas have nothing more to fear from the fury of this gulf, in spite of contrary trade-winds. The captain and passengers do not prepare for their departure by offering propitiatory sacrifices; and, on their return, they no longer go ornamented with wreaths and gilt fillets to thank the gods in the neighbouring temple.”

“I agree with you,” said I; “and steam seems to have killed all gratitude in the hearts of sailors. But, Captain, since you seem to have especially studied this sea, can you tell me the origin of its name?”
“There exist several explanations on the subject, M. Aronnax. Would you like to know the opinion of a chronicler of the fourteenth century?”
“Willingly.”
“This fanciful writer pretends that its name was given to it after the passage of the Israelites, when Pharaoh perished in the waves which closed at the voice of Moses.”
“A poet’s explanation, Captain Nemo,” I replied; “but I cannot content myself with that. I ask you for your personal opinion.”

“Here it is, M. Aronnax. According to my idea, we must see in this appellation of the Red Sea a translation of the Hebrew word ‘Edom’; and if the ancients gave it that name, it was on account of the particular colour of its waters.”
“But up to this time I have seen nothing but transparent waves and without any particular colour.”
“Very likely; but as we advance to the bottom of the gulf, you will see this singular appearance. I remember seeing the Bay of Tor entirely red, like a sea of blood.”
“And you attribute this colour to the presence of a microscopic seaweed?”
“Yes.”
“So, Captain Nemo, it is not the first time you have overrun the Red Sea on board the _Nautilus?_”
“No, sir.”
“As you spoke a while ago of the passage of the Israelites and of the catastrophe to the Egyptians, I will ask whether you have met with the traces under the water of this great historical fact?”
“No, sir; and for a good reason.”
“What is it?”

“It is that the spot where Moses and his people passed is now so blocked up with sand that the camels can barely bathe their legs there. You can well understand that there would not be water enough for my _Nautilus_.”
“And the spot?” I asked.

“The spot is situated a little above the Isthmus of Suez, in the arm which formerly made a deep estuary, when the Red Sea extended to the Salt Lakes. Now, whether this passage were miraculous or not, the Israelites, nevertheless, crossed there to reach the Promised Land, and Pharaoh’s army perished precisely on that spot; and I think that excavations made in the middle of the sand would bring to light a large number of arms and instruments of Egyptian origin.”

“That is evident,” I replied; “and for the sake of archaeologists let us hope that these excavations will be made sooner or later, when new towns are established on the isthmus, after the construction of the Suez Canal; a canal, however, very useless to a vessel like the _Nautilus_.”

“Very likely; but useful to the whole world,” said Captain Nemo. “The ancients well understood the utility of a communication between the Red Sea and the Mediterranean for their commercial affairs: but they did not think of digging a canal direct, and took the Nile as an intermediate. Very probably the canal which united the Nile to the Red Sea was begun by Sesostris, if we may believe tradition. One thing is certain, that in the year 615 before Jesus Christ, Necos undertook the works of an alimentary canal to the waters of the Nile across the plain of Egypt, looking towards Arabia. It took four days to go up this canal, and it was so wide that two triremes could go abreast. It was carried on by Darius, the son of Hystaspes, and probably finished by Ptolemy II. Strabo saw it navigated: but its decline from the point of departure, near Bubastes, to the Red Sea was so slight that it was only navigable for a few months in the year. This canal answered all commercial purposes to the age of Antonius, when it was abandoned and blocked up with sand. Restored by order of the Caliph Omar, it was definitely destroyed in 761 or 762 by Caliph Al-Mansor, who wished to prevent the arrival of provisions to Mohammed-ben-Abdallah, who had revolted against him. During the expedition into Egypt, your General Bonaparte discovered traces of the works in the Desert of Suez; and, surprised by the tide, he nearly perished before regaining Hadjaroth, at the very place where Moses had encamped three thousand years before him.”

“Well, Captain, what the ancients dared not undertake, this junction between the two seas, which will shorten the road from Cadiz to India, M. Lesseps has succeeded in doing; and before long he will have changed Africa into an immense island.”

“Yes, M. Aronnax; you have the right to be proud of your countryman. Such a man brings more honour to a nation than great captains. He began, like so many others, with disgust and rebuffs; but he has triumphed, for he has the genius of will. And it is sad to think that a work like that, which ought to have been an international work and which would have sufficed to make a reign illustrious, should have succeeded by the energy of one man. All honour to M. Lesseps!”
“Yes! honour to the great citizen,” I replied, surprised by the manner in which Captain Nemo had just spoken.
“Unfortunately,” he continued, “I cannot take you through the Suez Canal; but you will be able to see the long jetty of Port Said after to-morrow, when we shall be in the Mediterranean.”
“The Mediterranean!” I exclaimed.
“Yes, sir; does that astonish you?”
“What astonishes me is to think that we shall be there the day after to-morrow.”
“Indeed?”
“Yes, Captain, although by this time I ought to have accustomed myself to be surprised at nothing since I have been on board your boat.”
“But the cause of this surprise?”

“Well! it is the fearful speed you will have to put on the _Nautilus_, if the day after to-morrow she is to be in the Mediterranean, having made the round of Africa, and doubled the Cape of Good Hope!”
“Who told you that she would make the round of Africa and double the Cape of Good Hope, sir?”
“Well, unless the _Nautilus_ sails on dry land, and passes above the isthmus——”
“Or beneath it, M. Aronnax.”
“Beneath it?”
“Certainly,” replied Captain Nemo quietly. “A long time ago Nature made under this tongue of land what man has this day made on its surface.”
“What! such a passage exists?”
“Yes; a subterranean passage, which I have named the Arabian Tunnel. It takes us beneath Suez and opens into the Gulf of Pelusium.”
“But this isthmus is composed of nothing but quicksands?”
“To a certain depth. But at fifty-five yards only there is a solid layer of rock.”
“Did you discover this passage by chance?” I asked more and more surprised.

“Chance and reasoning, sir; and by reasoning even more than by chance. Not only does this passage exist, but I have profited by it several times. Without that I should not have ventured this day into the impassable Red Sea. I noticed that in the Red Sea and in the Mediterranean there existed a certain number of fishes of a kind perfectly identical. Certain of the fact, I asked myself was it possible that there was no communication between the two seas? If there was, the subterranean current must necessarily run from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean, from the sole cause of difference of level. I caught a large number of fishes in the neighbourhood of Suez. I passed a copper ring through their tails, and threw them back into the sea. Some months later, on the coast of Syria, I caught some of my fish ornamented with the ring. Thus the communication between the two was proved. I then sought for it with my _Nautilus;_ I discovered it, ventured into it, and before long, sir, you too will have passed through my Arabian tunnel!”
translated_paragraphs: 一月二十九日这一天，锡兰岛沉到地平线以下。“鹦鹉螺号”以每小时二十英里的速度，滑入马尔代夫与拉克代夫两群岛之间迷宫般的水道。我们甚至贴着基尔坦岛的岸边驶过。这块土地原由珊瑚形成，一四九九年被瓦斯科·达·伽马发现，是拉克代夫群岛十九个主岛之一。群岛位于北纬十度至十四度三十分、东经六十九度五十分七十二秒一带。
自从在日本海域启程，我们已走过一万六千二百二十英里，合七千五百法里格。
次日一月三十日，“鹦鹉螺号”升到洋面，视野中已无陆地。航向北东北，指向阿拉伯与印度半岛之间的阿曼海，波斯湾便由那里通往外洋。这方向显然要走进一个不可能另有出口的死胡同。尼摩船长要带我们去什么地方，我说不上。可这答复不能叫加拿大人满意。他当天就来找我，问起我们正要往哪儿去。
“尼德师傅，船长的兴致到哪里，我们就去哪里。”
“那他的兴致可带我们走不了多少路，”加拿大人说，“波斯湾没有别的出口。真要进去，不多久就得原路回来。”
“好嘛，兰德师傅，那咱们就原路回来。逛了波斯湾以后，倘若‘鹦鹉螺号’又想游红海，曼德海峡不是在那里等着让我们进去吗？”
“先生，不用我提醒您，”尼德·兰德说，“红海跟那波斯湾一样是封死的。苏伊士地峡的运河尚未挖通。就算挖通，咱们这么神秘的一条船，也不会冒险开进一道设有水闸的运河。再说，走红海，并不是带咱们回欧洲的路。”
“可我从没说过我们要回欧洲。”
“那您猜怎样？”
“我猜，等看完阿拉伯和埃及的奇异海岸，‘鹦鹉螺号’便会折回印度洋往南去。也许穿过莫桑比克海峡，也许从马斯克林群岛近旁经过，总之是去好望角。”
“到了好望角以后呢？”加拿大人把那几个字咬得分外重。
“那么，就进入我们还不曾见识的大西洋。啊，尼德朋友，这趟海底旅行你已经厌倦了。海底奇观虽然变换不休，你也看腻了。我可不同。一个世上少有人有缘一尝的航程，眼看它结束，我会很舍不得。”
一连四天，直到二月三日，“鹦鹉螺号”在阿曼海的各处，以不等速度在不同深度来去，仿佛漫无目的，还犹豫着不知该选哪条路。不过我们始终没有越过北回归线。
离开这片海时，我们短暂望见了马斯喀特，阿曼最要紧的城市之一。我欣赏它那奇异的相貌。黑色岩石围着城镇，白屋和堡垒从上面鲜明地凸显出来。清真寺浑圆的穹顶、宣礼塔优美的尖顶、清新而葱绿的台地，我都瞥见了。可那不过是一道幻影！“鹦鹉螺号”不多时就潜入那片海水之下。
我们沿阿拉伯的马赫拉和哈德拉毛海岸驶过六英里。起伏的山脉轮廓，时不时被几处古代遗址打破。二月五日，我们终于进入亚丁湾。它像个漏斗，插在曼德海峡的细颈上，印度洋海水便从这里流入红海。
二月六日，从“鹦鹉螺号”上看得见亚丁了。这城市高踞于一处海岬，与大陆之间由一道狭窄地峡相接，活像一座不可攻入的直布罗陀。一八三九年英国人占领这里之后，重建了防御工事。我依稀看见城里那些八角形的宣礼塔。从前，亚丁曾是这段海岸上最富庶的商贸集散地。
我满以为尼摩船长到了这一点便会掉头出去。可他根本不肯掉头。出乎我的意料，是我想错了。
第二天，二月七日，我们进入曼德海峡。这个名称在阿拉伯语中意为“泪之门”。
它宽二十英里，长度不过三十二英里。对全速前进的“鹦鹉螺号”而言，用不了一个小时便能穿过。可我什么也没看见，甚至没有看见丕林岛，英国政府正靠它加强亚丁的防务。往来苏伊士和孟买、加尔各答和墨尔本、波旁岛和毛里求斯的英法轮船，在狭道中犁浪者太多，“鹦鹉螺号”不肯冒险露面，谨慎地停在水下。终于，约莫正午时分，我们已身处红海水域。
尼摩船长是起了什么兴致决定进入这个海湾，我连追究的念头都没有。不过对于“鹦鹉螺号”走进来，我倒完全赞成。船速减缓，时而浮在水面，时而为避船只下潜。我因此有机会将这片奇特海洋的水上水下都看一看。
二月八日，天刚破晓，摩卡便出现在眼前。如今这已是一座凋敝的城镇，城墙挨一炮怕就要倒，四处倒还护着一些青翠的海枣树。可它曾是重要的城市，内有六个公共市场、二十六座清真寺，城墙由十四座堡垒拱卫，围成一圈，周长两英里。

“鹦鹉螺号”接着靠近非洲一岸，那里水要深些。我们从开启的护板中间，透过清澈如水晶的海水，欣赏亮丽的珊瑚灌丛和巨大岩块。海藻和褐藻替岩石披上了一层华贵的绿色皮裘。沿着环护非洲海岸的沙洲和火山岛，风物景致千变万化，简直无法形容！然而这些灌丛尽显其美的地方，却是“鹦鹉螺号”很快抵达的东岸，就在帖哈麦海滨。那里，种种植形动物不只在海面以下茂盛繁育，还在水面以上约六十英尺高处展开优美的交织。露出水面的形状比水中更加变幻，色彩却不及那些由海水的滋养保持鲜活的同类浓艳。
我就这样守在客厅舷窗边，度过了多少叫人快活的时辰！在我们的电灯光中，又得以欣赏多少以前没见过的海底动植物标本！
二月九日，“鹦鹉螺号”驶在红海最宽的一段，位于西岸萨瓦金和东岸贡福宰之间，横宽九十英里。
那天正午，船位测定以后，尼摩船长登上平台。我恰好在那里，打定主意，在他再下去之前，总得追问一下往后的打算。他一见我便走近，和气地递来一支雪茄。
“那么，先生，这片红海可使您满意？它藏着的奇观，鱼、植形动物、海绵花坛和珊瑚森林，您看够了吗？岸边的城市，是否也瞧见一两眼？”
“是的，尼摩船长，”我答道，“要做这种研究，‘鹦鹉螺号’的装备好得出奇。啊！多聪明的一条船！”
“是啊，先生，既聪明，又刀枪不入。红海的可怕风暴、洋流和沙洲，它一样也不怕。”
“确实，”我说，“这片海向来有凶险之名。如果我没记错，古代对它的评价真是糟透了。”
“糟透了，阿龙纳斯先生。希腊和拉丁史家提起它，无一肯说句好话。斯特拉博说，夏季季风吹起或者雨季降临时，这里特别危险。阿拉伯人伊德里西以‘库勒祖姆湾’之名描画它，讲述多少船只在沙洲上毁灭，夜间更无人敢冒险航行。照他的说法，这片海饱受可怕飓风的袭击，散布着不肯款待来者的荒岛，‘无论海面还是深处，都拿不出一样好东西来。’”
“由此可见，”我回答，“这些史家从来没搭‘鹦鹉螺号’航行过。”
“正是这样，”船长微笑着回答，“而在这一点上，今人也没有比古人长进。人类费了多少个世纪才发现，蒸汽能够推动机器！谁知道再过一百年，能不能看到第二艘‘鹦鹉螺号’？进步是缓慢的，阿龙纳斯先生。”
“确实，”我回答，“您的船至少走在时代前面一百年，也许还超前了整整一个时代。这样的发明如果随发明人一同带进坟墓，那是何等的憾事！”
尼摩船长没有答话。沉默了几分钟，他又说：
“您方才在说，古代史家把红海航行看作怎样的危险。”
“是的，”我答道，“不过他们的恐惧会不会有些夸大？”

“既是，又不是，阿龙纳斯先生。”尼摩船长答道。他仿佛对红海的一切都了如指掌。“有些地方，造得结实、索具齐备、又有驯服的蒸汽帮它掌握自己航向的现代船只已经不怕。放到古人的船上，却一样都是危险。请您想想最早那些海员，用棕树纤维绳把木板缝成船，浸透海豹油，外面涂上树脂粉，就敢出来冒险！他们连测定方位的仪器也没有，走在几乎一无所知的海流中，全凭猜测。在这种条件下，船难从前很多，也势必很多。可在我们这个时代，往来苏伊士与南方诸海的轮船，尽管会遇上逆向的信风，却已经不用再怕这个海湾发怒。舰长和乘客在动身前不再要献上供品求得神灵庇佑，回来时也不再戴着花冠和金饰发带，到邻近的神庙里向诸神致谢。”
“我赞同，”我说，“看样子蒸汽把水手心中的感恩都给抹去了。可船长，您似乎特别研究过这片海，能告诉我它的名字怎么来的吗？”
“关于这件事，有好几种解释，阿龙纳斯先生。一位十四世纪编年史家怎样说，您愿意听听吗？”
“很愿意。”
“这位想象力丰富的作家硬说，红海之名，是在以色列人通过以后才取得的。那时摩西发声，海水重新合拢，法老葬身于波浪。”
“诗人的解释，尼摩船长，”我回答，“可我不能满足于此。我想听您个人的见解。”
“那么，阿龙纳斯先生，请听。依我看，‘红海’这个名称，应当是希伯来语‘以东’的翻译。古人给它取这个名字，是因为海水的颜色独特。”
“可是我到现在只看见清澈的海水，没什么特别的颜色。”
“这很有可能。不过等我们向海湾的尽头走，您会看见那奇特的景象。我记得我见过整个图尔湾全变成红色，像一海的血。”
“您认为这颜色是显微镜下才能看见的一种海藻造成的？”
“这么看来，尼摩船长，您不是头一次乘‘鹦鹉螺号’遍游红海了？”
“不是，先生。”
“您刚讲到以色列人的渡海和埃及人的覆灭，我想请问，您可曾在水底找到过这桩历史大事的遗迹？”
“没有，先生，而且理由很充分。”
“是什么理由？”
“摩西和他的人民走过的那地方，如今被泥沙壅塞得厉害，水只够骆驼蘸蘸腿。您自然懂得，这点水浮不起我的‘鹦鹉螺号’。”
“地点究竟在哪儿？”我问。
“在苏伊士地峡稍北，过去红海一直深入盐湖时，曾在那里形成一个很深的河口，地点便在那条水臂中。那次渡海究竟有什么神迹姑且不论，以色列人总归是从那里跨过去，到达应许之地的。法老的大军也恰恰丧生在那里。我相信，若能在沙地中部动手发掘，就会出土数量可观的埃及武器和器具。”
“这很明白，”我回答，“为考古学家着想，但愿这样的发掘早晚能办成。等苏伊士运河修好，地峡上会建起新城。不过对‘鹦鹉螺号’这样的船而言，这条运河倒实在无用。”

“也许吧，可它对全世界都有用，”尼摩船长说，“古人已深知红海与地中海若能相通，对他们的商贸大有益处。不过他们没有打算直接挖一条运河，而是取道尼罗河作中介。如果传说可信，那条沟通尼罗河与红海的水道，很可能由塞索斯特里斯首先兴建。可以确定的是，公元前六一五年，尼科斯着手开挖一条引水渠，从埃及平原横过，朝阿拉伯方向引来尼罗河水。逆流走完需要四天，河道宽得可以让两艘三层桨船并排而行。希斯塔斯佩斯的儿子大流士接续了工程，大概到托勒密二世手里完工。斯特拉博亲眼见它通航。不过从布巴斯提斯附近的起点到红海，落差太小，一年中只有几个月可以行船。直到安东尼时期，这条运河一直担负了全部商贸之需，后来废弃，渐渐淤满了沙。哈里发欧麦尔曾命人疏浚恢复。七六一或七六二年，哈里发曼苏尔为了不让粮食送到举兵反叛他的穆罕默德·本·阿卜杜拉手里，彻底毁掉了它。远征埃及时，贵国波拿巴将军曾在苏伊士沙漠发现这项工程的遗迹。他却被猝然涌来的潮水袭击，险些没能活着回到哈贾罗特；三千年前摩西扎营的，正是同一个地方。”
“那么，船长，古人没敢动手的事，使两海直接相通、缩短加的斯至印度的航程，雷赛布先生却办成功了。不久，他就将把非洲变成一座巨大的岛。”
“是的，阿龙纳斯先生，您有理由为您的同胞骄傲。这样一个人为国家挣得的荣耀，超过伟大的统帅。他同许多人一样，一开头饱尝嫌恶和拒绝，可他毕竟胜利了，因为他的天才在意志。想到一项本该由各国共同负担、足够为一个君王的治世增光的工程，竟只能凭一个人的精力才办成，也真令人伤感。所有的荣誉，都该给雷赛布先生！”
“对！向这位伟大的公民致敬！”我答道。尼摩船长方才说话的口气，很叫我诧异。
“可惜，”他继续说，“我不能把您从苏伊士运河带过去。不过后天抵达地中海时，您能看见塞得港那道长长的防波堤。”
“地中海！”我叫道。
“是的，先生。这让您惊奇吗？”
“让我惊奇的是，后天咱们就会在那里。”
“当真吗？”
“是的，船长。虽说自从登上您的船，我早就该养成什么也不惊奇的习惯了。”
“可您惊奇的理由是什么？”
“唉！要是后天‘鹦鹉螺号’便须到达地中海，中间还得绕行非洲、兜过好望角，那么您得把速度提到多么可怕的地步啊！”
“先生，谁告诉您它会绕行非洲、兜过好望角呢？”
“那么，除非‘鹦鹉螺号’能在干地上航行，从地峡上面过去——”
“或者从它下面过去，阿龙纳斯先生。”
“从下面？”
“当然，”尼摩船长平静地回答，“大自然早已在这条舌形陆地的底下，做成了人类今天才在地表做成的事情。”
“什么！这样一条通路真的存在？”
“是的。一道地下的通路，我命名为阿拉伯隧道。它从苏伊士下面带我们通过，出口开在佩卢西翁湾。”
“可是这条地峡不是全由流沙构成吗？”
“只到某种深度是这样。往下不过五十五码，已有一层坚硬的岩石。”
“您是偶然发现这条通道的吗？”我越来越惊讶，问道。

“凭偶然，也凭推理，先生。推理的功劳又大过偶然。这条通道不只存在，我还早已从中受益过几次。没有它，今天我就不会贸然闯进没有去路的红海。我留意到，红海和地中海里有若干种鱼，品种一模一样。既然认准这点，我便问自己，这两片海之间可能毫不相通吗？倘若相通，单因两边海面高低不同，地下水流就一定会从红海流向地中海。我在苏伊士附近捕了很多鱼，把铜环穿过它们的尾巴，再放回海里。几个月之后，我在叙利亚沿岸捕到了几条佩着铜环的老相识。两海相通便有了实据。接下来我驾‘鹦鹉螺号’搜寻，找到通道，又冒险驶了进去。不久，先生，您也将从我的阿拉伯隧道通过了！”
