sections.title_en: PART TWO / CHAPTER XIII — THE ICEBERG
source_paragraphs: The _Nautilus_ was steadily pursuing its southerly course, following the fiftieth meridian with considerable speed. Did he wish to reach the pole? I did not think so, for every attempt to reach that point had hitherto failed. Again, the season was far advanced, for in the Antarctic regions the 13th of March corresponds with the 13th of September of northern regions, which begin at the equinoctial season. On the 14th of March I saw floating ice in latitude 55°, merely pale bits of debris from twenty to twenty-five feet long, forming banks over which the sea curled. The _Nautilus_ remained on the surface of the ocean. Ned Land, who had fished in the Arctic Seas, was familiar with its icebergs; but Conseil and I admired them for the first time. In the atmosphere towards the southern horizon stretched a white dazzling band. English whalers have given it the name of “ice blink.” However thick the clouds may be, it is always visible, and announces the presence of an ice pack or bank. Accordingly, larger blocks soon appeared, whose brilliancy changed with the caprices of the fog. Some of these masses showed green veins, as if long undulating lines had been traced with sulphate of copper; others resembled enormous amethysts with the light shining through them. Some reflected the light of day upon a thousand crystal facets. Others shaded with vivid calcareous reflections resembled a perfect town of marble. The more we neared the south the more these floating islands increased both in number and importance.

At 60° lat. every pass had disappeared. But, seeking carefully, Captain Nemo soon found a narrow opening, through which he boldly slipped, knowing, however, that it would close behind him. Thus, guided by this clever hand, the _Nautilus_ passed through all the ice with a precision which quite charmed Conseil; icebergs or mountains, ice-fields or smooth plains, seeming to have no limits, drift-ice or floating ice-packs, plains broken up, called palchs when they are circular, and streams when they are made up of long strips. The temperature was very low; the thermometer exposed to the air marked 2 deg. or 3° below zero, but we were warmly clad with fur, at the expense of the sea-bear and seal. The interior of the _Nautilus_, warmed regularly by its electric apparatus, defied the most intense cold. Besides, it would only have been necessary to go some yards beneath the waves to find a more bearable temperature. Two months earlier we should have had perpetual daylight in these latitudes; but already we had had three or four hours of night, and by and by there would be six months of darkness in these circumpolar regions. On the 15th of March we were in the latitude of New Shetland and South Orkney. The Captain told me that formerly numerous tribes of seals inhabited them; but that English and American whalers, in their rage for destruction, massacred both old and young; thus, where there was once life and animation, they had left silence and death.

About eight o’clock on the morning of the 16th of March the _Nautilus_, following the fifty-fifth meridian, cut the Antarctic polar circle. Ice surrounded us on all sides, and closed the horizon. But Captain Nemo went from one opening to another, still going higher. I cannot express my astonishment at the beauties of these new regions. The ice took most surprising forms. Here the grouping formed an oriental town, with innumerable mosques and minarets; there a fallen city thrown to the earth, as it were, by some convulsion of nature. The whole aspect was constantly changed by the oblique rays of the sun, or lost in the greyish fog amidst hurricanes of snow. Detonations and falls were heard on all sides, great overthrows of icebergs, which altered the whole landscape like a diorama. Often seeing no exit, I thought we were definitely prisoners; but, instinct guiding him at the slightest indication, Captain Nemo would discover a new pass. He was never mistaken when he saw the thin threads of bluish water trickling along the ice-fields; and I had no doubt that he had already ventured into the midst of these Antarctic seas before. On the 16th of March, however, the ice-fields absolutely blocked our road. It was not the iceberg itself, as yet, but vast fields cemented by the cold. But this obstacle could not stop Captain Nemo: he hurled himself against it with frightful violence. The _Nautilus_ entered the brittle mass like a wedge, and split it with frightful crackings. It was the battering ram of the ancients hurled by infinite strength. The ice, thrown high in the air, fell like hail around us. By its own power of impulsion our apparatus made a canal for itself; some times carried away by its own impetus, it lodged on the ice-field, crushing it with its weight, and sometimes buried beneath it, dividing it by a simple pitching movement, producing large rents in it. Violent gales assailed us at this time, accompanied by thick fogs, through which, from one end of the platform to the other, we could see nothing. The wind blew sharply from all parts of the compass, and the snow lay in such hard heaps that we had to break it with blows of a pickaxe. The temperature was always at 5 deg. below zero; every outward part of the _Nautilus_ was covered with ice. A rigged vessel would have been entangled in the blocked up gorges. A vessel without sails, with electricity for its motive power, and wanting no coal, could alone brave such high latitudes. At length, on the 18th of March, after many useless assaults, the _Nautilus_ was positively blocked. It was no longer either streams, packs, or ice-fields, but an interminable and immovable barrier, formed by mountains soldered together.
“An iceberg!” said the Canadian to me.

I knew that to Ned Land, as well as to all other navigators who had preceded us, this was an inevitable obstacle. The sun appearing for an instant at noon, Captain Nemo took an observation as near as possible, which gave our situation at 51° 30′ long. and 67° 39′ of S. lat. We had advanced one degree more in this Antarctic region. Of the liquid surface of the sea there was no longer a glimpse. Under the spur of the _Nautilus_ lay stretched a vast plain, entangled with confused blocks. Here and there sharp points and slender needles rising to a height of 200 feet; further on a steep shore, hewn as it were with an axe and clothed with greyish tints; huge mirrors, reflecting a few rays of sunshine, half drowned in the fog. And over this desolate face of nature a stern silence reigned, scarcely broken by the flapping of the wings of petrels and puffins. Everything was frozen—even the noise. The _Nautilus_ was then obliged to stop in its adventurous course amid these fields of ice. In spite of our efforts, in spite of the powerful means employed to break up the ice, the _Nautilus_ remained immovable. Generally, when we can proceed no further, we have return still open to us; but here return was as impossible as advance, for every pass had closed behind us; and for the few moments when we were stationary, we were likely to be entirely blocked, which did indeed happen about two o’clock in the afternoon, the fresh ice forming around its sides with astonishing rapidity. I was obliged to admit that Captain Nemo was more than imprudent. I was on the platform at that moment. The Captain had been observing our situation for some time past, when he said to me:
“Well, sir, what do you think of this?”
“I think that we are caught, Captain.”
The _Nautilus_ was blocked up
“So, M. Aronnax, you really think that the _Nautilus_ cannot disengage itself?”
“With difficulty, Captain; for the season is already too far advanced for you to reckon on the breaking of the ice.”

“Ah! sir,” said Captain Nemo, in an ironical tone, “you will always be the same. You see nothing but difficulties and obstacles. I affirm that not only can the _Nautilus_ disengage itself, but also that it can go further still.”
“Further to the South?” I asked, looking at the Captain.
“Yes, sir; it shall go to the pole.”
“To the pole!” I exclaimed, unable to repress a gesture of incredulity.
“Yes,” replied the Captain, coldly, “to the Antarctic pole—to that unknown point from whence springs every meridian of the globe. You know whether I can do as I please with the _Nautilus!_”

Yes, I knew that. I knew that this man was bold, even to rashness. But to conquer those obstacles which bristled round the South Pole, rendering it more inaccessible than the North, which had not yet been reached by the boldest navigators—was it not a mad enterprise, one which only a maniac would have conceived? It then came into my head to ask Captain Nemo if he had ever discovered that pole which had never yet been trodden by a human creature?

“No, sir,” he replied; “but we will discover it together. Where others have failed, I will not fail. I have never yet led my _Nautilus_ so far into southern seas; but, I repeat, it shall go further yet.”

“I can well believe you, Captain,” said I, in a slightly ironical tone. “I believe you! Let us go ahead! There are no obstacles for us! Let us smash this iceberg! Let us blow it up; and, if it resists, let us give the _Nautilus_ wings to fly over it!”
“Over it, sir!” said Captain Nemo, quietly; “no, not over it, but under it!”
“Under it!” I exclaimed, a sudden idea of the Captain’s projects flashing upon my mind. I understood; the wonderful qualities of the _Nautilus_ were going to serve us in this superhuman enterprise.

“I see we are beginning to understand one another, sir,” said the Captain, half smiling. “You begin to see the possibility—I should say the success—of this attempt. That which is impossible for an ordinary vessel is easy to the _Nautilus_. If a continent lies before the pole, it must stop before the continent; but if, on the contrary, the pole is washed by open sea, it will go even to the pole.”

“Certainly,” said I, carried away by the Captain’s reasoning; “if the surface of the sea is solidified by the ice, the lower depths are free by the Providential law which has placed the maximum of density of the waters of the ocean one degree higher than freezing-point; and, if I am not mistaken, the portion of this iceberg which is above the water is as one to four to that which is below.”

“Very nearly, sir; for one foot of iceberg above the sea there are three below it. If these ice mountains are not more than 300 feet above the surface, they are not more than 900 beneath. And what are 900 feet to the _Nautilus?_”
“Nothing, sir.”
“It could even seek at greater depths that uniform temperature of sea-water, and there brave with impunity the thirty or forty degrees of surface cold.”
“Just so, sir—just so,” I replied, getting animated.
“The only difficulty,” continued Captain Nemo, “is that of remaining several days without renewing our provision of air.”
“Is that all? The _Nautilus_ has vast reservoirs; we can fill them, and they will supply us with all the oxygen we want.”
“Well thought of, M. Aronnax,” replied the Captain, smiling. “But, not wishing you to accuse me of rashness, I will first give you all my objections.”
“Have you any more to make?”
“Only one. It is possible, if the sea exists at the South Pole, that it may be covered; and, consequently, we shall be unable to come to the surface.”
“Good, sir! but do you forget that the _Nautilus_ is armed with a powerful spur, and could we not send it diagonally against these fields of ice, which would open at the shocks.”
“Ah! sir, you are full of ideas to-day.”

“Besides, Captain,” I added, enthusiastically, “why should we not find the sea open at the South Pole as well as at the North? The frozen poles of the earth do not coincide, either in the southern or in the northern regions; and, until it is proved to the contrary, we may suppose either a continent or an ocean free from ice at these two points of the globe.”
“I think so too, M. Aronnax,” replied Captain Nemo. “I only wish you to observe that, after having made so many objections to my project, you are now crushing me with arguments in its favour!”

The preparations for this audacious attempt now began. The powerful pumps of the _Nautilus_ were working air into the reservoirs and storing it at high pressure. About four o’clock, Captain Nemo announced the closing of the panels on the platform. I threw one last look at the massive iceberg which we were going to cross. The weather was clear, the atmosphere pure enough, the cold very great, being 12° below zero; but, the wind having gone down, this temperature was not so unbearable. About ten men mounted the sides of the _Nautilus_, armed with pickaxes to break the ice around the vessel, which was soon free. The operation was quickly performed, for the fresh ice was still very thin. We all went below. The usual reservoirs were filled with the newly-liberated water, and the _Nautilus_ soon descended. I had taken my place with Conseil in the saloon; through the open window we could see the lower beds of the Southern Ocean. The thermometer went up, the needle of the compass deviated on the dial. At about 900 feet, as Captain Nemo had foreseen, we were floating beneath the undulating bottom of the iceberg. But the _Nautilus_ went lower still—it went to the depth of four hundred fathoms. The temperature of the water at the surface showed twelve degrees, it was now only ten; we had gained two. I need not say the temperature of the _Nautilus_ was raised by its heating apparatus to a much higher degree; every manœuvre was accomplished with wonderful precision.
“We shall pass it, if you please, sir,” said Conseil.
“I believe we shall,” I said, in a tone of firm conviction.

In this open sea, the _Nautilus_ had taken its course direct to the pole, without leaving the fifty-second meridian. From 67° 30′ to 90 deg., twenty-two degrees and a half of latitude remained to travel; that is, about five hundred leagues. The _Nautilus_ kept up a mean speed of twenty-six miles an hour—the speed of an express train. If that was kept up, in forty hours we should reach the pole.

For a part of the night the novelty of the situation kept us at the window. The sea was lit with the electric lantern; but it was deserted; fishes did not sojourn in these imprisoned waters; they only found there a passage to take them from the Antarctic Ocean to the open polar sea. Our pace was rapid; we could feel it by the quivering of the long steel body. About two in the morning I took some hours’ repose, and Conseil did the same. In crossing the waist I did not meet Captain Nemo: I supposed him to be in the pilot’s cage. The next morning, the 19th of March, I took my post once more in the saloon. The electric log told me that the speed of the _Nautilus_ had been slackened. It was then going towards the surface; but prudently emptying its reservoirs very slowly. My heart beat fast. Were we going to emerge and regain the open polar atmosphere? No! A shock told me that the _Nautilus_ had struck the bottom of the iceberg, still very thick, judging from the deadened sound. We had in deed “struck,” to use a sea expression, but in an inverse sense, and at a thousand feet deep. This would give three thousand feet of ice above us; one thousand being above the water-mark. The iceberg was then higher than at its borders—not a very reassuring fact. Several times that day the _Nautilus_ tried again, and every time it struck the wall which lay like a ceiling above it. Sometimes it met with but 900 yards, only 200 of which rose above the surface. It was twice the height it was when the _Nautilus_ had gone under the waves. I carefully noted the different depths, and thus obtained a submarine profile of the chain as it was developed under the water. That night no change had taken place in our situation. Still ice between four and five hundred yards in depth! It was evidently diminishing, but, still, what a thickness between us and the surface of the ocean! It was then eight. According to the daily custom on board the _Nautilus_, its air should have been renewed four hours ago; but I did not suffer much, although Captain Nemo had not yet made any demand upon his reserve of oxygen. My sleep was painful that night; hope and fear besieged me by turns: I rose several times. The groping of the _Nautilus_ continued. About three in the morning, I noticed that the lower surface of the iceberg was only about fifty feet deep. One hundred and fifty feet now separated us from the surface of the waters. The iceberg was by degrees becoming an ice-field, the mountain a plain. My eyes never left the manometer. We were still rising diagonally to the surface, which sparkled under the electric rays. The iceberg was stretching both above and beneath into lengthening slopes; mile after mile it was getting thinner. At length, at six in the morning of that memorable day, the 19th of March, the door of the saloon opened, and Captain Nemo appeared.
“The sea is open!” was all he said.
translated_paragraphs: “鹦鹉螺号”沿第五十度经线以相当快的速度稳稳南行。船长真想抵达南极？我不这么以为，因为此前每一次前往极点的尝试都失败了。何况季节已经很晚。南极地区的三月十三日，相当于北方的九月十三日，已是秋分前后的时节。三月十四日，在南纬五十五度，我看见了浮冰。最先只是些苍白的碎片，长二十至二十五英尺，聚成一片片小冰滩，浪头在上面卷起。“鹦鹉螺号”仍停在海面。尼德·兰德曾在北冰洋捕鲸，冰山是他的熟相识；我和康塞尔却是第一次欣赏。南方地平线上空横着一道耀眼的白带。英国捕鲸人给它取名“冰光”。云再厚也能望见，它预告着浮冰群或冰岸的存在。果然，很快就出现了更大的冰块，光彩随雾气的无常变化。有的冰体带着绿色纹脉，像有人用硫酸铜描上长长的波纹；有的像硕大的紫水晶，透着光。有些冰在成千上万的晶面上反射日光。有的在明亮的白垩色光影中深浅错落，简直像一座大理石的城市。越向南行，这些漂浮的岛屿不但数量增多，体积也越来越大。

到了南纬六十度，一切通道都消失了。然而尼摩船长悉心寻觅，很快又找出一道狭窄裂口，毅然钻了进去，明知它会在身后重新合拢。在这双巧手引导下，“鹦鹉螺号”一路穿过各色冰区，精准得叫康塞尔佩服不已。有浮动的冰山，有平滑如无边平原的冰原，有漂流的碎冰或浮冰群；从平原断裂下来的冰块，聚成圆片状的称冰斑，聚成长条状的称冰流。气温很低。暴露在空气中的温度计标着零下两三度，可我们穿着海熊和海豹贡献的暖和毛皮。“鹦鹉螺号”里面由电力装置保持温暖，最厉害的寒冷也不在话下。再说，只要往水下潜上几码，便能找到温和些的温度。早两个月，这些纬度还享有不落的白昼；眼下每天却已有三四个小时的夜，不久极地又将面临为期半年的黑暗。三月十五日，我们到了南设得兰群岛和南奥克尼群岛的纬度。船长告诉我，从前这几处栖息着庞大的海豹群。英国和美国捕鲸人杀红了眼，老小一并屠戮，原先生命活跃的地方，留给后来的只有沉寂和死亡。

三月十六日上午约八点，“鹦鹉螺号”沿第五十五度经线越过南极圈。四面为冰所围，天边也被封闭。但尼摩船长从一道缺口找到另一道缺口，仍向更高纬度挺进。这陌生地区的美叫我惊异到无从形容。冰块结成最出奇的形态。这一堆像东方城市，清真寺和宣礼塔多得数不过来；那一丛像一座倾覆的城池，仿佛一场自然界的痉挛将它推倒在地。太阳斜射，整幅图画随时都给改了一副面貌，又会在雪暴之中隐没于灰蒙蒙的雾气里。四下响着爆裂和崩坠的声音。大冰山一翻，整片风景便被改换，像活动景片换了一幕。经常眼看找不到出口，我以为我们已彻底成了囚徒，尼摩船长却能凭一点点征兆，让直觉领他找出新通路。他从来没有看错过冰原上蜿蜒而行的细线般的蓝水。我毫不怀疑，他从前已经冒险进入过这些南极海域。
然而就在三月十六日，冰原终于将道路完全封住了。还不是冰山本身横在面前，而是一片又一片叫严寒黏合起来的广大冰原。这个障碍却仍挡不住尼摩船长。他以吓人的猛劲冲上去。“鹦鹉螺号”像楔子那样插入易脆的冰体，在可怕的劈啪声中豁开一条口子。活像古人的攻城槌，有无穷的力量将它掷出。冰给掀到半空，雹子似的掉在我们周围。我们这台机器只凭冲劲，竟给自己开出一条航道。有时被自己的冲力推得骑上冰原，用体重把冰压碎；有时又一头钻到冰底，船首只须上下点动，便将冰分开，造成宽大的裂缝。
这当口，我们同时遭到狂风和浓雾的袭击，从平台的一头向另一头，竟看不见东西。风从罗盘的各个方向凶猛地吹，积雪堆得硬实，非用十字镐才能敲开。气温始终在零下五度，“鹦鹉螺号”露在外面的每一处都封了冰。寻常装帆挂索的船，必定会在堵塞的冰峡里缠得动弹不得。只有不用帆、不用煤、以电力推动的船才能在这样高的纬度冒险。终于到了三月十八日，在一次次冲击都无结果以后，“鹦鹉螺号”真正给堵住了。面前已不是条状浮冰、冰群或冰原，而是一道看不到尽头、也推不动的屏障，整座整座冰山焊成了一体。
“一道冰山！”加拿大人对我说。

我知道，在尼德·兰德和我们之前所有海员的眼里，这都是无法越过的一道障碍。正午太阳露了片刻。尼摩船长尽可能准确地作了观测，得知船位是经度五十一度三十分、南纬六十七度三十九分。我们在南极地区又深入了一度。液态的海面一眼也看不见。“鹦鹉螺号”的撞角底下，延伸着一片巨大的平原，杂乱的冰块交结在一起。这里那里，有尖峰和冰针伸上两百英尺高空；更远是一处斧削般的陡岸，披着灰影；又有些巨镜，将半淹在雾里的几缕日光反射回来。大自然这一派荒寒面容上，笼罩着严厉的寂静，偶尔才被海燕和海鹦扑动翅膀的声音打破。一切都冻住了，连声音都像结了冰。
“鹦鹉螺号”这时不得不停下冰原间的冒险行程。不管我们怎样努力，采用多么强有力的破冰手段，它还是纹丝不动。平常前面走不通，总还容得下往回走，可在这里后退和前进一样不可能，因为来路上每一道水隙都已在身后关闭。只消停驻片刻，我们就可能被完全封死。下午约两点，事情真就如此发生了。新冰以惊人的速度，在船的四周合拢。我不得不承认，尼摩船长已不是“不够谨慎”这几个字就能形容的了。当时我正在平台上。船长注视我们的处境已有一阵，忽然向我开了口。
“那么，先生，您对此有什么看法？”
“我看我们是被困住了，船长。”
图注　“鹦鹉螺号”为冰所困
“这么说，阿龙纳斯先生，您真以为‘鹦鹉螺号’不能脱身？”
“要脱身可难，船长。季节已经太晚，您也不能指望冰层化开。”
“啊，先生，”尼摩船长略带讥讽地说，“您总是一个样，满眼只看见困难和阻挡。我却断言，‘鹦鹉螺号’不但能脱身，还能继续前进。”
“再往南？”我望着船长问。
“是的，先生。它要一直到极点。”
“到极点！”我叫道，不由得做出一个难以置信的手势。
“是的，”船长冷冷地回答，“到南极。到那个尚未有人认识的点；地球的每一条经线都从那里伸出。您知道我能不能叫‘鹦鹉螺号’听我如意行事！”
是的，这我知道。我知道这个人勇敢，甚至敢到莽撞。可是环绕南极有那么多障碍密密竖起，使它比北极更难抵达，而北极至今连最勇敢的海员也还没到过。要把那些障碍一一征服，岂非一个疯狂的事业，只有疯子才能想得出？随即我心头起了一个念头，便问尼摩船长，以前他难道已经发现过这个从未有人踏过的极点吗？
“没有，先生，”他答道，“不过我们会一起发现它。别人失败的地方，我不会失败。我还从没有驾‘鹦鹉螺号’深入南方海洋到这个地步，但我再说一次，它还要再往前。”
“我当然相信您，船长，”我以略带讥意的口吻说，“我信！往前走吧！咱们面前哪有什么障碍！把这冰山撞碎！把它炸掉！要是还不肯退让，给‘鹦鹉螺号’装上翅膀，飞过去！”
“飞过去，先生？”尼摩船长平静地说，“不。不是从上面过去，而是从下面！”
“从下面！”我叫道。关于船长的计划，一个念头猛地闪过脑际。我懂了。“鹦鹉螺号”那些独特奇妙的本领，正要给这桩超出人力的事业效劳。
“我看，先生，我们开始彼此了解了，”船长似笑非笑地说，“您开始看得见这次尝试的可能——我该说，看得见它会成功。普通船只办不到的事，对‘鹦鹉螺号’却很容易。如果极点前面横着一块大陆，它势必在大陆跟前停下；反过来，如果冲洗着南极的是一片开阔海洋，它便会直抵极点。”
“当然，”我说。我已被船长的推理带得兴奋起来。“海面就算冻成固体，下层的深水仍然畅通。这是造物的安排，大洋海水在比结冰点高一度的时候密度最大。我若没记错，这冰山在水面以上的部分，同水面以下的部分约为一比四。”
“相当接近，先生。冰山每露出水面一英尺，水下就有三英尺。假使这些冰山伸出水面不超过三百英尺，水面以下也就不会超过九百英尺。九百英尺对‘鹦鹉螺号’算得了什么？”
“什么也算不上，先生。”
“它甚至还可以到更深处寻找均匀的海水温度，任凭海面上零下三四十度，也能安安稳稳地通过。”
“是这样，先生，岂不正是这样！”我越说越热烈。
“唯一的困难，”尼摩船长说下去，“就是要好几天不能更新船里的空气。”
“就这一样吗？‘鹦鹉螺号’有大储气罐。我们把罐装满，就能供给所需的全部氧气。”
“想得好，阿龙纳斯先生，”船长微笑着回答，“不过我不想让您说我轻率，还是先把一切反对意见都向您提出为妙。”
“您还有别的要提吗？”
“只有一个。即便南极真有海洋，它也可能被冰覆盖。那样，我们便没法浮上海面。”
“好吧，先生！可别忘记，‘鹦鹉螺号’安着强劲的撞角。难道不能使它斜着朝冰原冲去，由它随撞击而开裂？”
“啊，先生，您今天主意可真多。”
“何况，船长，”我满腔热情地补充，“为什么我们不能在南极像在北极一样，找到一片开阔海洋？地球上最寒冷的极点，无论南北，都不与地理极点重合。在有反证以前，我们完全可以设想，地球这两个地点是一片大陆，或是一片无冰的海洋。”
“我也是这样想，阿龙纳斯先生，”尼摩船长回答，“我只请您留意这一点：您方才还在反对我的计划，提出了那么多疑难，如今倒拿拥护它的道理来把我压倒了！”

这项大胆尝试的准备工作开始了。“鹦鹉螺号”的强力泵把空气打进储气罐，高压保存。约四点，尼摩船长宣布，平台上的舱盖快要关闭。我朝即将横穿的庞大冰山投去最后一眼。天气晴，空气相当清透，气温极冷，零下十二度；但风已减弱，体感还没有那样难捱。十来个人手拿十字镐，沿“鹦鹉螺号”的两舷凿开环绕船体的冰。船很快就脱了束缚。新结的冰还薄，所以这事干得快。大家下舱。寻常所用的压载舱引入刚破冰流出的海水，“鹦鹉螺号”迅速下沉。我和康塞尔已坐定在客厅。隔着敞开护板的窗，我们看见南大洋较深的水层。温度计的液柱升高，罗盘指针在盘面上偏转。正如船长预料，大约九百英尺深处，我们已经浮在冰山起伏不平的底面以下。可“鹦鹉螺号”还要更深，一直下至四百英寻。水温在表面记作十二度，此时只有十度，我们得了两度的温差。不必说，船内有供暖装置，温度比外面高得多。一切操作都完成得精确而漂亮。
“恕我说一句，先生，咱们会穿过去的。”康塞尔说。
“我也相信会。”我的口气中满是确信。
在这片畅通的海水里，“鹦鹉螺号”沿第五十二度经线，径直驶往极点。从南纬六十七度三十分到九十度，还要走过二十二度半，约五百里格。“鹦鹉螺号”保持每小时二十六英里的平均速度，跟特快列车一样快。保持下去，四十小时就能抵达极点。

夜里有好长一段，我们被处境的新奇吸引，舍不得离开窗口。海水给电灯照得明亮，却空空荡荡。鱼儿不栖身在这样受禁锢的海里，只是借它作一条通道，从南大洋游到开放的极地海洋中去。我们速度很快，长长的钢制船身发着颤，能感觉得出。凌晨约两点，我才去休息几个钟头，康塞尔也一样。经过船腰通道时，我没有遇见尼摩船长，猜他在舵手室里。
次日，三月十九日早晨，我又回到客厅里自己的岗位。电动计程仪告诉我，“鹦鹉螺号”已减速。它正朝水面升去，不过极为谨慎，水舱里的水一点点才抽出。我的心怦怦跳。我们要冲出水面，重新呼吸极地开放的空气了吗？不！一次撞击告诉我，“鹦鹉螺号”碰到了冰山的底面。撞声沉闷，那冰想来仍很厚。照水手的说法，我们的确“触礁”了，却是颠倒着触的礁，而且在一千英尺深处。照这个算法，我们头顶上方有三千英尺的冰，其中一千英尺在水线以上。冰山在这里比边缘还高，这可不是令人安心的事。
那天“鹦鹉螺号”又试过几回，每一次都撞上那道天花板一样盖在头顶的墙。有时量得冰厚只有九百码，露出水面的只占两百码。它的高度已是“鹦鹉螺号”下潜之初的两倍。我把每一次测得的深度仔细记下，竟能画出这道冰山链在水下起伏的剖面图。到了夜里，处境仍旧未变。冰层厚度还有四五百码！分明是在减薄，可我们与洋面之间，依旧隔着那么厚的一层！
当时是八点。按“鹦鹉螺号”平时的习惯，早在四个钟头以前就该换气。虽然船长还没动用储氧，我倒也没有觉得十分难受。这一夜我睡得很苦，希望和恐惧轮番围攻，好几次爬起身。“鹦鹉螺号”一路摸索着。凌晨约三点，我留意到冰底伸下去已只有约五十英尺。现在我们与海面之间隔着一百五十英尺。冰山渐变为冰原，高山渐变为平地。我的眼睛一刻不离压力计。我们仍斜向上升，接近电光下闪亮的表面。冰的上下两面都延伸成越来越长的缓坡，每过一英里，厚度便又减一点。终于，在那值得纪念的三月十九日早晨六点，客厅的门开了，尼摩船长出现。
“前面是开阔的海。”他只说了这一句。

sections.title_zh: 下部 / 第14章　南极
sections.title_en: PART TWO / CHAPTER XIV — THE SOUTH POLE
source_paragraphs: I rushed on to the platform. Yes! the open sea, with but a few scattered pieces of ice and moving icebergs—a long stretch of sea; a world of birds in the air, and myriads of fishes under those waters, which varied from intense blue to olive green, according to the bottom. The thermometer marked 3° C. above zero. It was comparatively spring, shut up as we were behind this iceberg, whose lengthened mass was dimly seen on our northern horizon.
“Are we at the pole?” I asked the Captain, with a beating heart.
“I do not know,” he replied. “At noon I will take our bearings.”
“But will the sun show himself through this fog?” said I, looking at the leaden sky.
“However little it shows, it will be enough,” replied the Captain.

About ten miles south a solitary island rose to a height of one hundred and four yards. We made for it, but carefully, for the sea might be strewn with banks. One hour afterwards we had reached it, two hours later we had made the round of it. It measured four or five miles in circumference. A narrow canal separated it from a considerable stretch of land, perhaps a continent, for we could not see its limits. The existence of this land seemed to give some colour to Maury’s theory. The ingenious American has remarked that, between the South Pole and the sixtieth parallel, the sea is covered with floating ice of enormous size, which is never met with in the North Atlantic. From this fact he has drawn the conclusion that the Antarctic Circle encloses considerable continents, as icebergs cannot form in open sea, but only on the coasts. According to these calculations, the mass of ice surrounding the southern pole forms a vast cap, the circumference of which must be, at least, 2,500 miles. But the _Nautilus_, for fear of running aground, had stopped about three cable-lengths from a strand over which reared a superb heap of rocks. The boat was launched; the Captain, two of his men, bearing instruments, Conseil, and myself were in it. It was ten in the morning. I had not seen Ned Land. Doubtless the Canadian did not wish to admit the presence of the South Pole. A few strokes of the oar brought us to the sand, where we ran ashore. Conseil was going to jump on to the land, when I held him back.
“Sir,” said I to Captain Nemo, “to you belongs the honour of first setting foot on this land.”
“Yes, sir,” said the Captain, “and if I do not hesitate to tread this South Pole, it is because, up to this time, no human being has left a trace there.”

Saying this, he jumped lightly on to the sand. His heart beat with emotion. He climbed a rock, sloping to a little promontory, and there, with his arms crossed, mute and motionless, and with an eager look, he seemed to take possession of these southern regions. After five minutes passed in this ecstasy, he turned to us.
“When you like, sir.”

I landed, followed by Conseil, leaving the two men in the boat. For a long way the soil was composed of a reddish sandy stone, something like crushed brick, scoriae, streams of lava, and pumice-stones. One could not mistake its volcanic origin. In some parts, slight curls of smoke emitted a sulphurous smell, proving that the internal fires had lost nothing of their expansive powers, though, having climbed a high acclivity, I could see no volcano for a radius of several miles. We know that in those Antarctic countries, James Ross found two craters, the Erebus and Terror, in full activity, on the 167th meridian, latitude 77° 32′. The vegetation of this desolate continent seemed to me much restricted. Some lichens lay upon the black rocks; some microscopic plants, rudimentary diatomas, a kind of cells placed between two quartz shells; long purple and scarlet weed, supported on little swimming bladders, which the breaking of the waves brought to the shore. These constituted the meagre flora of this region. The shore was strewn with molluscs, little mussels, and limpets. I also saw myriads of northern clios, one-and-a-quarter inches long, of which a whale would swallow a whole world at a mouthful; and some perfect sea-butterflies, animating the waters on the skirts of the shore.

There appeared on the high bottoms some coral shrubs, of the kind which, according to James Ross, live in the Antarctic seas to the depth of more than 1,000 yards. Then there were little kingfishers and starfish studding the soil. But where life abounded most was in the air. There thousands of birds fluttered and flew of all kinds, deafening us with their cries; others crowded the rock, looking at us as we passed by without fear, and pressing familiarly close by our feet. There were penguins, so agile in the water, heavy and awkward as they are on the ground; they were uttering harsh cries, a large assembly, sober in gesture, but extravagant in clamour. Albatrosses passed in the air, the expanse of their wings being at least four yards and a half, and justly called the vultures of the ocean; some gigantic petrels, and some damiers, a kind of small duck, the underpart of whose body is black and white; then there were a whole series of petrels, some whitish, with brown-bordered wings, others blue, peculiar to the Antarctic seas, and so oily, as I told Conseil, that the inhabitants of the Ferroe Islands had nothing to do before lighting them but to put a wick in.
“A little more,” said Conseil, “and they would be perfect lamps! After that, we cannot expect Nature to have previously furnished them with wicks!”

About half a mile farther on the soil was riddled with ruffs’ nests, a sort of laying-ground, out of which many birds were issuing. Captain Nemo had some hundreds hunted. They uttered a cry like the braying of an ass, were about the size of a goose, slate-colour on the body, white beneath, with a yellow line round their throats; they allowed themselves to be killed with a stone, never trying to escape. But the fog did not lift, and at eleven the sun had not yet shown itself. Its absence made me uneasy. Without it no observations were possible. How, then, could we decide whether we had reached the pole? When I rejoined Captain Nemo, I found him leaning on a piece of rock, silently watching the sky. He seemed impatient and vexed. But what was to be done? This rash and powerful man could not command the sun as he did the sea. Noon arrived without the orb of day showing itself for an instant. We could not even tell its position behind the curtain of fog; and soon the fog turned to snow.
“Till to-morrow,” said the Captain, quietly, and we returned to the _Nautilus_ amid these atmospheric disturbances.

The tempest of snow continued till the next day. It was impossible to remain on the platform. From the saloon, where I was taking notes of incidents happening during this excursion to the polar continent, I could hear the cries of petrels and albatrosses sporting in the midst of this violent storm. The _Nautilus_ did not remain motionless, but skirted the coast, advancing ten miles more to the south in the half-light left by the sun as it skirted the edge of the horizon. The next day, the 20th of March, the snow had ceased. The cold was a little greater, the thermometer showing 2° below zero. The fog was rising, and I hoped that that day our observations might be taken. Captain Nemo not having yet appeared, the boat took Conseil and myself to land. The soil was still of the same volcanic nature; everywhere were traces of lava, scoriae, and basalt; but the crater which had vomited them I could not see. Here, as lower down, this continent was alive with myriads of birds. But their rule was now divided with large troops of sea-mammals, looking at us with their soft eyes. There were several kinds of seals, some stretched on the earth, some on flakes of ice, many going in and out of the sea. They did not flee at our approach, never having had anything to do with man; and I reckoned that there were provisions there for hundreds of vessels.
“Sir,” said Conseil, “will you tell me the names of these creatures?”
“They are seals and morses.”

It was now eight in the morning. Four hours remained to us before the sun could be observed with advantage. I directed our steps towards a vast bay cut in the steep granite shore. There, I can aver that earth and ice were lost to sight by the numbers of sea-mammals covering them, and I involuntarily sought for old Proteus, the mythological shepherd who watched these immense flocks of Neptune. There were more seals than anything else, forming distinct groups, male and female, the father watching over his family, the mother suckling her little ones, some already strong enough to go a few steps. When they wished to change their place, they took little jumps, made by the contraction of their bodies, and helped awkwardly enough by their imperfect fin, which, as with the lamantin, their cousins, forms a perfect forearm. I should say that, in the water, which is their element—the spine of these creatures is flexible; with smooth and close skin and webbed feet—they swim admirably. In resting on the earth they take the most graceful attitudes. Thus the ancients, observing their soft and expressive looks, which cannot be surpassed by the most beautiful look a woman can give, their clear voluptuous eyes, their charming positions, and the poetry of their manners, metamorphosed them, the male into a triton and the female into a mermaid. I made Conseil notice the considerable development of the lobes of the brain in these interesting cetaceans. No mammal, except man, has such a quantity of brain matter; they are also capable of receiving a certain amount of education, are easily domesticated, and I think, with other naturalists, that if properly taught they would be of great service as fishing-dogs. The greater part of them slept on the rocks or on the sand. Amongst these seals, properly so called, which have no external ears (in which they differ from the otter, whose ears are prominent), I noticed several varieties of seals about three yards long, with a white coat, bulldog heads, armed with teeth in both jaws, four incisors at the top and four at the bottom, and two large canine teeth in the shape of a fleur-de-lis. Amongst them glided sea-elephants, a kind of seal, with short, flexible trunks. The giants of this species measured twenty feet round and ten yards and a half in length; but they did not move as we approached.
“These creatures are not dangerous?” asked Conseil.
“No; not unless you attack them. When they have to defend their young their rage is terrible, and it is not uncommon for them to break the fishing-boats to pieces.”
“They are quite right,” said Conseil.
“I do not say they are not.”
Two miles farther on we were stopped by the promontory which shelters the bay from the southerly winds. Beyond it we heard loud bellowings such as a troop of ruminants would produce.
“Good!” said Conseil; “a concert of bulls!”
“No; a concert of morses.”
“They are fighting!”
“They are either fighting or playing.”

We now began to climb the blackish rocks, amid unforeseen stumbles, and over stones which the ice made slippery. More than once I rolled over at the expense of my loins. Conseil, more prudent or more steady, did not stumble, and helped me up, saying:
“If, sir, you would have the kindness to take wider steps, you would preserve your equilibrium better.”
Arrived at the upper ridge of the promontory, I saw a vast white plain covered with morses. They were playing amongst themselves, and what we heard were bellowings of pleasure, not of anger.

As I passed these curious animals I could examine them leisurely, for they did not move. Their skins were thick and rugged, of a yellowish tint, approaching to red; their hair was short and scant. Some of them were four yards and a quarter long. Quieter and less timid than their cousins of the north, they did not, like them, place sentinels round the outskirts of their encampment. After examining this city of morses, I began to think of returning. It was eleven o’clock, and, if Captain Nemo found the conditions favourable for observations, I wished to be present at the operation. We followed a narrow pathway running along the summit of the steep shore. At half-past eleven we had reached the place where we landed. The boat had run aground, bringing the Captain. I saw him standing on a block of basalt, his instruments near him, his eyes fixed on the northern horizon, near which the sun was then describing a lengthened curve. I took my place beside him, and waited without speaking. Noon arrived, and, as before, the sun did not appear. It was a fatality. Observations were still wanting. If not accomplished to-morrow, we must give up all idea of taking any. We were indeed exactly at the 20th of March. To-morrow, the 21st, would be the equinox; the sun would disappear behind the horizon for six months, and with its disappearance the long polar night would begin. Since the September equinox it had emerged from the northern horizon, rising by lengthened spirals up to the 21st of December. At this period, the summer solstice of the northern regions, it had begun to descend; and to-morrow was to shed its last rays upon them. I communicated my fears and observations to Captain Nemo.

“You are right, M. Aronnax,” said he; “if to-morrow I cannot take the altitude of the sun, I shall not be able to do it for six months. But precisely because chance has led me into these seas on the 21st of March, my bearings will be easy to take, if at twelve we can see the sun.”
“Why, Captain?”
“Because then the orb of day described such lengthened curves that it is difficult to measure exactly its height above the horizon, and grave errors may be made with instruments.”
“What will you do then?”

“I shall only use my chronometer,” replied Captain Nemo. “If to-morrow, the 21st of March, the disc of the sun, allowing for refraction, is exactly cut by the northern horizon, it will show that I am at the South Pole.”
“Just so,” said I. “But this statement is not mathematically correct, because the equinox does not necessarily begin at noon.”
“Very likely, sir; but the error will not be a hundred yards and we do not want more. Till to-morrow, then!”

Captain Nemo returned on board. Conseil and I remained to survey the shore, observing and studying until five o’clock. Then I went to bed, not, however, without invoking, like the Indian, the favour of the radiant orb. The next day, the 21st of March, at five in the morning, I mounted the platform. I found Captain Nemo there.
“The weather is lightening a little,” said he. “I have some hope. After breakfast we will go on shore and choose a post for observation.”

That point settled, I sought Ned Land. I wanted to take him with me. But the obstinate Canadian refused, and I saw that his taciturnity and his bad humour grew day by day. After all, I was not sorry for his obstinacy under the circumstances. Indeed, there were too many seals on shore, and we ought not to lay such temptation in this unreflecting fisherman’s way. Breakfast over, we went on shore. The _Nautilus_ had gone some miles further up in the night. It was a whole league from the coast, above which reared a sharp peak about five hundred yards high. The boat took with me Captain Nemo, two men of the crew, and the instruments, which consisted of a chronometer, a telescope, and a barometer. While crossing, I saw numerous whales belonging to the three kinds peculiar to the southern seas; the whale, or the English “right whale,” which has no dorsal fin; the “humpback,” with reeved chest and large, whitish fins, which, in spite of its name, do not form wings; and the fin-back, of a yellowish brown, the liveliest of all the cetacea. This powerful creature is heard a long way off when he throws to a great height columns of air and vapour, which look like whirlwinds of smoke. These different mammals were disporting themselves in troops in the quiet waters; and I could see that this basin of the Antarctic Pole serves as a place of refuge to the cetacea too closely tracked by the hunters. I also noticed large medusæ floating between the reeds.

At nine we landed; the sky was brightening, the clouds were flying to the south, and the fog seemed to be leaving the cold surface of the waters. Captain Nemo went towards the peak, which he doubtless meant to be his observatory. It was a painful ascent over the sharp lava and the pumice-stones, in an atmosphere often impregnated with a sulphurous smell from the smoking cracks. For a man unaccustomed to walk on land, the Captain climbed the steep slopes with an agility I never saw equalled and which a hunter would have envied. We were two hours getting to the summit of this peak, which was half porphyry and half basalt. From thence we looked upon a vast sea which, towards the north, distinctly traced its boundary line upon the sky. At our feet lay fields of dazzling whiteness. Over our heads a pale azure, free from fog. To the north the disc of the sun seemed like a ball of fire, already horned by the cutting of the horizon. From the bosom of the water rose sheaves of liquid jets by hundreds. In the distance lay the _Nautilus_ like a cetacean asleep on the water. Behind us, to the south and east, an immense country and a chaotic heap of rocks and ice, the limits of which were not visible. On arriving at the summit Captain Nemo carefully took the mean height of the barometer, for he would have to consider that in taking his observations. At a quarter to twelve the sun, then seen only by refraction, looked like a golden disc shedding its last rays upon this deserted continent and seas which never man had yet ploughed. Captain Nemo, furnished with a lenticular glass which, by means of a mirror, corrected the refraction, watched the orb sinking below the horizon by degrees, following a lengthened diagonal. I held the chronometer. My heart beat fast. If the disappearance of the half-disc of the sun coincided with twelve o’clock on the chronometer, we were at the pole itself.
“Twelve!” I exclaimed.
“The South Pole!” replied Captain Nemo, in a grave voice, handing me the glass, which showed the orb cut in exactly equal parts by the horizon.
I looked at the last rays crowning the peak, and the shadows mounting by degrees up its slopes. At that moment Captain Nemo, resting with his hand on my shoulder, said:
“I, Captain Nemo, on this 21st day of March, 1868, have reached the South Pole on the ninetieth degree; and I take possession of this part of the globe, equal to one-sixth of the known continents.”
“In whose name, Captain?”
“In my own, sir!”
Saying which, Captain Nemo unfurled a black banner, bearing an “N” in gold quartered on its bunting. Then, turning towards the orb of day, whose last rays lapped the horizon of the sea, he exclaimed:
“Adieu, sun! Disappear, thou radiant orb! rest beneath this open sea, and let a night of six months spread its shadows over my new domains!”
translated_paragraphs: 我冲上平台。果然是开阔的海！海上只零零星星漂着几片浮冰、几座移动的冰山，眼前展着一大片海面。空中是鸟的天下，水底有无数游鱼。海水随着海底景物的不同，时而深蓝，时而橄榄绿。温度计指在摄氏零上三度。北方天际，依稀看得到那绵长的冰体。我们虽被它隔在这边，同先前相比，这里已是春天了。
“我们到南极点了吗？”我心跳得厉害，问船长。
“还不知道，正午我会测定船位。”他答道。
“可是太阳肯从这层雾里露脸吗？”我望着铅灰色的天问。
“只消露一点儿就够了。”船长答道。

南边大约十英里处，一座孤岛耸立在海上，高一百零四码。我们朝它驶去，走得很小心，因为海里可能到处有浅滩。一小时后，我们到达岛边。又过两小时，我们已经绕岛一周。岛的周长四五英里，一道窄水道把它同一大片陆地隔开。那也许是块大陆，因为我们根本望不到它的尽头。这片陆地的存在，似乎给莫里的学说添了一点依据。那位颇有见地的美国人曾经指出，南极点到南纬六十度之间，海上遍布巨大浮冰，北大西洋却看不到那种规模。他由此推断，南极圈内一定有相当广阔的大陆，因为冰山只能沿海岸形成，不能在外海中凭空长出来。照这样推算，南极四周的冰体构成一个巨大的冰盖，周长至少有二千五百英里。“鹦鹉螺号”怕搁浅，在离海滩约三链的地方停下。滩头耸立着壮观的石堆。小艇放下水去，船长、两个携带仪器的船员、康塞尔和我都坐了进去。那时是上午十点。我没见着尼德·兰德，想必这加拿大人不肯承认脚下当真有个南极点。几桨划去，小艇直上沙滩。康塞尔正要跳上陆地，我伸手拉住了他。
“船长，”我对尼摩说，“第一个踏上这片土地的荣誉，应当属于您。”
“是的，先生，”船长说，“我之所以毫不迟疑要踏上这个南极点，是因为直到今天，还没有一个人在这里留下过足迹。”
说完，他轻快地跳上沙地。激动使他的心颤动着。他沿一块斜岩登上一处小岬，交抱双臂，一言不发，一动不动，目光热切，好像正把整个南方的疆域收归己有。这样出神了五分钟，他才转向我们。
“先生，您现在请自便。”

我上了岸，康塞尔随后，那两个水手留在小艇里。很长一段地面全由微红的砂岩构成，像是碎砖，另有火山渣、一道道凝固的熔岩和浮石。这里出于火山作用，一望即知。有些地方冒着几缕带硫黄味的轻烟，足以证明地下的火仍蕴着当初向外喷发的力量。可是我登上一处高坡，放眼周围几英里内，却看不见火山。我们知道，詹姆斯·罗斯曾在南极一带、东经一百六十七度、南纬七十七度三十二分的地方，发现过两个正在活动的火山口，即埃里伯斯和特罗尔。这片荒凉大陆的植物，在我看来实在有限。黑岩上附着些地衣，另有几种显微镜下才看得见的植物，是些结构简单的硅藻，仿佛细胞夹在两片石英质的壳中；还有紫色和猩红色的长藻，靠小浮囊托起，被浪花推上岸。这便是此地稀薄的植物面貌。滩上散布着软体动物，小小的贻贝和帽贝。我还见到成千上万的北方裸海蝶，每个一又四分之一英寸长，鲸只消一口就能吞去整整一个世界。近岸的水中还有真正如蝶的翼足类，将一带海水点缀得生意盎然。

浅水处的海底，冒出一些灌木般的珊瑚。据詹姆斯·罗斯说，这类珊瑚生活在南极海中，深处可到一千多码。又有小翠鸟，海星则星星点点，撒满地面。但最具生气的地方还在空中。各种各样的鸟，有成千只在那里振翅飞舞，叫得我们耳朵发聋。还有些挤满岩石，见我们经过也不害怕，反倒很熟络地挤到脚边。企鹅在地上笨拙沉重，入了水却那么灵活。它们聚成一大群，动作庄重不多，发出的刺耳叫嚷可一点也不肯节省。信天翁掠过天空，双翼展开至少四码半，无怪人们叫它海洋的秃鹫。也有巨大的海燕，有名叫棋盘鸟的小鸭，身体下方黑白相间。再有各种海燕，有的微白，翼缘是棕色，有的是南极海域特有的蓝色品种。我告诉康塞尔，那些鸟油脂多到什么地步呢？在法罗群岛，人们要拿它们照明，只须添一根灯芯，划火点着就是了。
“再差一点，它们就是十全十美的灯啦！”康塞尔说，“可总不好指望大自然连灯芯也预先给它们配上吧！”

再向前约半英里，地面布满流苏鹬的巢穴，好像一片产卵场，许多鸟正从里面钻出。尼摩船长让人猎取了几百只。它们叫得像驴嘶，个头跟鹅差不多，身披石板灰的羽毛，腹部白色，喉间围着一圈黄线。拿石头便能打死，竟不知要跑。雾却不散。十一点了，太阳还没露面。我为它迟迟不出着起急来。没有太阳便不能观测，我们靠什么来确定究竟到没到极点？我回到尼摩船长身边时，他正倚着一块岩石，默默望天，看来也有些不耐烦，有些烦恼。可又能怎么办？这人胆子再大，力量再强，也只能指挥大海，不能指挥太阳。正午到了，白日的光轮一瞬也没露。我们甚至辨不出它藏在雾幕后什么方位。没过多久，雾又变成了雪。
“等明天吧。”船长安静地说。我们就在这风雪纷扰中回到了“鹦鹉螺号”。

暴雪下到次日。平台上没法立足。我在客厅里笔录这次南极大陆之行的见闻，从那里还能听见海燕和信天翁在暴风雪里嬉游的叫声。“鹦鹉螺号”并没有停着不动。太阳贴着地平线走过，剩下一点微光，船就在这微光中沿岸又往南驶了十英里。次日，三月二十日，雪停了。天气更冷了一点，温度计指在零下二度。雾正往上散，我盼着今天有望进行观测。尼摩船长还没出现，小艇便先送康塞尔和我上岸。地面依旧是火山造就的，到处是熔岩、火山渣和玄武岩的痕迹，唯独喷出这些东西的火山口，我无从看见。这里和下边那一带一样，陆上挤满了鸟。不过如今分掌地盘的还有一大群一大群海生哺乳动物，都用温和的眼睛望着我们。海豹有好几种，有的卧在地上，有的卧在浮冰上，许多在海里出出进进。我们走近也没惊走它们，这些动物根本没有跟人打过交道。我心里算了算，眼前这些就够几百艘船备足给养。
“先生，”康塞尔说，“能告诉我这些动物的名字吗？”
“它们是海豹和海象。”

这时才早晨八点。离观测太阳的好时辰还有四个钟头。我领着康塞尔往一道宽阔的海湾走，那湾深嵌在陡峭的花岗岩岸间。我敢说，到了那里，陆地也看不见，冰也看不见，统统让无数海生哺乳动物盖住了。我不由自主寻望起老普罗透斯来，神话里正是这位牧者看守海神涅普顿的浩大畜群。最多的还是海豹，雌雄自成一簇簇的家族，父亲守卫全家，母亲哺育幼儿，有几个小家伙已经强壮到能自己挪上几步。它们要换地方，就把身子一缩，一小跳一小跳地向前，笨拙地借发育不全的鳍帮忙。这鳍和它们的亲戚海牛一样，其实是一条完整的前肢。话虽这样，在水中——那才是它们的天地——它们脊骨柔韧，皮肤光滑紧密，脚有蹼，游起来妙极了。在陆地上休息时，姿态又那么优雅。难怪古人见了它们那温柔传情、连最美的女子也难以超越的目光，看见亮而妩媚的眼睛，迷人的姿势，富于诗意的举止，便把雄的想象成特里同海神，把雌的想象成人鱼。我还指给康塞尔看，这些有趣的鲸类动物，大脑的脑叶发育得多么充分。除了人，没有哪种哺乳动物有这么多脑质。它们也能受相当程度的教育，很容易驯养。我和另一些博物学家都以为，加以适当训练，它们一定很能充作帮人捕鱼的猎犬。大部分海豹睡在岩上或沙地上。真正的海豹没有外耳，和耳朵突出的水獭不同。我在其中认出几个品种，体长约三码，白毛，脑袋像斗牛犬，上下两颚都长着牙齿，上四枚门齿，下四枚门齿，又有两枚百合花形的大犬齿。象海豹也滑行在其间，这一类海豹长着短短的、灵活的鼻子。最大的一头身围二十英尺，从头到尾十码半，我们走近时，它们却纹丝不动。
“这些家伙没有危险吧？”康塞尔问。
“你不攻击它们就没有。要是非得护住幼崽，它们发起怒来可怕得很，把渔船撞碎也是常有的事。”
“它们做得很对。”康塞尔说。
“我也没说它们不对。”
又走了两英里，挡住我们去路的是一座岬角。海湾所以不受南风侵袭，靠的便是它。岬角另一边传来震耳的吼声，像一群反刍的牲畜同时开了嗓。
“好哇！”康塞尔说，“公牛开音乐会啦！”
“不，是海象开音乐会。”
“它们在打架呢！”
“不是在打架，就是在玩耍。”
我们开始往那些发黑的岩石上爬。冰把石面弄得溜滑，脚底下冷不防就是一个趔趄。我翻滚下去不止一次，吃亏的总是自己那副腰杆。康塞尔比我谨慎，也许是脚步比我稳，一次没跌。他扶我起身，嘴里说：
“先生若肯把步子迈得再宽些，平衡也就比较容易保住了。”
登上岬角的高脊，我望见一大片白色平原，上面全是海象。它们确实在彼此嬉戏，我们听到的吼叫不是愤怒，而是欢喜。

这些有趣的动物一动不动，我从它们身旁经过，尽可以从容端详。皮厚而粗糙，黄中泛红，体毛短且稀疏。有些体长四又四分之一码。比起北方的亲戚来，这些海象更安静，也不那么胆怯。它们不像北方海象那样，要在营地外围布置岗哨。考察完这座海象城，我想该回去了。已是十一点，假如天气许可船长观测，我希望在场亲眼看一看。我们沿峭岸顶上的一条窄径往回走。十一点半，就到了先前登陆的地方。船长乘来的小艇已经冲上沙滩。我看见他站在一块玄武岩上，仪器就放在近旁，双眼盯着北方的地平线，太阳这时正贴着那一带划出一道长弧。我站到他身边，默默等待。正午到了，太阳仍像上回一样，不肯露面。真像有意跟我们过不去！我们还是缺少观测。明天再做不成，就得放弃一切观测的念头。因为今天恰好是三月二十日，明天二十一日，便是昼夜平分之日。太阳将沉在地平线后，一去六个月，与之同来的，是漫长的极夜。自从九月昼夜平分之日，太阳从北方地平线升起，沿着一圈又一圈细长的螺线往高处爬，一直升到十二月二十一日。那时正值北部地区的夏至，它便开始下降；明天，它将向这些地方洒下最后的光芒。我向尼摩船长讲了自己的观察与忧虑。
“阿龙纳斯先生，您说得对，”他说，“假如明天不能测到太阳的高度，我就得等六个月才能再做这件事。不过，既然机缘恰在三月二十一日把我引到这片海上，那么只要十二点能看见太阳，测定船位其实会相当容易。”
“为什么呢，船长？”
“因为这段时候太阳运行的弧线拉得太长，很难精确量出它在地平线上的高度。只靠仪器测量，会产生相当可观的误差。”
“那么您打算怎么做？”
“我只用航海精密时计，”尼摩船长答，“假如明天，三月二十一日，把折射的影响算进去，太阳圆面正好被北方地平线切为两半，那便表明我已身在南极点。”
“不错，”我说，“只是从数学上讲，这个说法还不能完全精确，因为昼夜平分的时刻并不一定恰在正午。”
“很可能是这样，先生。可误差不会有一百码，我们也不必要求更精确。明天见吧！”
尼摩船长回到艇上。我和康塞尔留下来探勘海岸，一边观察，一边研究，直到五点。我这才上床，睡前也忘不了像印度人那样，祈求这轮光辉的太阳眷顾我们。次日，三月二十一日，清晨五点，我登上平台，看见尼摩船长已在那里。
“天有些放晴了，”他说，“还有希望。吃过早饭就上岸，选一个观测点。”

这桩事说定，我去找尼德·兰德，想带他同去。这位倔脾气的加拿大人偏不，我看他的沉默和郁郁不乐简直与日俱增。不过就眼下的情形而言，他这番固执也不见得叫我遗憾。岸上海豹确实太多，不该把这样的诱惑白白摆到这个做事不多想的渔人面前。早饭过后，我们上了小艇。夜间“鹦鹉螺号”已往前驶了几英里。如今它离岸足有一里格，岸上耸着一座尖峰，高约五百码。和我同乘小艇的有尼摩船长、两名船员和那些仪器，即一具航海精密时计、一架望远镜和一具气压计。渡海时，我看见许多鲸，属于南方海域的三个品种。一是英国人称作“露脊鲸”的鲸，没有背鳍。二是座头鲸，胸前有纵褶，鳍很大，泛白；这类鲸也叫大翅鲸，可那对鳍终究不是翅膀。三是长须鲸，黄褐色，是鲸类里最活跃的。它们有力地向高处喷出一束束空气与水汽，看着像旋转的烟柱，老远就能听见声响。这几种哺乳动物成群结队在安静的水面嬉游。看来，这座南极海盆正是鲸类的一处避难所，让它们躲开追踪得太紧的捕鲸人。我还看见大水母漂浮在水草间。

九点钟我们登岸。天空渐渐明亮，云往南飞去，雾像是正从冰冷的海面退走。尼摩船长向尖峰走去，想必是要选峰顶为观测站。攀登可不好受。脚下是锋利的熔岩和浮石，裂隙还在冒烟，空气中不时渗着硫黄味。若说这是个不常走陆路的人，船长爬起陡坡来却矫健得让人从没见过，即使猎人看了也会羡慕。我们花两小时登上山顶，峰体一半是斑岩，一半是玄武岩。从峰上望去，大海辽阔，北方海面与天空的分界清楚得很。脚下是一片片耀眼的雪白，头顶是没有雾的淡蓝。在北面，太阳圆面像个火球，下方已被地平线切出两只尖角。几百束水柱，一捆捆从海里喷上来。远处“鹦鹉螺号”像一头鲸，枕着水面安睡。我们身后朝南、朝东，是大片土地，是乱纷纷堆叠的冰与岩石，一眼看不到头。登顶后，尼摩船长仔细读取气压计的平均读数，观测时得把这项因素算进去。十一点四十五分，我们已经只能借折射看见太阳。它像一面金盘，把最后的光照在这荒无人烟的大陆，照在这从没有人驾船耕过的海上。尼摩船长拿一具带透镜的观测器，以镜面校正折射，盯着太阳沿一道斜长的轨迹，一点点沉到地平线以下。我手里拿着精密时计，心跳得很快。假如半个日轮沉下的瞬间与时计的十二点分毫不差，那么我们就在极点本身。
“十二点！”我喊道。
“南极点！”尼摩船长庄重地回答，把观测镜递给我。镜中，地平线恰好把日轮平分为二。
我望着落在尖峰顶上的最后一抹日光，望着渐次爬上山坡的阴影。就在这时，尼摩船长一只手按着我的肩头，开口宣告：
“我，尼摩船长，于一八六八年三月二十一日，抵达南纬九十度的南极点。我在此宣告，占有地球上这一片疆域。它相当于已知大陆的六分之一。”
“船长，以谁的名义？”
“先生，以我自己的名义！”
说罢，尼摩船长展开一面黑旗，旗面的一格上绣着金色的“N”。随后转向那轮白日，它最后的几束光仍轻拂着海天交界之处。他高声道：
“再见，太阳！沉下去吧，发光的日轮！到这片开阔海面下安息，让长夜把六个月的阴影，铺遍我的新领地！”

sections.title_zh: 下部 / 第15章　意外还是事故？
sections.title_en: PART TWO / CHAPTER XV — ACCIDENT OR INCIDENT?
source_paragraphs: The next day, the 22nd of March, at six in the morning, preparations for departure were begun. The last gleams of twilight were melting into night. The cold was great, the constellations shone with wonderful intensity. In the zenith glittered that wondrous Southern Cross—the polar bear of Antarctic regions. The thermometer showed 12 below zero, and when the wind freshened it was most biting. Flakes of ice increased on the open water. The sea seemed everywhere alike. Numerous blackish patches spread on the surface, showing the formation of fresh ice. Evidently the southern basin, frozen during the six winter months, was absolutely inaccessible. What became of the whales in that time? Doubtless they went beneath the icebergs, seeking more practicable seas. As to the seals and morses, accustomed to live in a hard climate, they remained on these icy shores. These creatures have the instinct to break holes in the ice-field and to keep them open. To these holes they come for breath; when the birds, driven away by the cold, have emigrated to the north, these sea mammals remain sole masters of the polar continent. But the reservoirs were filling with water, and the _Nautilus_ was slowly descending. At 1,000 feet deep it stopped; its screw beat the waves, and it advanced straight towards the north at a speed of fifteen miles an hour. Towards night it was already floating under the immense body of the iceberg. At three in the morning I was awakened by a violent shock. I sat up in my bed and listened in the darkness, when I was thrown into the middle of the room. The _Nautilus_, after having struck, had rebounded violently. I groped along the partition, and by the staircase to the saloon, which was lit by the luminous ceiling. The furniture was upset. Fortunately the windows were firmly set, and had held fast. The pictures on the starboard side, from being no longer vertical, were clinging to the paper, whilst those of the port side were hanging at least a foot from the wall. The _Nautilus_ was lying on its starboard side perfectly motionless. I heard footsteps, and a confusion of voices; but Captain Nemo did not appear. As I was leaving the saloon, Ned Land and Conseil entered.
“What is the matter?” said I, at once.
“I came to ask you, sir,” replied Conseil.

“Confound it!” exclaimed the Canadian, “I know well enough! The _Nautilus_ has struck; and, judging by the way she lies, I do not think she will right herself as she did the first time in Torres Straits.”
“But,” I asked, “has she at least come to the surface of the sea?”
“We do not know,” said Conseil.
“It is easy to decide,” I answered. I consulted the manometer. To my great surprise, it showed a depth of more than 180 fathoms. “What does that mean?” I exclaimed.
“We must ask Captain Nemo,” said Conseil.
“But where shall we find him?” said Ned Land.
“Follow me,” said I, to my companions.

We left the saloon. There was no one in the library. At the centre staircase, by the berths of the ship’s crew, there was no one. I thought that Captain Nemo must be in the pilot’s cage. It was best to wait. We all returned to the saloon. For twenty minutes we remained thus, trying to hear the slightest noise which might be made on board the _Nautilus_, when Captain Nemo entered. He seemed not to see us; his face, generally so impassive, showed signs of uneasiness. He watched the compass silently, then the manometer; and, going to the planisphere, placed his finger on a spot representing the southern seas. I would not interrupt him; but, some minutes later, when he turned towards me, I said, using one of his own expressions in the Torres Straits:
“An incident, Captain?”
“No, sir; an accident this time.”
“Serious?”
“Perhaps.”
“Is the danger immediate?”
“No.”
“The _Nautilus_ has stranded?”
“Yes.”
“And this has happened—how?”

“From a caprice of nature, not from the ignorance of man. Not a mistake has been made in the working. But we cannot prevent equilibrium from producing its effects. We may brave human laws, but we cannot resist natural ones.”
Captain Nemo had chosen a strange moment for uttering this philosophical reflection. On the whole, his answer helped me little.
“May I ask, sir, the cause of this accident?”

“An enormous block of ice, a whole mountain, has turned over,” he replied. “When icebergs are undermined at their base by warmer water or reiterated shocks their centre of gravity rises, and the whole thing turns over. This is what has happened; one of these blocks, as it fell, struck the _Nautilus_, then, gliding under its hull, raised it with irresistible force, bringing it into beds which are not so thick, where it is lying on its side.”
“But can we not get the _Nautilus_ off by emptying its reservoirs, that it might regain its equilibrium?”

“That, sir, is being done at this moment. You can hear the pump working. Look at the needle of the manometer; it shows that the _Nautilus_ is rising, but the block of ice is floating with it; and, until some obstacle stops its ascending motion, our position cannot be altered.”

Indeed, the _Nautilus_ still held the same position to starboard; doubtless it would right itself when the block stopped. But at this moment who knows if we may not be frightfully crushed between the two glassy surfaces? I reflected on all the consequences of our position. Captain Nemo never took his eyes off the manometer. Since the fall of the iceberg, the _Nautilus_ had risen about a hundred and fifty feet, but it still made the same angle with the perpendicular. Suddenly a slight movement was felt in the hold. Evidently it was righting a little. Things hanging in the saloon were sensibly returning to their normal position. The partitions were nearing the upright. No one spoke. With beating hearts we watched and felt the straightening. The boards became horizontal under our feet. Ten minutes passed.
“At last we have righted!” I exclaimed.
“Yes,” said Captain Nemo, going to the door of the saloon.
“But are we floating?” I asked.
“Certainly,” he replied; “since the reservoirs are not empty; and, when empty, the _Nautilus_ must rise to the surface of the sea.”

We were in open sea; but at a distance of about ten yards, on either side of the _Nautilus_, rose a dazzling wall of ice. Above and beneath the same wall. Above, because the lower surface of the iceberg stretched over us like an immense ceiling. Beneath, because the overturned block, having slid by degrees, had found a resting-place on the lateral walls, which kept it in that position. The _Nautilus_ was really imprisoned in a perfect tunnel of ice more than twenty yards in breadth, filled with quiet water. It was easy to get out of it by going either forward or backward, and then make a free passage under the iceberg, some hundreds of yards deeper. The luminous ceiling had been extinguished, but the saloon was still resplendent with intense light. It was the powerful reflection from the glass partition sent violently back to the sheets of the lantern. I cannot describe the effect of the voltaic rays upon the great blocks so capriciously cut; upon every angle, every ridge, every facet was thrown a different light, according to the nature of the veins running through the ice; a dazzling mine of gems, particularly of sapphires, their blue rays crossing with the green of the emerald. Here and there were opal shades of wonderful softness, running through bright spots like diamonds of fire, the brilliancy of which the eye could not bear. The power of the lantern seemed increased a hundredfold, like a lamp through the lenticular plates of a first-class lighthouse.
“How beautiful! how beautiful!” cried Conseil.
“Yes,” I said, “it is a wonderful sight. Is it not, Ned?”

“Yes, confound it! Yes,” answered Ned Land, “it is superb! I am mad at being obliged to admit it. No one has ever seen anything like it; but the sight may cost us dear. And, if I must say all, I think we are seeing here things which God never intended man to see.”
Ned was right, it was too beautiful. Suddenly a cry from Conseil made me turn.
“What is it?” I asked.
“Shut your eyes, sir! Do not look, sir!” Saying which, Conseil clapped his hands over his eyes.
“But what is the matter, my boy?”
“I am dazzled, blinded.”

My eyes turned involuntarily towards the glass, but I could not stand the fire which seemed to devour them. I understood what had happened. The _Nautilus_ had put on full speed. All the quiet lustre of the ice-walls was at once changed into flashes of lightning. The fire from these myriads of diamonds was blinding. It required some time to calm our troubled looks. At last the hands were taken down.
“Faith, I should never have believed it,” said Conseil.

It was then five in the morning; and at that moment a shock was felt at the bows of the _Nautilus_. I knew that its spur had struck a block of ice. It must have been a false manœuvre, for this submarine tunnel, obstructed by blocks, was not very easy navigation. I thought that Captain Nemo, by changing his course, would either turn these obstacles or else follow the windings of the tunnel. In any case, the road before us could not be entirely blocked. But, contrary to my expectations, the _Nautilus_ took a decided retrograde motion.
“We are going backwards?” said Conseil.
“Yes,” I replied. “This end of the tunnel can have no egress.”
“And then?”
“Then,” said I, “the working is easy. We must go back again, and go out at the southern opening. That is all.”
In speaking thus, I wished to appear more confident than I really was. But the retrograde motion of the _Nautilus_ was increasing; and, reversing the screw, it carried us at great speed.
“It will be a hindrance,” said Ned.
“What does it matter, some hours more or less, provided we get out at last?”
“Yes,” repeated Ned Land, “provided we do get out at last!”

For a short time I walked from the saloon to the library. My companions were silent. I soon threw myself on an ottoman, and took a book, which my eyes overran mechanically. A quarter of an hour after, Conseil, approaching me, said, “Is what you are reading very interesting, sir?”
“Very interesting!” I replied.
“I should think so, sir. It is your own book you are reading.”
“My book?”
And indeed I was holding in my hand the work on the Great Submarine Depths. I did not even dream of it. I closed the book and returned to my walk. Ned and Conseil rose to go.
“Stay here, my friends,” said I, detaining them. “Let us remain together until we are out of this block.”
“As you please, sir,” Conseil replied.

Some hours passed. I often looked at the instruments hanging from the partition. The manometer showed that the _Nautilus_ kept at a constant depth of more than three hundred yards; the compass still pointed to south; the log indicated a speed of twenty miles an hour, which, in such a cramped space, was very great. But Captain Nemo knew that he could not hasten too much, and that minutes were worth ages to us. At twenty-five minutes past eight a second shock took place, this time from behind. I turned pale. My companions were close by my side. I seized Conseil’s hand. Our looks expressed our feelings better than words. At this moment the Captain entered the saloon. I went up to him.
“Our course is barred southward?” I asked.
“Yes, sir. The iceberg has shifted and closed every outlet.”
“We are blocked up then?”
“Yes.”
translated_paragraphs: 次日，三月二十二日，早晨六点，艇上着手准备离去。最后几丝微光正融进黑夜。天气严寒，星座亮得惊人。天顶闪烁着奇妙的南十字，那是南极地区的“大熊星座”。温度计指在零下十二度，风势一紧，寒气便格外刺骨。开阔的水面上浮冰渐多。大海放眼望去，处处是同一幅景象，水面上铺开无数发黑的斑块，那是新冰正在生成。显然，南极的海盆在漫长的六个月冬季会全部冻结，绝无通行的可能。鲸在那时候去了哪里？想必从冰山底下钻走，寻找更容易游动的水域。至于海豹和海象，既然惯于严寒气候，就留在这些冰封的海岸。它们天生便会在冰原上凿出孔洞，并设法不让洞口封死。它们来这些孔洞里呼吸。当寒气赶走飞鸟，鸟群纷纷往北迁徙，这些海生哺乳动物就成了南极大陆唯一的主人。这当儿，压载水舱正在进水，“鹦鹉螺号”缓缓下沉。到一千英尺深处，它停住了，螺旋桨搅动海水，以每小时十五英里的速度径直向北。傍晚前后，艇已浮行在那巨大的冰体下方。凌晨三点，一次猛撞把我从睡梦中震醒。我从床上坐起，正在黑暗中听动静，又一下给抛到了房间中央。“鹦鹉螺号”撞上东西以后，猛烈地弹了回来。我沿舱壁摸索着走到扶梯，再到了客厅。天花板上有光，照见家具全都翻了。幸亏舷窗装得结实，经住了这番撞击。艇身歪斜，画也不再垂直，右舷的画紧贴在墙纸上，左舷的画离墙至少有一英尺。“鹦鹉螺号”向右舷倾侧，一动不动。我听见脚步和一片嘈杂的人声，尼摩船长却没有出现。我正要从客厅出去，尼德·兰德和康塞尔进来了。
“出什么事了？”我立刻问。
“先生，我正是来问您的。”康塞尔回答。
“见鬼！”加拿大人喊道，“我倒清楚得很！‘鹦鹉螺号’撞上东西了。看它这副歪法，我觉得这次怕不能像头回在托雷斯海峡那样自己正过来。”
“可是，”我问，“它至少上了海面吗？”
“我们不知道。”康塞尔说。
“这倒容易确定。”我答着，看了看压力表。不料，它指示我们还在一百八十英寻以下。“这是什么意思！”我惊呼道。
“那就得请教尼摩船长了。”康塞尔说。
“可得上哪儿去找他？”尼德·兰德问。
“跟我来。”我对两个伙伴说。

我们离开了客厅。图书室里没人，到了中央扶梯，船员铺位附近也没有人。我想尼摩船长一定在驾驶舱。还是等着为好。我们三个便都折回客厅。这么待了二十分钟，竭力倾听“鹦鹉螺号”上哪怕最轻微的一点响动。后来尼摩船长进来了，像是没有看见我们。一向不动声色的脸上，这时却现出了不安。他先默默察看罗盘，再看压力表，又走到世界平面图前，用手指按在标示南方海域的一处。我不愿打扰他。过了几分钟，他转向我，我才借用他自己在托雷斯海峡说过的那句话问：
“船长，是个小插曲？”
“不，先生。这一回，是出了事故。”
“严重吗？”
“也许。”
“眼前就有危险？”
“没有。”
“‘鹦鹉螺号’搁浅了？”
“是的。”
“这究竟——是怎么发生的？”
“大自然一时变了性子，并非人不懂操船。我们的操作毫无差错。可物体要恢复平衡，我们不能阻止。人的法律我们可以冒犯，自然的法则我们无从抗拒。”
尼摩船长选在这么个奇异的时刻，说出这番哲理。总的说来，他的回答对我帮助不大。
“船长，能否请教究竟是什么造成了事故？”
“一块巨冰，整整一座山，翻转过来了。”他答道，“海水较暖，或是接连不断的撞击，都能从下边侵削冰山的基部。重心升高，整个冰体就会倾覆。我们碰见的正是这种情形。那样一块巨冰翻倒时撞上了‘鹦鹉螺号’，又滑进艇壳下面，以绝大的力气把艇向上托，托入不那么厚的冰层。现在艇就在那上面侧躺着。”
“把压载水舱排空，能不能叫‘鹦鹉螺号’浮脱出来，重新找回平衡？”
“先生，我们此刻正在这样做。您听得见水泵在运转。看那压力表指针，它表明‘鹦鹉螺号’正在上升。可是大冰块也跟着它往上浮。没有东西挡住冰块上升，情形就不会改变。”

果然，“鹦鹉螺号”还是原样向右舷倾斜。等冰块停住，它无疑会扶正。可是到了那一步，谁能担保我们不被夹在两道玻璃般的冰面之间，可怕地挤碎？我思量着这种处境的一切后果。尼摩船长的眼睛始终没离开压力表。从冰山翻倒起，“鹦鹉螺号”已上升约一百五十英尺，可它偏离垂线的角度始终不变。忽然，船底传来一点轻微的动静。显然，船身扶正了些。客厅里悬挂的东西渐渐回到原来该在的位置，舱壁也越来越接近竖直。没人说话。我们心怦怦跳，眼看着、也亲身感受着艇一点点正过来。脚下的地板终于平了。十分钟过去了。
“总算正过来了！”我喊道。
“对。”尼摩船长已走到客厅门边。
“可我们现在浮起来了吗？”我问。
“当然。压载水舱还没排空我们就已经浮起。等排空了，‘鹦鹉螺号’自然该升上海面。”他答道。

我们确实浮在水中。可是“鹦鹉螺号”两边各约十码远，就耸起一道耀眼的冰墙。上面、下面，也全是同样的冰墙。上方是冰山的底面，像一块无边的天花板，伸展在我们头上。下方是翻倒的那块巨冰，一点点滑动之后，架在两侧冰墙上，由冰墙支撑在那里。“鹦鹉螺号”实实在在给囚在一条完整的冰隧道里，隧道宽二十多码，当中充满静水。看起来，要出去并不难，往前走或者往后退，接着再往深处下潜几百码，就能在冰山底下自由通行了。天花板上的灯已经熄灭，客厅之中却仍一片辉煌。探照灯的光射在冰壁上，再强烈地反射回来，透过隔窗照进来。电光落在那些削凿得千姿百态的冰块上，产生的效果，我简直无法描述。随着冰中纹理不同，每个角、每道棱、每一块晶面，都映出不同的光。这是一座耀眼的宝石矿，尤其像蓝宝石，放出的蓝光同祖母绿的翠光交错。这里那里，又流转着蛋白石般柔和得出奇的色泽，穿过一颗颗火钻似的光点，亮得眼睛根本受不了。探照灯的威力仿佛一下放大百倍，就像一等灯塔的灯火穿过一层层透镜。
“真美！真美！”康塞尔叫道。
“是呀，”我说，“真是一番奇景。尼德，你说呢？”
“是呀，见鬼，是呀！”尼德·兰德回答，“真是壮观！非得亲口承认这点，我就来气。谁也没看过这种东西，可看这一眼，恐怕要付出不小的代价。若要我把话全说透，我觉得我们眼下所见，原是上帝从没打算叫人看到的。”
尼德说得对，实在美得过分。忽然康塞尔一声喊，叫我回过头来。
“怎么了？”我问。
“先生，快闭上眼睛！别看，先生！”康塞尔说着，拿两只手捂住了眼。
“好小伙儿，到底出了什么事？”
“晃得我睁不开眼，什么都看不见了。”
我的眼睛不由自主又转向舷窗，可那股火光仿佛要把双眼吞噬，我根本受不了。我明白了，“鹦鹉螺号”开足了速度。冰壁上原先沉静的光彩，顿时统统化成一道道闪电。那千千万万颗钻石迸出的火，直要把人刺瞎。我们的双眼好一阵才缓过来。这才把遮眼的手放下。
“老天爷，我原先怎么也不会相信！”康塞尔说。
那是凌晨五点。就在这时，“鹦鹉螺号”的艇首又是一震。我知道准是撞角碰上了一块冰。大约是操纵时没转得过来，因为这水下隧道里冰块横梗，很不好走。我想尼摩船长只须改变航向，或绕开这些障碍，或依隧道的弯折而行即可。无论如何，前路总不至于堵死了吧。出乎我意料，“鹦鹉螺号”却断然向后退去。
“我们在倒着走？”康塞尔问。
“是，”我回答，“隧道这一头恐怕没有出口。”
“然后呢？”
“然后？”我说，“操作起来很容易，沿原路倒回去，从南边的口子出去。就这么回事。”
我这样讲，是想显得比心里更有把握些。“鹦鹉螺号”退得越来越快，螺旋桨逆转，带着我们飞速向后。
“这下可耽误了。”尼德说。
“多几个钟头，少几个钟头，有什么要紧？只要最后能出去。”
“是啊，”尼德·兰德重复着我的话，“只要我们最后真能出去！”
我从客厅踱到图书室，来回走了一阵。两个伙伴一言不发。我很快一头靠进一张软榻，拿起本书，眼睛机械地扫过字行。一刻钟后，康塞尔走到跟前问：“先生读的书是不是很有意思？”
“很有意思！”我答。
“那是自然，先生。您在读自己的著作呢。”
“我自己的书？”
果然，我手里正拿着自己所著的《海底深处的奥秘》。我一丁点也没意识到。我合上书，重新踱起步来。尼德和康塞尔起身要走。
“留下吧，朋友们。”我把他们拦住，“在脱离这道冰障以前，我们就待在一起。”
“听先生的。”康塞尔答道。

几小时过去。我三番五次看舱壁上挂着的仪器。压力表显示，“鹦鹉螺号”一直保持在三百多码的深度，罗盘仍指向南，计程仪显示航速每小时二十英里。在这样狭窄的地方，这个速度快得很。可尼摩船长知道，怎么赶都不嫌快；对我们来说，一分钟抵得好长的岁月。八点二十五分，又传来一次撞击，这回是在艇尾。我的脸倏地白了。两个伙伴紧挨在我身边。我一把抓住康塞尔的手。我们相对的一眼，比说什么话都更能表明心情。就在这时，船长走进客厅。我向他迎去。
“往南的路也被截断了？”我问。
“是的，先生。冰山移了位置，把每一个出口都封死了。”
“那么，我们给堵在里头了？”
“是的。”
