sections.title_en: PART TWO / CHAPTER XXII — THE LAST WORDS OF CAPTAIN NEMO
source_paragraphs: The panels had closed on this dreadful vision, but light had not returned to the saloon: all was silence and darkness within the _Nautilus_. At wonderful speed, a hundred feet beneath the water, it was leaving this desolate spot. Whither was it going? To the north or south? Where was the man flying to after such dreadful retaliation? I had returned to my room, where Ned and Conseil had remained silent enough. I felt an insurmountable horror for Captain Nemo. Whatever he had suffered at the hands of these men, he had no right to punish thus. He had made me, if not an accomplice, at least a witness of his vengeance. At eleven the electric light reappeared. I passed into the saloon. It was deserted. I consulted the different instruments. The _Nautilus_ was flying northward at the rate of twenty-five miles an hour, now on the surface, and now thirty feet below it. On taking the bearings by the chart, I saw that we were passing the mouth of the Manche, and that our course was hurrying us towards the northern seas at a frightful speed. That night we had crossed two hundred leagues of the Atlantic. The shadows fell, and the sea was covered with darkness until the rising of the moon. I went to my room, but could not sleep. I was troubled with dreadful nightmare. The horrible scene of destruction was continually before my eyes. From that day, who could tell into what part of the North Atlantic basin the _Nautilus_ would take us? Still with unaccountable speed. Still in the midst of these northern fogs. Would it touch at Spitzbergen, or on the shores of Nova Zembla? Should we explore those unknown seas, the White Sea, the Sea of Kara, the Gulf of Obi, the Archipelago of Liarrov, and the unknown coast of Asia? I could not say. I could no longer judge of the time that was passing. The clocks had been stopped on board. It seemed, as in polar countries, that night and day no longer followed their regular course. I felt myself being drawn into that strange region where the foundered imagination of Edgar Poe roamed at will. Like the fabulous Gordon Pym, at every moment I expected to see “that veiled human figure, of larger proportions than those of any inhabitant of the earth, thrown across the cataract which defends the approach to the pole.” I estimated (though, perhaps, I may be mistaken)—I estimated this adventurous course of the _Nautilus_ to have lasted fifteen or twenty days. And I know not how much longer it might have lasted, had it not been for the catastrophe which ended this voyage. Of Captain Nemo I saw nothing whatever now, nor of his second. Not a man of the crew was visible for an instant. The _Nautilus_ was almost incessantly under water. When we came to the surface to renew the air, the panels opened and shut mechanically. There were no more marks on the planisphere. I knew not where we were. And the Canadian, too, his strength and patience at an end, appeared no more. Conseil could not draw a word from him; and, fearing that, in a dreadful fit of madness, he might kill himself, watched him with constant devotion. One morning (what date it was I could not say) I had fallen into a heavy sleep towards the early hours, a sleep both painful and unhealthy, when I suddenly awoke. Ned Land was leaning over me, saying, in a low voice, “We are going to fly.” I sat up.
“When shall we go?” I asked.
“To-night. All inspection on board the _Nautilus_ seems to have ceased. All appear to be stupefied. You will be ready, sir?”
“Yes; where are we?”
“In sight of land. I took the reckoning this morning in the fog—twenty miles to the east.”
“What country is it?”
“I do not know; but, whatever it is, we will take refuge there.”
“Yes, Ned, yes. We will fly to-night, even if the sea should swallow us up.”
“The sea is bad, the wind violent, but twenty miles in that light boat of the _Nautilus_ does not frighten me. Unknown to the crew, I have been able to procure food and some bottles of water.”
“I will follow you.”
“But,” continued the Canadian, “if I am surprised, I will defend myself; I will force them to kill me.”
“We will die together, friend Ned.”

I had made up my mind to all. The Canadian left me. I reached the platform, on which I could with difficulty support myself against the shock of the waves. The sky was threatening; but, as land was in those thick brown shadows, we must fly. I returned to the saloon, fearing and yet hoping to see Captain Nemo, wishing and yet not wishing to see him. What could I have said to him? Could I hide the involuntary horror with which he inspired me? No. It was better that I should not meet him face to face; better to forget him. And yet—— How long seemed that day, the last that I should pass in the _Nautilus_. I remained alone. Ned Land and Conseil avoided speaking, for fear of betraying themselves. At six I dined, but I was not hungry; I forced myself to eat in spite of my disgust, that I might not weaken myself. At half-past six Ned Land came to my room, saying, “We shall not see each other again before our departure. At ten the moon will not be risen. We will profit by the darkness. Come to the boat; Conseil and I will wait for you.”

The Canadian went out without giving me time to answer. Wishing to verify the course of the _Nautilus_, I went to the saloon. We were running N.N.E. at frightful speed, and more than fifty yards deep. I cast a last look on these wonders of nature, on the riches of art heaped up in this museum, upon the unrivalled collection destined to perish at the bottom of the sea, with him who had formed it. I wished to fix an indelible impression of it in my mind. I remained an hour thus, bathed in the light of that luminous ceiling, and passing in review those treasures shining under their glasses. Then I returned to my room.

I dressed myself in strong sea clothing. I collected my notes, placing them carefully about me. My heart beat loudly. I could not check its pulsations. Certainly my trouble and agitation would have betrayed me to Captain Nemo’s eyes. What was he doing at this moment? I listened at the door of his room. I heard steps. Captain Nemo was there. He had not gone to rest. At every moment I expected to see him appear, and ask me why I wished to fly. I was constantly on the alert. My imagination magnified everything. The impression became at last so poignant that I asked myself if it would not be better to go to the Captain’s room, see him face to face, and brave him with look and gesture.

It was the inspiration of a madman; fortunately I resisted the desire, and stretched myself on my bed to quiet my bodily agitation. My nerves were somewhat calmer, but in my excited brain I saw over again all my existence on board the _Nautilus;_ every incident, either happy or unfortunate, which had happened since my disappearance from the _Abraham Lincoln_—the submarine hunt, the Torres Straits, the savages of Papua, the running ashore, the coral cemetery, the passage of Suez, the Island of Santorin, the Cretan diver, Vigo Bay, Atlantis, the iceberg, the South Pole, the imprisonment in the ice, the fight among the poulps, the storm in the Gulf Stream, the Avenger, and the horrible scene of the vessel sunk with all her crew. All these events passed before my eyes like scenes in a drama. Then Captain Nemo seemed to grow enormously, his features to assume superhuman proportions. He was no longer my equal, but a man of the waters, the genie of the sea.

It was then half-past nine. I held my head between my hands to keep it from bursting. I closed my eyes; I would not think any longer. There was another half-hour to wait, another half-hour of a nightmare, which might drive me mad.

At that moment I heard the distant strains of the organ, a sad harmony to an undefinable chant, the wail of a soul longing to break these earthly bonds. I listened with every sense, scarcely breathing; plunged, like Captain Nemo, in that musical ecstasy, which was drawing him in spirit to the end of life.

Then a sudden thought terrified me. Captain Nemo had left his room. He was in the saloon, which I must cross to fly. There I should meet him for the last time. He would see me, perhaps speak to me. A gesture of his might destroy me, a single word chain me on board.
But ten was about to strike. The moment had come for me to leave my room, and join my companions.

I must not hesitate, even if Captain Nemo himself should rise before me. I opened my door carefully; and even then, as it turned on its hinges, it seemed to me to make a dreadful noise. Perhaps it only existed in my own imagination.

I crept along the dark stairs of the _Nautilus_, stopping at each step to check the beating of my heart. I reached the door of the saloon, and opened it gently. It was plunged in profound darkness. The strains of the organ sounded faintly. Captain Nemo was there. He did not see me. In the full light I do not think he would have noticed me, so entirely was he absorbed in the ecstasy.
I crept along the carpet, avoiding the slightest sound which might betray my presence. I was at least five minutes reaching the door, at the opposite side, opening into the library.

I was going to open it, when a sigh from Captain Nemo nailed me to the spot. I knew that he was rising. I could even see him, for the light from the library came through to the saloon. He came towards me silently, with his arms crossed, gliding like a spectre rather than walking. His breast was swelling with sobs; and I heard him murmur these words (the last which ever struck my ear):
“Almighty God! enough! enough!”
Was it a confession of remorse which thus escaped from this man’s conscience?

In desperation, I rushed through the library, mounted the central staircase, and, following the upper flight, reached the boat. I crept through the opening, which had already admitted my two companions.
“Let us go! let us go!” I exclaimed.
“Directly!” replied the Canadian.

The orifice in the plates of the _Nautilus_ was first closed, and fastened down by means of a false key, with which Ned Land had provided himself; the opening in the boat was also closed. The Canadian began to loosen the bolts which still held us to the submarine boat.
Suddenly a noise was heard. Voices were answering each other loudly. What was the matter? Had they discovered our flight? I felt Ned Land slipping a dagger into my hand.
“Yes,” I murmured, “we know how to die!”

The Canadian had stopped in his work. But one word many times repeated, a dreadful word, revealed the cause of the agitation spreading on board the _Nautilus_. It was not we the crew were looking after!

“The maelstrom! the maelstrom!” Could a more dreadful word in a more dreadful situation have sounded in our ears! We were then upon the dangerous coast of Norway. Was the _Nautilus_ being drawn into this gulf at the moment our boat was going to leave its sides? We knew that at the tide the pent-up waters between the islands of Ferroe and Loffoden rush with irresistible violence, forming a whirlpool from which no vessel ever escapes. From every point of the horizon enormous waves were meeting, forming a gulf justly called the “Navel of the Ocean,” whose power of attraction extends to a distance of twelve miles. There, not only vessels, but whales are sacrificed, as well as white bears from the northern regions.
It is thither that the _Nautilus_, voluntarily or involuntarily, had been run by the Captain.

It was describing a spiral, the circumference of which was lessening by degrees, and the boat, which was still fastened to its side, was carried along with giddy speed. I felt that sickly giddiness which arises from long-continued whirling round.

We were in dread. Our horror was at its height, circulation had stopped, all nervous influence was annihilated, and we were covered with cold sweat, like a sweat of agony! And what noise around our frail bark! What roarings repeated by the echo miles away! What an uproar was that of the waters broken on the sharp rocks at the bottom, where the hardest bodies are crushed, and trees worn away, “with all the fur rubbed off,” according to the Norwegian phrase!
What a situation to be in! We rocked frightfully. The _Nautilus_ defended itself like a human being. Its steel muscles cracked. Sometimes it seemed to stand upright, and we with it!
“We must hold on,” said Ned, “and look after the bolts. We may still be saved if we stick to the _Nautilus_.”
He had not finished the words, when we heard a crashing noise, the bolts gave way, and the boat, torn from its groove, was hurled like a stone from a sling into the midst of the whirlpool.
My head struck on a piece of iron, and with the violent shock I lost all consciousness.
translated_paragraphs:
舷窗护板已经关上，遮去了可怕的景象，客厅里却没有恢复灯光。“鹦鹉螺号”内部一片寂静，一片黑暗。它正在水面下一百英尺处，以惊人的速度离开这片凄凉的海域。它要往哪儿去？向北，向南？那个人刚完成如此可怕的报复，又要奔往何方？我回到自己的房间。尼德和康塞尔也一直沉默着。我对尼摩船长生出一股无法克服的恐惧和厌恶。不论他从这些人手里受过什么苦，也没有权利这样惩罚他们。他就算没把我变成帮凶，至少也让我见证了他的复仇。
十一点，电灯重新亮了。我走进客厅，里面空无一人。我看过各种仪表。“鹦鹉螺号”正以每小时二十五英里的速度向北疾驰，一时浮在水面，一时又沉到水下三十英尺。我对照海图定了方位，发现我们正驶过英吉利海峡入口，沿一道把我们急速送往北方海域的航线飞驰。那一夜，我们在大西洋上跑了二百里格。夜幕降临，直到月亮升起之前，海面为黑暗所笼罩。
我回到舱房，却无法安睡，尽被可怕的噩梦纠缠。那场毁灭的惨景一直浮在眼前。从今天起，谁说得出“鹦鹉螺号”要把我们带到北大西洋的哪一个角落？速度还是快得叫人费解。包围我们的，还是北方的浓雾。它会停靠斯匹次卑尔根岛，还是新地岛的海岸？我们会不会驶进那些陌生水域，探索白海、喀拉海、鄂毕湾、利亚罗夫群岛，乃至亚洲那不为人知的海岸？我答不出来。连时间流逝的快慢我都判断不了。艇上的钟已经停了。仿佛置身极地，黑夜与白昼不再照常更替。我觉得自己被卷向一片奇异的天地，埃德加·坡那沉沦于深海的想象力曾在那里恣意漫游。和故事中的戈登·皮姆一样，我时时以为就要看见“那个蒙着面纱，比地上任何人都高大的身影，横亘在一道阻断通往极地之路的瀑布上”。
我估计——也许估错了——“鹦鹉螺号”这段狂乱的航行持续了十五或二十天。若非最后那场灾变为这次航行画下句点，还要这样持续多久，我不知道。从此，我再也没见过尼摩船长，也没见过他的大副。哪怕一瞬间，没有一名船员出现。“鹦鹉螺号”几乎始终待在水下。浮上来换气时，舱盖也只是机械地开合。平面世界图上不再留下航迹。我不知道我们身在何处。加拿大人的体力和耐心同样耗尽，也不再露面。康塞尔没法从他嘴里问出半个字，怕他疯狂发作起来，会寻短见，片刻不离地守护着他。
一天早晨——几月几日，我说不清——我天快亮时才落进一场沉重、令人痛苦又不舒服的睡梦，忽然醒了过来。尼德·兰德正俯身在我跟前，压低嗓子说：“咱们要逃了。”我坐了起来。
“什么时候走？”我问。
“今晚。‘鹦鹉螺号’上似乎已经无人巡查。大家都像失了神。先生，您会准备好的吧？”
“会。我们在哪里？”
“已经望得见陆地。今早我在雾里估了方位，陆地在东面，约二十英里。”
“那是什么国家？”
“不知道。不管是什么地方，咱们都到那里避难。”
“好，尼德，好。今晚咱们就走，哪怕大海要吞掉我们。”
“海况坏，风又猛。不过搭‘鹦鹉螺号’那只轻便的小艇走二十英里，还吓不倒我。瞒着船员，我已经预备好食物，还有几瓶水。”
“我跟你走。”
“不过，”加拿大人接着说，“要叫人撞见，我可会还手。我会逼他们杀死我。”
“那咱们一道死，尼德朋友。”

一切我都打定了主意。加拿大人离开我。我走上平台，在狂浪的冲击下，几乎站立不住。天色阴沉可怕。但在那些浓重褐暗的阴影里，已经有了陆地，我们非逃不可。我又回到客厅，既害怕看见尼摩船长，却又盼着见他，想见，又不想见。见了又能说什么？我难道能掩饰他给我带来的、出于本能的恐惧和憎恶？不能。最好不要同他面对面，最好将他忘记。可是——
那一天显得多么漫长。这是我在“鹦鹉螺号”上度过的最后一天。我独自待着。尼德·兰德和康塞尔尽量不开口，怕露了行迹。六点，我吃晚饭，毫无饥意，尽管厌食，还是逼自己吃下去，免得体力不支。六点半，尼德·兰德来到我房里说：“动身前不再见面了。十点钟月亮还没升起，咱们借着夜色走。您到小艇那里来，康塞尔和我等您。”
加拿大人不等我回答便走了。我想核实“鹦鹉螺号”的航向，便到客厅查看。艇正在五十多码深处以可怕的速度向北偏东北驶去。我最后一次望着那些自然界的奇观、聚在这座博物馆里的艺术珍品。这些世无其匹的收藏，注定要同收集它们的人一并葬身海底。我想将它们永不磨灭地印在脑海里。就这样，我待了一个钟头，沐浴在顶棚洒下的灯光里，将玻璃罩下闪亮的宝物一件一件再看过去，然后才回到自己的房间。

我换上结实耐穿的航海衣服，将笔记收好，小心放在身上。心跳声那么响，我根本无力叫它慢一点。在尼摩眼前，这样的心烦意乱肯定会将我出卖。这会儿他在做什么？我在他房门旁倾听，听见了脚步声。尼摩还在屋里，尚未就寝。我每时每刻都预期他会出现，问我为什么要逃。我一刻也没能放松警觉。想象把什么都夸大起来。那感受最后变得这样尖锐，我甚至问自己，是否还不如直接走进船长的房间，同他面对面，看着他，用一举一动迎接他的目光？

是个疯子的念头。所幸我忍住了，躺到床上，想将浑身的不安镇住。神经稍稍平静，激动的脑中却重新映出了整个艇上的生活。自从我从“亚伯拉罕·林肯号”上失踪，那一件件幸与不幸的事：海底打猎、托雷斯海峡、巴布亚的土人、搁浅、珊瑚墓地、穿过苏伊士、圣托里尼岛、克里特潜水者、维戈湾、亚特兰蒂斯、冰山、南极、被封在冰里、激战章鱼、墨西哥湾流上的风暴、“复仇者号”，再到那艘军舰连同全体舰员一起沉没的可怕一幕。一切像戏剧中的一场场景象，在我眼前过去。随后，尼摩船长似乎变得极大，连他的五官都放大到了超人的地步。他已不再是同我一样的凡人。他属于水，是海的精灵。
那时是九点半。我双手捧住脑袋，怕它会爆裂。我闭上眼，不愿再想。还有半个钟头要等。再熬半个钟头这样的噩梦，足以把我逼疯。
正在这时，远远传来管风琴声。一支说不出名目的咏唱，伴着悲凉的和声，如一个灵魂在地上哀哭，渴望挣脱尘世的束缚。我凝聚浑身的感官听着，几乎不再呼吸。我和尼摩船长一样，沉入那种乐声唤来的出神状态。他的精神仿佛已被琴声引向生命的尽头。
又一个念头骤然叫我害怕。尼摩已经离开自己的舱房。他在客厅里，我要逃走，非穿过那里不可。我会最后一次碰见他。他会看见我，也许还会跟我说话。他的一个手势就能毁了我，一句话就能将我锁在艇上。
十点就要敲响。我离开房间去会合同伴的时刻到了。
我不能迟疑，就是尼摩自己在面前站起来拦路，也不能。我小心地打开房门。即便这么小心，门扇在铰链上一转，我仍觉得声响可怕。也许那声音只存在于我的想象中。
我贴着“鹦鹉螺号”昏暗的阶梯挨下去，每走一级就停一停，想按住心跳。我到了客厅门前，轻轻推开。厅中是深沉的黑暗。管风琴声隐隐约约。尼摩船长就在那里。他没看见我。我想，就算四周灯火通明，他也不会留意我。他已完全沉浸在忘我的境地。
我沿地毯轻轻移动，竭力防着一丁点响动泄露我的行迹。客厅另一头有道门通往图书室。我至少走了五分钟，才到门旁。
我正要开门，尼摩船长一声叹息，将我钉在原地。我知道他正在起身。我竟还能看见他，图书室的灯光透进了客厅。他交叉着双臂，悄然朝我这边来。与其说是在走，不如说像个幽灵飘过。他的胸膛因啜泣而起伏。我听见他低声吐出这几个字，那是他的声音最后一次落进我耳中：
“全能的上帝！够了！够了！”
这句话是否从这人的良心深处漏出，是在承认心中的悔恨？
我不顾一切，冲过图书室，登上中央扶梯，再沿最上面一段梯级攀去，到了小艇跟前。两位同伴已经先我从那个孔口进去。我也钻了进去。
“走吧！快走！”我喊道。
“马上！”加拿大人答。
我们先封闭“鹦鹉螺号”艇壳钢板上的通口，用尼德·兰德事前备好的一把配制钥匙将它锁紧。小艇自身的舱口也关上了。随后加拿大人开始松动仍将小艇固定在潜艇上的螺栓。
突然传来一阵嘈杂。有人大声呼喊，彼此应答。出什么事了？难道我们的逃走被发现了？我感觉尼德·兰德往我手里塞了一把匕首。
“好，”我低声说，“怎么面对死亡，我们也知道！”
加拿大人已停下手里的工作。一个词反反复复地响起，一个可怕的词，解释了“鹦鹉螺号”上迅速蔓延的惊慌。船员们要找的，并不是我们！

“大漩涡！大漩涡！”在这样可怕的处境中，还有比这更叫人害怕的字眼能撞进耳朵吗！我们已在挪威危险的海岸外。莫非正当小艇要离开潜艇侧旁时，“鹦鹉螺号”就要被这个深渊吸进去了？我们知道，潮汐一至，法罗与罗弗敦群岛之间积聚的水会势不可当地奔涌，形成一个还从未有船能逃出的大漩涡。从天际的各个方向，巨浪会合在一处，构成一座深渊，人称“海洋之脐”，实在名副其实。它的吸力远及十二英里。葬身其中的，除了船只，还有鲸，乃至北方来的白熊。
有意也罢，无意也罢，船长竟把“鹦鹉螺号”驶到了这里。
潜艇正在描画一条螺旋线，一圈比一圈小。小艇仍紧扣在一旁，也被带着疾转，速度令人头晕目眩。长时间一圈圈打转，那种恶心、晕眩的感觉已经涌了上来。
我们骇到了极点。血液仿佛不再流动，知觉仿佛全给消灭了，浑身都是冷汗，如同临死时的汗！我们这只薄弱的小艇周围，又是何等巨响！咆哮声在几英里外轰然回荡！海水打在海底尖锐的礁岩上，碎裂成一片震耳欲聋的吼声。最坚固的物体在那里都被碾碎，树木也给磨平，照挪威人的说法，“连身上的皮毛都磨光了”！
这是何等境地！我们被摇晃得厉害。“鹦鹉螺号”像一个活人般奋力抵抗，它的钢筋铁骨咯咯作响。有时，潜艇像要直立起来，连着我们一起！
“抓牢！”尼德说，“看住螺栓！只要还贴在‘鹦鹉螺号’上，也许尚有救。”
他话没说完，我们耳边猛地一声崩响。螺栓脱落，小艇从凹槽中扯出，像投石索抛出的一块石头，被甩进那漩涡正中。
我的头撞到一块铁上。那一记猛烈的撞击，使我完全丧失了知觉。

sections.title_en: PART TWO / CHAPTER XXIII — CONCLUSION
source_paragraphs: Thus ends the voyage under the seas. What passed during that night—how the boat escaped from the eddies of the maelstrom—how Ned Land, Conseil, and myself ever came out of the gulf, I cannot tell.
But when I returned to consciousness, I was lying in a fisherman’s hut, on the Loffoden Isles. My two companions, safe and sound, were near me holding my hands. We embraced each other heartily.

At that moment we could not think of returning to France. The means of communication between the north of Norway and the south are rare. And I am therefore obliged to wait for the steamboat running monthly from Cape North.

And, among the worthy people who have so kindly received us, I revise my record of these adventures once more. Not a fact has been omitted, not a detail exaggerated. It is a faithful narrative of this incredible expedition in an element inaccessible to man, but to which Progress will one day open a road.

Shall I be believed? I do not know. And it matters little, after all. What I now affirm is, that I have a right to speak of these seas, under which, in less than ten months, I have crossed 20,000 leagues in that submarine tour of the world, which has revealed so many wonders.

But what has become of the _Nautilus?_ Did it resist the pressure of the maelstrom? Does Captain Nemo still live? And does he still follow under the ocean those frightful retaliations? Or, did he stop after the last hecatomb?

Will the waves one day carry to him this manuscript containing the history of his life? Shall I ever know the name of this man? Will the missing vessel tell us by its nationality that of Captain Nemo?

I hope so. And I also hope that his powerful vessel has conquered the sea at its most terrible gulf, and that the _Nautilus_ has survived where so many other vessels have been lost! If it be so—if Captain Nemo still inhabits the ocean, his adopted country, may hatred be appeased in that savage heart! May the contemplation of so many wonders extinguish for ever the spirit of vengeance! May the judge disappear, and the philosopher continue the peaceful exploration of the sea! If his destiny be strange, it is also sublime. Have I not understood it myself? Have I not lived ten months of this unnatural life? And to the question asked by Ecclesiastes three thousand years ago, “That which is far off and exceeding deep, who can find it out?” two men alone of all now living have the right to give an answer——
CAPTAIN NEMO AND MYSELF.
translated_paragraphs: 我的海底航行到这里就结束了。那一夜究竟出了什么事，小艇怎样挣脱了大漩涡里一道道回旋的急流，尼德·兰德、康塞尔和我又是怎样逃出那片深渊的，我都说不上来。
等我恢复知觉，已经躺在罗弗敦群岛一间渔人的小屋里了。两位同伴都平安无恙，正在我身旁握着我的手。我们紧紧地拥抱在一起。
眼下我们还不能打算回法国。挪威北部和南部之间交通稀少，我只得等候那艘从北角开来的轮船，每月才有一班。
如今，住在这些好心收留我们的人中间，我又把这段历险的记录从头修订了一遍。没有一件事实遗漏，也没有一处细节夸大。这是一次令人难以置信的远征，我把它如实记了下来。我们所到的水下世界，今天的人还无从进入，总有一天，人类的进步会为它开出一条路来。
人们会相信我吗？我不知道。说到底，这倒无关紧要。有一点我敢断言：谈起这一片片海，我是有资格开口的。在还不到十个月的海底环球航行中，我在这些海洋的水下走过了两万里格，见识了多少奇观！
可是，“鹦鹉螺号”怎么样了？它顶住了大漩涡的力量吗？尼摩船长还活着吗？他可还在海底进行那可怕的复仇？还是上一次大开杀戒以后，他就此罢手了？
将来，会不会有一天，海浪把这部记着他生平事迹的手稿送到他手中？我还能知道这个人的姓名吗？那艘失踪的船究竟属于哪个国家，会不会由此揭开尼摩船长的国籍之谜？

我希望能。我也希望，他那艘强大的潜艇已经在大海最可怕的深渊里战胜了大海，希望在无数船只葬身的地方，“鹦鹉螺号”能够幸存下来！果真如此，果真尼摩船长还生活在他认作第二故乡的海洋里，那么，愿他那颗刚烈的心渐渐平息仇恨！愿眼前的种种奇观永远熄灭他的复仇之念！愿他放下审判者的身份，以一位哲人的心境，继续平静地探寻海洋！他的命运固然离奇，却也崇高。这一点，我自己岂会不明白？如此异乎寻常的生活，我不是也亲身过了十个月吗？三千年前，《传道书》曾经发问：“那遥远而又深不可测的，谁能探得明白？”如今活在世上的人中，只有两个人有资格回答——
尼摩船长和我。
